ENROLLMENT AND LOCK-IN GATES. IBKR requires a margin account or a cash account with liquid net worth above $25,000, and imposes a 90-day wait before re-enrolling if you leave. Schwab requires $100,000 in household assets AND is invitation-only, subject to Schwab's approval — you may simply not be allowed in. ERISA accounts (401(k)s) are excluded entirely.

COUNTERPARTY AND REHYPOTHECATION RISK — THE ASYMMETRY THAT MATTERS. Securities on loan are NOT covered by SIPC. You are unsecured against your own broker, protected only by collateral: IBKR posts 100% in US Treasuries or cash in a segregated pledge account; Fidelity posts a minimum of 100% USD collateral with a third-party custodian. Note that 100% collateral against a position marked daily still leaves gap risk in a fast market, and the collateral is marked to yesterday's close. You are accepting a small probability of a large loss in exchange for 53bp — a profoundly unattractive risk shape, and one that is worst precisely in the stressed markets where a retail sector ETF would gap.

LOSS OF VOTING RIGHTS AND QUALIFIED DIVIDEND TREATMENT while on loan, with only Fidelity offering partial (26.98%) compensation.

EARLY ASSIGNMENT ON THE SHORT CALL. American-style XRT options mean the short call in a conversion can be assigned around ex-dividend, stripping the stock, killing the lending income, and leaving a naked long put. This is not theoretical — it is the standard outcome for a deep-ITM short call before a dividend.

OPERATIONAL COMPLEXITY WILDLY DISPROPORTIONATE TO REWARD. Managing a rolling conversion, monitoring assignment risk, tracking lending accruals and cash-in-lieu tax lots, all to underperform a T-bill ladder by ~3%/yr.
referee.confidence:
HIGH — and higher than I am normally willing to be on a rejection, for three specific reasons.

1. THE CORE RESULT IS ALGEBRAIC, NOT STATISTICAL. It requires no backtest, no sample period, and no distributional assumption. An options-hedged lender earns rf − borrow × (1 − split × util). For any positive borrow fee and any split below 100%, that is strictly less than rf. There is no parameter choice — no borrow fee, no utilization rate, no volatility regime — that flips the sign. This is not "the edge is probably too small"; it is "the edge has the wrong sign by construction." I stress-tested it at 50% and 60% splits and at 25%, 50% and 100% utilization; all nine combinations lose to T-bills before costs.

2. THE FACTUAL PREMISE IS DIRECTLY FALSIFIED BY OBSERVED DATA, NOT INFERENCE. The strategy is predicated on XRT being persistently hard to borrow with a high sustained fee. The measured fee is 1.07% with 500,000 shares freely available (ChartExchange/IBKR, 2026-08-12). Even at the peak of the 2021 meme-stock episode, S3's Ihor Dusaniwsky publicly noted XRT at 2.32% — cheaper to short than GME at 1.70%. The premise is not merely optimistic; it is inverted, and the academic literature explains why: XRT is the "short favorite" that intermediates most shorting AT LOW FEES, which is exactly why its short interest is 568% of float.

3. I VERIFIED THE HEDGE-PRICING CLAIM EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. Rather than asserting that options price the borrow, I pulled live CBOE quotes and inverted put-call parity across every liquid strike with a proper dividend schedule. Implied borrow came out at 0.79%, 1.11%, 1.43% and 1.57% against a 1.07% quoted cash fee. The options market has it right to within the bid-ask. That closes the only loophole through which this trade could have worked.

CALIBRATION AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND. My confidence is in the VERDICT, not in every input. Three numbers I could not verify and have flagged rather than fabricated: XRT-specific realized SYEP utilization (no broker publishes it; IBKR's own pages returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, so all IBKR program terms here come from secondary sources and IBKR's own guides subdomain rather than the primary pricing page); IBKR's wholesale lending rate versus the 1.07% retail short charge; and the paywalled long-run XRT fee history. Critically, all three uncertainties push the conclusion in the SAME direction — the wholesale rate is typically below the retail short charge, and lower utilization means less income — so resolving them can only make the trade worse.

I would revisit only on a genuinely different setup: a lender split above 100% (does not exist), an ETF where option-implied borrow sits materially BELOW the achievable lending rate (I found the opposite), or AP status enabling real create-to-lend with full fee capture and redemption optionality. None is available to a small trader. This same failure mode — a dramatic surface statistic (568% short interest) that is a mechanical artifact rather than evidence of scarcity — is precisely the pattern the analyst's FTD work already identified. Recommend declining without further work.

referee.strategy: Illiquid-Underlying ETF NAV-Discount Convergence — buying HY/muni/bank-loan/EM bond ETFs when they trade at a wide, persistent discount to NAV during market stress, on the thesis that APs will eventually arbitrage the gap closed (March 2020 as case study).
referee.edge_case:
The discounts are real, large, and documented. Verified magnitudes from March 2020: LQD traded at a 5.08% discount on 3/19/2020; AGG and BND at 4.43% and 6.17% on 3/16/2020; IG corporate bond ETFs averaged roughly a 3.4% discount in mid-March with some products beyond 8%. BIS (Quarterly Review, March 2021, "The anatomy of bond ETF arbitrage") reports bond ETF tracking error exceeded 200bp for some funds in March-April 2020 versus a 0.7bp historical sector average — a ~300x dislocation. The mechanism that should produce convergence is genuine and mechanical: APs can redeem in kind and sell the bonds, which is a far harder constraint to evade than in closed-end funds.

The economic case is that during a dash-for-cash, forced sellers pay a large premium for immediacy while the natural buyers (AP/dealer balance sheets) are simultaneously constrained. Pan & Zeng ("ETF Arbitrage under Liquidity Mismatch") document precisely this: most APs are also bond dealers using one balance sheet for both roles, and large bond flow shocks to AP balance sheets limit ETF arbitrage, "leading to persistent relative mispricings." That is a textbook limits-to-arbitrage setup, and someone with unconstrained capital genuinely does get paid for supplying liquidity there.

And the discounts did resolve: BIS notes steep discounts "transformed into large premiums" within days. Prices did rebound hard — LQD +16.8% in 5 days from 3/19, EMB +14.2% from 3/18, MUB +13.3% from 3/19 (my computation, Yahoo daily closes).

That is the strongest form of the case. It does not survive contact with the actual timing evidence below.
referee.against_case:
Three independent kills.

1) THE DISCOUNT IS A CORRECT PRICE, NOT A MISPRICING. Bond ETF NAV is struck once daily off vendor matrix marks (ICE/IHS Markit/BVAL) built from surveys and models, not executable bids. BlackRock's own SEC-FIAC deck (July 2020) shows the standard deviation of dealer quotes versus actual trade prices exploding in March 2020 — the NAV inputs themselves were unreliable. The decisive logic, which I found stated plainly in the practitioner literature: if NAV prices were actionable and market makers could sell those bonds meaningfully above the ETF price, the dislocation would have normalized immediately. It did not. BIS confirms the gap "was not arbitraged away" by APs. APs had both the ability and the incentive and declined — revealed preference that the NAV was fiction. Notably, >92% of LQD's underlying bonds DID trade on 3/19/2020 and 74% had an observable print within ~2 hours of the close, so this was not mainly a staleness problem: the marks were simply above where bonds cleared. You are not buying a dollar for 95 cents; you are buying a dollar for a dollar and being told by an accountant it is worth 1.05.

2) SIGNAL IS SWAMPED BY NOISE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE. My computation from Yahoo daily closes: March 2020 annualized realized vol was LQD 58%, HYG 50%, BKLN 56%, EMB 66%, MUB 44% (versus 1-4% in calm February). LQD's DAILY standard deviation was 3.65%. The entire peak discount was 5.08%. One day of noise is ~72% of the whole signal. Over a 5-day convergence window the noise is ~8.2% against a 5% best-case signal. And the crisis-average discount was far smaller than the headline: BlackRock's own data gives average ABSOLUTE premium/discount for March-April 2020 of just LQD 1.39%, HYG 1.06%, TLT 0.86% (versus 0.13-0.21% in Jan-Feb). So the typical trade is a ~1% signal against 50-60% annualized vol.

3) THE ACTUAL FORWARD RETURNS ARE NEGATIVE. This is the FTD result all over again. I took the entry dates a trader could actually identify ex ante as "wide discount" — 3/11, 3/12, 3/16, 3/17/2020, when the press was already reporting 3-6% discounts — across LQD, HYG, BKLN, EMB, MUB (n=20). Mean 5-day return: -7.88%. Median: -8.91%. Percent negative: 95%. Mean worst drawdown within 10 days: -11.70%. Buying the discount on the dates the discount was visibly wide lost money 19 times out of 20. Only 3/18 and 3/19 — the exact bottom, identifiable only in hindsight — were profitable, and that P&L was created on 3/23 when the Fed announced the SMCCF. HYG then jumped +6.5% in a single day on 4/9/2020 when the Fed extended the facility to high-yield ETFs. This strategy's entire historical track record is a bet on the timing of a central bank announcement, wearing an arbitrage costume.

Exactly parallel to the FTD finding: the naive spike signal has no predictive power because the signal is generated by the same stress that keeps causing losses. But note the disanalogy that makes ETFs worse — the FTD work found a surviving "chronic persistence" pattern. In ETFs the create/redeem mechanism specifically prevents chronic persistence, so the analogous surviving signal does not exist here. Closed-end funds, which lack create/redeem, do sustain persistent structural discounts — but that is a different strategy than the one proposed.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
The seller into the discount is a rational, informed, liquidity-motivated seller — not a patsy. Bond mutual funds meeting redemptions, risk-parity and vol-target programs mechanically deleveraging, insurers and corporates raising cash. For them the ETF at a 4% discount was the CHEAPEST available exit, not an expensive one: over February-March 2020 the bid-ask on individual IG bonds widened from ~25bp to over 100bp while LQD's own bid-ask stayed below 2bp. Selling the ETF at a discount to a stale mark was strictly better than selling the actual bonds, where the achievable bid was lower still. They are trading a mark they know is not real for cash they know is real. That is rational, and it means the "discount" is largely the difference between an accounting mark and a clearing price.

The buyer is a market maker or AP demanding compensation for warehousing credit and gap risk at the exact moment its own balance sheet, VaR limits and repo funding are most constrained. Pan & Zeng show the dual dealer/AP role creates an inventory-management motive that can distort ETF arbitrage rather than correct it. So the buyer is being paid a genuine, earned liquidity risk premium for balance sheet capacity — a capacity a small fund does not possess and therefore cannot rent out.

The critical point: the people best positioned to arbitrage this — the APs, who alone can redeem in kind and hit the NAV — looked at a supposed 5% free lunch and declined to eat it, for two straight weeks, in size. Any thesis here requires believing you see something the APs did not, using worse data, with no access to the redemption mechanism they hold and you do not.
referee.frictions:
Verified where possible; flagged where not.

ETF SPREAD. Calm markets: HYG and LQD both show a 30-day median bid/ask of 0.01% (iShares product pages, Aug 2026) — effectively free. Stress: LQD stayed under 2bp through Feb-Mar 2020; BND's spread peaked at 0.13% on 3/16/2020, back to 0.01% by 5/21. Call it 5-25bp round trip on mega-cap names in stress. But the widest discounts occur in the SMALLER, less liquid funds, where stressed spreads of 50-150bp are realistic (I could not verify per-fund stressed spreads for those; treat as an estimate).

COMMISSIONS. ~$0 at US retail brokers for ETF shares. Not a factor.

SLIPPAGE. The binding cost. In a tape with 3.65% daily sigma (LQD, March 2020) and intraday ranges to match — LQD printed a 115.21 low against a 121.30 close on 3/16 alone, a 5% intraday span — realistic execution slippage is 25-100bp per side for anything above token size. This alone equals or exceeds the average 1.0-1.4% crisis discount.

BORROW (for any hedged/pair version). HYG cost-to-borrow was 0.82% annualized with only 3,900,000 shares available at IBKR (ChartExchange, 8/12/2026) — against 32M shares/day ADV. That is a thin borrow pool in calm conditions; it will not be there in a panic when everyone is shorting HY. I could NOT verify actual March 2020 borrow rates for HYG or LQD and will not invent them; general reporting indicates some fixed-income ETFs exceeded 10% fees during heavy hedging periods. Add recall risk at the worst moment.

OPTIONS — THE DECISIVE COST. I pulled a live HYG and LQD chain (Aug 2026, calm market, HYG spot 79.61). Near-dated at-the-money HYG options quote 12-30% of mid in bid-ask (77.5 call 2.02/2.27 = 11.7%; 79 call 0.54/0.72 = 28.6%). LQD options are effectively untradeable: the 105.5 call quoted 0.29 bid / 1.37 ask — 130% of mid — with most strikes 200% of mid and open interest in the hundreds. That is in a CALM market. In March 2020 with realized vol at 50-58% annualized, a 1-month ATM HYG put costs roughly 0.4 x 0.55 x sqrt(1/12) x 79 ≈ $5.0, about 6-7% of notional, before paying a spread on it. You would spend 6-7% of notional hedging to capture a 1-5% discount. Structurally impossible. (I could not retrieve VXHYG history — the index returned no time series — so the crisis IV level is inferred from realized vol, which is a floor, not a verified print.)

TAXES. Any winning trade here is short-term by construction (days to weeks), taxed at ordinary income — up to ~40.8% federal for a US individual. That converts a 1% gross discount capture into ~0.6% net before every cost above.

FULL STACK, hedged version: 2 ETF spreads (10-50bp) + slippage (50-200bp) + borrow (80bp+ annualized, spiking) + option premium if used (600bp+) versus a 100-140bp average crisis signal. Negative before you start.
referee.capacity:
Execution capacity is enormous and completely beside the point. HYG trades ~$2.5bn/day (32.0M shares x $79.61) and LQD ~$3.1bn/day (29.7M x $106.12), with AUM of $17.70bn and $33.14bn respectively (iShares, Aug 2026). A small fund could move $10-50m in either without meaningful impact even in stress. Bond ETFs collectively traded ~$60bn/day in 2026 versus ~$20bn/day in 2020 (BlackRock).

The binding constraint is OPPORTUNITY FREQUENCY, and it is brutal. Discounts wide enough to matter net of the cost stack — call it >3% — have appeared essentially once in the history of bond ETFs, for a handful of days in March 2020. Even during that once-in-a-generation event, the average absolute premium/discount over the full March-April window was only 1.39% (LQD), 1.06% (HYG), 0.86% (TLT). In normal conditions the figure is 0.13-0.21%, i.e. inside the spread and inside the noise.

Realistic capacity per trade: $10-50m of ETF you can buy, against a gross signal of ~1% that is negative-expectancy at the entry points you can actually identify. Realistic capacity per year: in a typical year, ZERO dollars — there is nothing to trade. Over a decade you might get one legitimate window lasting under two weeks. Amortized annual gross opportunity, generously assuming you nail a once-per-decade 3% capture on $25m: ~$75k gross, once per decade, or ~$7.5k/year expected, before costs that exceed it. You cannot build a book on this, and you certainly cannot justify the operational infrastructure to monitor for it.

The less-liquid funds where discounts run widest (small muni, bank-loan, EM funds) have ADV in the low single-digit millions of dollars, so the wider the discount you target, the smaller the size you can execute — capacity is inversely correlated with signal, which is the classic signature of an illusory edge.
referee.decay_evidence:
Already commercialized by the only parties who can actually run it, and structurally decaying on four fronts.

1) THE ARB IS THE APs' BUSINESS MODEL, NOT AN UNDISCOVERED SIGNAL. Creation/redemption arbitrage is the mechanical core of the ETF wrapper, operated continuously by a concentrated set of AP/dealer firms (Bank of Canada Staff Analytical Note 2020-27 documents this concentration in US fixed-income ETFs). There is no discovery here — the trade is fully industrialized, and its operators are the ones who declined to take it in March 2020.

2) MARKET-MAKING CAPACITY HAS ROUGHLY TRIPLED. Bond ETF ADV went from ~$20bn/day in 2020 to ~$60bn/day in 2026 (BlackRock). Portfolio trading and custom-basket creation/redemption have since become standard, explicitly letting APs transact partial baskets rather than being forced to source every bond — directly attacking the balance-sheet constraint that Pan & Zeng identify as the cause of the 2020 persistence. The exact friction that generated the 2020 opportunity has been engineered against.

3) DEDICATED HEDGING INSTRUMENTS NOW EXIST, WHICH COMPRESSES THE BASIS. CME launched US Corporate Bond Index futures in June 2024 on the Bloomberg US Corporate and US High Yield Very Liquid indices; ICE launched MSCI/MarketAxess corporate bond index futures in 2024; Eurex launched USD credit futures in September 2024. CME credit futures volume surpassed 450,000 contracts by September 2025. Institutions now have a clean, capital-efficient way to arbitrage ETF price against index value — a tool that did not exist in March 2020 and that mechanically narrows exactly this gap. Note these are institutional futures; they do not solve the retail hedging problem, they only accelerate the decay of the opportunity.

4) THE FED PUT SHORTENED THE HALF-LIFE. The SMCCF was announced 3/23/2020 and extended to high-yield ETFs on 4/9/2020. That precedent is now priced in: participants expect a backstop, which compresses the duration and depth of future dislocations. This cuts both ways for the strategy and both ways are bad — you get a smaller signal, and whatever remains is a bet on policy reaction function rather than on convergence.

5) VENDOR COMMERCIALIZATION. The intraday/real-time bond ETF NAV pricing problem is itself now a product — Virtu built a NAV pricing tool and signed up bond ETF issuers for it. The informational advantage of "knowing the real NAV" is a purchased utility for institutions, not an edge available to a small trader.

Counter-evidence check: I could NOT verify discount magnitudes during the April 2025 tariff shock, which would be the cleanest recent test of whether resilience has improved. HYG fell only ~4.1% in that episode, and I found no reporting of notable NAV dislocations — suggestive of decay but not proof. I flag this as an unverified gap.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Negative for every implementation a small trader can actually execute. Specifics:

UNHEDGED LONG (the only version genuinely available to retail). Measured, not modeled: across 5 ETFs (LQD, HYG, BKLN, EMB, MUB) x the 4 dates a trader could identify ex ante as wide-discount (3/11, 3/12, 3/16, 3/17/2020), mean 5-day return -7.88%, median -8.91%, 95% negative, mean worst drawdown within 10 days -11.70%. Including the two hindsight-only bottom dates (3/18, 3/19), the mean 5-day is still -2.07% with 63% negative. Net expectancy: roughly -8% per 5-day trade at realistic entries, minus 50-200bp of frictions. This is not an edge; it is a levered long credit-beta position initiated into a falling knife, with the payoff contingent on central bank timing.

HEDGED PAIR (long the wider-discount ETF vs short a peer on the same index — the only structurally sound variant). I tested HYG vs JNK, the two largest US HY ETFs, across the entire crisis. Maximum cumulative relative divergence: +1.96% (3/26/2020), typically under 1%. That ~1-2% gross is not even cleanly attributable to discount convergence — HYG tracks iBoxx Liquid HY and JNK tracks a Bloomberg HY index, so index composition drift accounts for a meaningful share. Against it: two ETF spreads, slippage on both legs in a 50%-vol tape, HYG borrow at 0.82% annualized with only 3.9M shares available, recall risk, and short-side dividend liability on a ~6.7%-yielding fund. Net expectancy: approximately zero to modestly negative, on a signal too small to survive a single bad fill.

OPTIONS-HEDGED. Definitively negative and not close. ~6-7% of notional in premium to hedge a 1-5% discount, before paying live bid-ask of 12-30% of mid on HYG options and 30-200% on LQD options.

Honest uncertainty: my forward-return test is a single episode, n=30 overlapping observations across 5 correlated funds in one event — statistically that is essentially n=1, and I want to be explicit that it cannot support a precise expectancy figure. But that cuts AGAINST the strategy, not for it: March 2020 is the single most favorable observation that will ever exist for this trade, and the trade lost money at every identifiable entry point within it. A strategy that fails on its own best-case case study does not need a larger sample to reject.

What IS knowable and unknowable: the cost stack is knowable and I have quantified it. The gross signal is knowable and is ~1.0-1.4% on average, ~5% at the once-in-history extreme. Whether the discount predicts convergence is, on the available evidence, answered NO for tradable entries. What is genuinely unknowable is the timing of the policy response that alone generated the 2020 recovery — and a strategy whose returns depend on an unknowable is not an edge.
referee.barriers:
Four hard structural barriers, the first two of which are absolute.

1) YOU CANNOT CREATE OR REDEEM. This is not a friction, it is a wall. The actual arbitrage requires being a registered Authorized Participant with a signed AP agreement with the fund and clearing capability at NSCC/DTC, transacting in creation units of typically 50,000-100,000 shares. Retail traders and small funds are structurally locked out of the ONLY mechanism that forces convergence. You are not doing the arbitrage; you are speculating that someone else will do it, on a timetable you cannot observe, for reasons you cannot verify.

2) YOU CANNOT SHORT NAV. There is no tradable instrument that pays the ETF's net asset value. Therefore the "convergence" leg cannot be isolated from the beta. Every retail implementation reduces to either (a) naked long credit risk at maximum stress, or (b) a proxy hedge whose basis error (I measured HYG/JNK divergence at up to 1.96%) is the same order of magnitude as the entire signal you are trying to capture. There is no version of this where you own the convergence and not the beta.

3) YOU CANNOT OBSERVE THE SIGNAL IN REAL TIME. Official NAV is struck once daily at 4pm off vendor matrix marks. Intraday iNAV is computed from those same unreliable inputs and is widely regarded as untrustworthy for bond ETFs — which is precisely why Virtu built and sold a commercial NAV pricing tool to issuers. So you are trading a stale, error-laden signal against a price moving 3.65% per day, and by the time the previous close's discount is published, the information is worthless. The published premium/discount that makes headlines is a backward-looking accounting artifact.

4) YOUR BROKER TIGHTENS EXACTLY WHEN THE TRADE APPEARS. Margin requirements on volatile credit ETFs rise in stress, borrow availability on any short leg evaporates (HYG shows only 3.9M borrowable shares against 32M ADV in a CALM market), and a small fund faces its own redemption and risk-limit pressure at the same moment. The trade demands you add risk at the point your capital base is least able to support it — which is the same balance-sheet constraint that stopped the APs, except you have a far worse balance sheet than they do.

Institutional hedges that would partially solve barrier 2 — CDX HY, and the new CME/ICE/Eurex credit index futures — require ISDA documentation or futures accounts with margin and minimum sizes that put them out of reach of a small trader, and their existence accelerates the decay of the opportunity for everyone else.
referee.confidence:
HIGH that the verdict is LIKELY-ILLUSORY, for a small trader or small fund.

Reasons for high confidence: (a) The direct empirical test is unambiguous and I computed it myself from raw price data — 95% of identifiable wide-discount entries lost money over 5 days, averaging -7.88%, in the single most favorable episode that has ever existed for this trade. A strategy that fails on its own best case study does not require further testing. (b) The structural barriers (no create/redeem, no way to short NAV) are absolute, not matters of degree, and they are independent of any statistical question. (c) The cost stack alone kills it: I verified live option quotes of 12-30% of mid on HYG and 30-200% on LQD, versus an average crisis signal of 1.0-1.4%, using BlackRock's own numbers. (d) The revealed preference of the APs — the only parties who could do the real arbitrage, who had every incentive, and who passed for two weeks — independently confirms the discount was compensation for risk rather than mispricing. Four independent lines of evidence converge on the same answer.

Reasons it is not stated as certainty: (a) My forward-return test is effectively one event across correlated instruments; overlapping windows on five funds in one crisis is closer to n=1 than n=30, and I have not run a multi-decade panel of daily premium/discount data — I attempted to obtain iShares' historical premium/discount series and the SEC/BIS underlying data and could not retrieve machine-readable history. (b) I could not verify March 2020 borrow rates, March 2020 option bid-ask widths, or the VXHYG implied-vol path (the index returned no time series), so the hedge cost is inferred from realized vol (50-58% annualized) rather than from observed IV prints. (c) I could not verify April 2025 tariff-shock discount magnitudes, which would be the cleanest test of decay.

Notably, every one of these gaps concerns evidence that would make the strategy look WORSE, not better — stressed borrow and stressed option spreads are strictly higher than the calm-market figures I used, so my cost stack is conservative. The verdict would only flip on evidence that discounts systematically predict positive risk-adjusted forward returns at identifiable entries, and I found the opposite.

I would upgrade to NO-EDGE if given a full daily premium/discount panel confirming no predictive power out of sample; the reason I stop at LIKELY-ILLUSORY is that a genuine liquidity risk premium does exist here — it is simply earned by balance sheet, and unavailable to the trader in question.

referee.strategy: Daily Short-Volume Reversal using FINRA's free daily short-sale volume file (short heavily short-sold names, buy lightly short-sold names), gated by an SEC fails-to-deliver (FTD) filter, motivated by Diether–Lee–Werner (2009, RFS 22:2).
referee.edge_case:
The academic pedigree is real. Diether, Lee & Werner (2009, RFS 22(2)) sorted stocks daily on relss = shorted shares / traded shares and found a Low-minus-High long-short portfolio earning 0.063%/day (1.39%/month) on NYSE and 0.064%/day (1.41%/month) on Nasdaq, with 3-factor alphas of 0.065%/day (t=2.98) NYSE and 0.060%/day (t=2.59) Nasdaq at t+2, and 5-day-hold alphas of 0.042%/day and 0.049%/day. Monotonic across quintiles. Boehmer–Jones–Zhang (2008) independently found heavily-shorted names underperform by 1.16% risk-adjusted over the following 20 trading days on NYSE SuperDOT data.

Crucially, the effect is not dead in the public-data era in *every* form: Wang, Yan & Zheng (JFE 2020, 135(1):191-212) confirm "Shorting flows remain a significant predictor of negative future stock returns during 2010-2015, when daily short-sale volume data are published in real time. This predictability decays slowly and lasts for a year."

The data is genuinely free, machine-readable, and low-latency: I downloaded 125 consecutive FINRA CNMS consolidated files directly (https://cdn.finra.org/equity/regsho/daily/CNMSshvolYYYYMMDD.txt), ~12,200 rows/day, no key required; FINRA posts them by 6:00pm ET on trade date. Free CDN history reaches back to ~Jan 2019 (I verified 20190102 returns 200, 20180102 returns 403). So the raw material for the strategy costs $0 and arrives same-day.

The analyst's own FTD work supplies a plausible gate: chronic-fail cheap names show a monotonic dose-response (-1.80% median 2wk at 81-100 fail-days), 16/17 years negative, and survives a within-name test (-1.19%, 60.6% of names worse in chronic spells).
referee.against_case:
Five independent kill shots, in descending order of severity.

1. THE ORIGINAL AUTHORS ALREADY SAID IT DOESN'T CLEAR COSTS. Verbatim from DLW's own paper: "The average return on Low-High strategies may seem 'too large,' but execution costs and commissions are likely to be significant because of daily rebalancing... With effective half-spreads of around 30 basis points, execution costs for the Low-High portfolio with the five-day holding period would be roughly 2.7% per month (not including commissions)... Thus, unless a trader managed her costs very effectively (maybe through the use of limit orders), she could easily wipe out the positive return from a Low-High portfolio strategy." Gross 1.39%/month vs. their own cost estimate 2.7%/month. The strategy was net-negative in the paper that discovered it, in 2005, on price>=$5 stocks, using better data than exists publicly today.

2. THE EXACT HORIZON THIS STRATEGY TRADES IS THE ONE THAT DIED. Wang-Yan-Zheng's abstract continues: "Long-term shorting flows are more informative than short-term shorting flows. Indeed, abnormal short-term shorting flows do not predict future returns or anticipate bad news... A comparison with the Regulation SHO data indicates that the predictability is much shorter-term during 2005-2007. Short sellers appear to have shifted from trading on short-term private information to trading on long-term public information." A *daily* short-volume reversal signal is precisely the "abnormal short-term shorting flow" they find has no predictive power once the data went public. What survives is a slow, year-long accumulation signal — a different, low-turnover trade that is effectively short interest.

3. THE FIELD IS NOT A DIRECTIONAL SHORTING MEASURE, AND THE SIGN MAY BE INVERTED. I computed the distribution from 1,406,093 symbol-days (121 trading days, Feb-Aug 2026, 13,777 symbols): median daily short-volume ratio = 48.0%, mean 47.6%. Half of all off-exchange volume is marked short. That is impossible as directional bearish activity; it is intermediation plumbing. FINRA's own Information Notice 5/10/19 explains the mechanism: when a firm facilitates a customer's long sale, "the trade between the two firms... is reported as short and included in the short sale volume calculations in the Daily File. The volume associated with the firm's purchase from its customer, however, is not reflected." SqueezeMetrics built an entire commercial product (DIX) on the *opposite* sign, arguing short volume proxies investor BUYING, and reporting that "as short volume rises above 35%, average intraday returns are uniformly positive." A naive short-the-high-short-volume trade may be systematically shorting into retail buying pressure.

4. THE CROSS-SECTIONAL SIGNAL IS A NOISE-SORTING ARTIFACT. I decomposed the ratio's variance: only 24.4% is between-name; 75.6% is within-name day-to-day noise. AR(1) of the name-demeaned ratio = 0.227. And dispersion collapses monotonically with liquidity — interquartile range of the ratio by off-exchange volume bucket: <1k shares/day 0.661; 1-10k 0.435; 10-100k 0.316; 100k-1M 0.242; 1-10M 0.203; >10M 0.171. On a representative day (20260811) the top and bottom deciles of the ratio had median off-exchange volume of ~3,174 and ~3,017 shares versus 36,614 for the median name. The extremes of the sort are 90%+ populated by near-untraded names where the ratio is a small-sample accident. Any backtest that finds an edge in the extreme deciles is almost certainly measuring microcap noise, illiquidity premia, and bid-ask bounce — the same failure mode the analyst already found in naive FTD spikes.

5. THE UNDERLYING MARKS ARE KNOWN TO BE WRONG AT SCALE. SEC press release 2023-192 (Sept 2023): Citadel Securities paid a $7M penalty because "for a five-year period, it is estimated that Citadel Securities incorrectly marked millions of orders, inaccurately denoting that certain short sales were long sales and vice versa," from an automated-system coding error. Those bad marks flowed into the public file undetected for five years, at the single largest retail wholesaler.

Add: the "~20 trading days" result in the strategy brief is a misattribution. That is Boehmer-Jones-Zhang (2008), built on proprietary NYSE SuperDOT order-level short-sale data for 2000-2004, not the public FINRA field. DLW's own horizons were t+2 to t+5.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Four counterparties, each rationally happy to take it.

1. THE WHOLESALER/INTERNALIZER WHO CREATED THE SIGNAL. Citadel Securities alone executes ~35% of US retail equity share volume. When it fills a retail buy, it sells short and that print is what lands in the FINRA file; its offsetting purchase is a non-media report and is invisible. It is flat by the close, earns the spread plus payment for order flow, and has no directional view. You are inferring bearish information from a bookkeeping byproduct of the market maker's inventory management. It takes the other side because it is being paid to, not because it disagrees.

2. RETAIL BUYERS. Under the DIX/"Short is Long" reading, high off-exchange short volume in a given name is a proxy for retail buying pressure being absorbed. The other side of your short is the retail flow itself, which is buying because it wants the stock.

3. SECURITIES LENDERS AND PRIME BROKERS. They collect the borrow fee whether you are right or wrong, and hold a recall option they can exercise at the worst moment. On the FTD-gated microcap names — where borrow is scarce — the lender is capturing most of the gross spread you are trying to earn, by construction (the analyst's own breakeven borrow of 25-55% annualized is the proof).

4. ISSUERS AND TOXIC-FINANCING COUNTERPARTIES IN THE GATED MICROCAPS. The FTD gate selects sub-$2 chronically-failing shells (median price $1.47 in my computation). These names are structurally short-biased — that is *why* the decay signal exists — which means the population of natural sellers is already crowded with convertible-note holders, ATM equity lines, and death-spiral financiers who short as a hedge and have far better information on dilution timing than you do. Meanwhile the residual 2.5% of the cohort that squeezes >+25% (analyst's own figure) is where the counterparty makes all its money at your expense. You are taking the crowded side of a trade whose payoff is skewed against latecomers.
referee.frictions:
Two cost stacks, because the strategy has two possible universes.

A) LIQUID UNIVERSE (off-exchange ADV >= 1M shares, ~1,244 names; the only version with capacity)
- Turnover: I measured next-day decile persistence at 30-35% across every universe filter, i.e. ~65-70% one-way daily turnover if rebalanced daily. For DLW's 5-day overlapping construction, turnover is 20%/day/leg (their footnote 18: 0.20 x 2 x 22 = 8.8 round trips/month).
- Spread: effective half-spreads have compressed enormously since DLW's 30bp assumption. For liquid non-S&P names a reasonable modern range is 3-10bp half-spread (I could NOT verify a current authoritative per-market-cap figure; the SEC's own small-cap study is Collver 2014 on 2013 data: 41% of small caps with mcap<$1B and price>=$2 had mean daily quoted spreads <=4.5 cents, 14% <=1.5 cents, but 25% had >=15 cents). At 5bp half-spread: 5-day version = 8.8 round trips x 10bp = 0.88%/month; daily version = ~28 round trips/month x 10bp = ~2.8%/month.
- Borrow: cheap here. D'Avolio (2002, JFE) benchmark: 91% of borrowed stock is general collateral at a 17bp/yr mean fee; the 9% specials averaged 4.30%/yr. Modern industry taxonomy: GC <100bp, Special >100bp, Deep Special >400bp. Call it 0.03%/month for GC.
- Commissions: negligible at retail scale (IBKR-class tiered pricing), but at 28 round trips/month per name across ~250 names both legs, per-share minimums start to bite for small accounts.
- Net drag: ~0.9%/month (5-day) to ~2.8%/month (daily) before any alpha.

B) FTD-GATED MICROCAP UNIVERSE (where the analyst's surviving signal lives)
- I intersected the FTD panel (chronic = on the fails file on >=63% of settlement dates in 2026, price <$5) with the FINRA file: 265 names, median price $1.65, median consolidated dollar volume ~$3.87M/day (p25 $1.27M, p75 $10.9M).
- Spread: the hard *theoretical floor* is one tick. Median gate name price $1.47 → minimum possible quoted spread is 0.29% of price (p75 0.54%); realized spreads on sub-$2 microcaps run several ticks wide, plausibly 1-3% round trip. At ~26 two-week turns/year that is 26-78%/year in spread alone.
- Borrow: these are precisely the deep-special population. The analyst's own breakeven borrow is 25-55% annualized in the $0.50-$5 bands. I could not verify per-name borrow fees (iborrowdesk and IBKR's rate pages both returned 403 through the proxy). Vendor aggregate (companiesmarketcap.com, methodology unverified): 8.18% average cost to borrow across 11,246 names, with the top of the distribution above 700-1,000%. Many of these names have no locate at all at retail brokers.
- MARGIN: this is the friction nobody models. FINRA Rule 4210(c): short stock under $5 requires maintenance margin of the GREATER of $2.50/share or 100% of market value. On a $1.47 stock you post $2.50 to carry $1.47 of short exposure — a 170% margin requirement. Return on capital is ~0.59x return on notional before anything else.
- Reg SHO Rule 201: any 10% intraday decline triggers a bid-price test for the rest of that day and the following day, meaning you cannot hit the bid. In sub-$2 microcaps this triggers constantly and it disables entry exactly when the signal is firing.
- Options (the "defined-risk" escape hatch) mostly does not exist. Cboe Rule 4.3 requires >=7,000,000 publicly held shares, >=2,000 holders, >=2,400,000 shares traded over the prior 12 months, and price >= $3.00. The gate universe has median price $1.47 — it fails the price test outright. Even ignoring price, I computed that 31.6% of top-short-volume-decile names fail the 2.4M-share volume test alone (vs 6.9% of mid-decile names). Where options do exist on such names, quoted widths are a large fraction of premium and IV is extreme — I could not source an authoritative width/IV figure and will not invent one.
- Taxes: all gains are short-term ordinary income (up to 37% federal + 3.8% NIIT), and short sales are ineligible for long-term treatment regardless of holding period. Constructive-sale and wash-sale mechanics add complexity. Post-tax, a marginal pre-tax edge becomes negative.
referee.capacity:
Per trade, gated version: I found that on a typical day only ~5.0 names (max 12 across 121 trading days) pass BOTH the chronic-cheap FTD gate AND the top decile of short-volume ratio. Median consolidated dollar volume for gate names is ~$3.87M/day. At a realistic 3% participation for a name that thin, that is ~$116k per name, ~$580k of gross short notional at any one time. At 170% margin (Rule 4210(c), sub-$5) that consumes ~$1.0M of capital to carry $0.58M of exposure. Pushing to 10% of ADV would move these names against you on entry and again on exit.

Per year, gated version: with ~2-week holds, ~26 turns, annual traded notional ~$15M against a ~$0.6M standing book. Even if the gross edge were the analyst's best-case mean (+0.47% per 2wk short gain, ~12.9%/yr on notional), that is ~$77k/year gross on $1M of committed capital — before 26-78%/yr in spread and 20-50%/yr in borrow. The arithmetic does not reach positive.

Liquid universe: capacity is genuinely large — ~1,244 names with >=1M off-exchange shares/day, top decile ~124 names with median 1.77M off-exchange shares/day (≈3.8M consolidated at the current ~46.5% TRF share). At 1% of ADV and a $25 assumed price that is roughly $95M/leg of standing exposure. But at 65-70% daily turnover you would be trading ~$60-80M/day per leg, which requires institutional execution infrastructure a small fund does not have — and the gross edge in this universe is the one Wang-Yan-Zheng show is approximately zero. Large capacity on a zero signal is worth nothing.

Bottom line: the capacity and the edge are in disjoint universes. Where the signal has dispersion, the names are untradeable. Where the names are tradeable, the signal has no dispersion (ratio IQR 0.171-0.203 clustered around 0.50).
referee.decay_evidence:
Direct, published, and specific to this signal:

1. Wang, Yan & Zheng (JFE 2020, 135(1):191-212), "Shorting flows, public disclosure, and market efficiency" — the definitive post-publication test. Verbatim: "abnormal short-term shorting flows do not predict future returns or anticipate bad news... A comparison with the Regulation SHO data indicates that the predictability is much shorter-term during 2005-2007. Short sellers appear to have shifted from trading on short-term private information to trading on long-term public information that is gradually incorporated into prices." The short-horizon signal DLW documented in 2005 is specifically what stopped working once the data became public.

2. McLean & Pontiff (JF 2016), 97 published predictors: returns are 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication, with the 32% gap attributed to publication-informed trading. DLW published in 2009; FINRA has published these files free for well over a decade. Applying the 58% haircut to DLW's 1.39%/month gives ~0.58%/month — still below even the modern liquid-universe cost stack for a daily-rebalanced book.

3. Regulatory acknowledgment that the field is misread: FINRA issued Information Notice 5/10/19 specifically to explain that the Daily File "includes only trades that are publicly disseminated," is "not consolidated" across markets, and that "short interest data reflects short positions held by market participants at a specific moment in time on two discrete days each month, while the Daily File reflects the aggregate volume of trades executed as short sales on each trade date." A regulator does not publish a notice like that unless the misinterpretation is already widespread.

ALREADY COMMERCIALIZED — this is not an undiscovered dataset:
- FINRA itself: free daily/monthly files, an interactive 365-day grid, AND a public Query API (developer.finra.org).
- SqueezeMetrics has sold DIX — built directly on TRF short volume — since roughly 2016, with a published white paper ("Short is Long") arguing the *opposite* sign to this strategy.
- Fintel sells "Short Volume Ratio" screens; ShortVolume.com, ChartExchange, stockgrid, ForcedAlpha and Quiver Quantitative all surface it free or near-free.
- Ortex publishes an explainer titled "Why Daily Short Volumes Are Often Misinterpreted."
- There is a public Kaggle dataset of FINRA short volumes, and TradingView community scripts implementing DIX-style indicators.
- Blocher, Haslag & Zhang (J. Empirical Finance 2020), "Short trading and short investing," already formalized the split between intermediation-driven short trading (weekly-scale, unconstrained) and genuine short investing (multi-month, constrained). Both academia and vendors have picked this over.

One asymmetry worth noting: SEC Rule 13f-2 / Form SHO — which would have published aggregated true short *positions* — has been repeatedly delayed; the first reporting period is now January 2028 with filings due 14 Feb 2028. So the informative version of this data does not yet exist publicly, and the uninformative version has been fully mined.
referee.net_edge_estimate:
Liquid universe (price >= $5, off-exchange ADV >= 1M shares): gross expected edge ≈ 0.0%/month, on the direct authority of Wang-Yan-Zheng for exactly this horizon. Even granting a generous post-decay 0.3-0.6%/month, cost is 0.9%/month at 5-day holds and ~2.8%/month at the daily rebalance the signal's 30-35% persistence actually implies. Net expectancy: roughly -0.5% to -2.5% per month. Negative with high confidence.

FTD-gated microcap universe: gross short gain, using the analyst's own honest MEAN (not median) of -0.47% per 2 weeks, ≈ +12.9%/year on notional. Costs: spread 26-78%/yr (26 turns x 1-3% round trip), borrow plausibly 20-50%/yr for chronic-fail sub-$2 names, plus a 0.59x haircut to return-on-capital from the 170% margin rule, plus Rule 201 blocking entry on exactly the down days. Net expectancy: approximately -25% to -55% per year on capital. Negative with high confidence, and the direction of the error is not close.

What I could NOT determine, stated plainly: I did not run my own return backtest. I could not obtain a free price feed through the environment's proxy (stooq's JS proof-of-work POST was reset; iborrowdesk and IBKR rate pages returned 403). So the return figures above are the published literature's plus the analyst's own FTD panel, not an independent replication. I also could not verify per-name borrow fees, current per-market-cap effective spreads (my best SEC source is 2013 data), or options bid-ask widths and IV levels on these names. Everything I state as measured — the ratio distribution, variance decomposition, decile persistence, liquidity-conditional dispersion, options-eligibility failure rates, and the FTD-gate overlap count — I computed directly from 125 downloaded FINRA files and the repository's 27.5M-row FTD parquet, and those are reproducible.

Given the sign uncertainty alone (DIX argues the signal is inverted), an honest expectancy interval for the naive daily version straddles zero on the gross and is decisively negative on the net.
referee.barriers:
1. LOCATE AND SHORTABILITY. The gate universe has median price $1.47. Most retail brokers will not lend sub-$1 and much sub-$2 stock at all; where they will, the locate disappears on the days the signal fires.
2. MARGIN. FINRA Rule 4210(c): short stock under $5 requires the greater of $2.50/share or 100% of market value. A $1.47 short consumes $2.50 of capital — 170%. This single rule cuts return-on-capital by ~41% before costs.
3. REG SHO RULE 201. A 10% intraday decline triggers the bid-price test for the remainder of that day and the next, so short orders can only be displayed or executed above the national best bid. In sub-$2 microcaps this fires routinely and specifically blocks entry when the thesis is playing out.
4. EXECUTION INFRASTRUCTURE. Measured next-day decile persistence of 30-35% means ~65-70% of the book turns over daily. Capturing anything requires passive/limit execution at scale — DLW themselves flagged that the only escape is if "a trader managed her costs very effectively (maybe through the use of limit orders)." A small trader crossing the spread has already lost.
5. NO DEFINED-RISK ALTERNATIVE. The options escape hatch is closed by Cboe Rule 4.3's $3.00 price floor for covered securities, plus 7M public shares / 2,000 holders / 2.4M shares per 12 months. I measured that 31.6% of top-short-volume-decile names fail the volume test alone; the gated microcaps fail the price test outright.
6. UNIVERSE SIZE. ~5 qualifying names per day means the portfolio is never diversified. With 2.48% of the chronic cohort returning >+25% (analyst's figure), a 5-name book has roughly a 12% chance per rebalance of holding a squeeze, and no way to diversify it away.
7. DATA HISTORY. Free FINRA CDN history reaches back only to ~January 2019 (verified: 20190102 → 200, 20180102 → 403). Roughly 7.5 years is enough to overfit a daily signal and not enough to distinguish it from noise; longer history requires paid transaction files or vendor reconstruction.
8. DATA INTEGRITY. Per SEC 2023-192, the largest wholesaler mismarked millions of long/short orders for five years. A small trader has no way to detect or correct such contamination.
9. VENUE INCOMPLETENESS. The FINRA file covers only off-exchange TRF/ADF/ORF prints (~46.5% of consolidated volume as of March 2026). Building the consolidated measure FINRA itself says is required means separately ingesting Nasdaq, NYSE and Cboe short-volume files — the "free FINRA data" premise is already false.
10. TAXES. Short-term ordinary income at up to 37% + 3.8% NIIT, with no long-term treatment available on short sales, applied to a strategy whose pre-tax edge is already marginal.
referee.confidence:
HIGH that there is no exploitable net-of-cost edge here for a small trader or small fund, for four converging reasons that do not depend on each other.

(a) The originating paper's own cost arithmetic is negative: 1.39%/month gross versus 2.7%/month execution cost, stated by DLW in the published text, in the best-case 2005 sample, on price>=$5 stocks, using exchange-marked tick data superior to anything public today.
(b) The specific horizon this strategy trades has a direct, peer-reviewed null result in the public-data era — Wang-Yan-Zheng (JFE 2020): "abnormal short-term shorting flows do not predict future returns or anticipate bad news."
(c) My own measurement of the current file shows the cross-sectional dispersion that a sort would exploit is a liquidity artifact — ratio IQR falls monotonically from 0.661 in sub-1k-share names to 0.171 in >10M-share names, 75.6% of variance is within-name daily noise, and the extreme deciles have ~1/12th the volume of the median name.
(d) The gate makes it worse, not better: only ~5 names/day pass both filters, at median $1.47/share where the 170% margin rule, Rule 201, absent options, and deep-special borrow all apply simultaneously.

MEDIUM on the precise magnitude of the negative expectancy, because I could not run an independent return backtest (no free price feed reachable through the proxy) and could not verify current per-name borrow fees or per-market-cap effective spreads with an authoritative source. My spread figures lean on a 2014 SEC study of 2013 data, and my borrow-fee framing leans on D'Avolio (2002) plus a vendor aggregate whose methodology I could not check. Those uncertainties affect how negative the answer is, not its sign.

LOW confidence only on one sub-question: whether the correct sign is negative or actively inverted. SqueezeMetrics' commercial DIX product asserts high short volume proxies BUYING, with intraday returns uniformly positive above a 35% ratio — but that is a vendor white paper, not peer-reviewed, and I did not independently verify it. Either way it argues against the trade as specified; it just changes whether the strategy is dead or backwards.

Recommendation: do not put this on the book. If any variant is worth further work, it is the slow one Wang-Yan-Zheng actually validated — long-horizon accumulated shorting flow with a one-year decay — which is a low-turnover signal in liquid names, is essentially a proxy for short interest, and is already sold by multiple vendors. The daily-reversal-plus-FTD-gate construction should be retired for the same reason the analyst retired naive FTD spikes: it is a sort on noise in names too small to trade.

referee.strategy: Section 103(k) Coal Tripwire — monitor MSHA Section 103(k) accident/control orders on msha.gov and short the affected US-listed coal issuer (HCC, AMR, BTU, METC) into the expected production disruption.
referee.edge_case: The honest strongest case, and it is thin. (1) 103(k) orders are real and can be severe: I pulled the full MSHA violations census (151MB zip, 3.09M rows, file dated 2026-08-07) and isolated 14,142 103(k) orders since 2000. Median duration is 6 days but the tail is fat — p90 = 93 days, p95 = 181 days, p99 = 446 days; 23.4% exceed 30 days and 10.3% exceed 90 days. A >90-day order at a single-asset issuer genuinely is an earnings event. (2) These are control orders, not penalty citations — only 107 of 14,249 carry any proposed penalty — so they are not "just paperwork"; they legally stop work until MSHA re-approves. (3) The MSHA channel is genuinely slower than the newswire, so a latency edge is at least conceptually available. (4) The one subset with the right sign: conditioning on duration > 90 days (N=28 across the four tickers, 2019+), the 21-day XME-adjusted return is mean -2.91% / median -5.82% entering on the issue date, and -4.03% / -8.58% entering after the flat-file lag. (5) Concentration risk is real at one name: Warrior Met's Mine No. 7 alone drew 27 of HCC's 50 orders since 2019, and No. 7 is its dominant longwall. That is the version of the trade that is not obviously stupid. Everything below says it still does not work.
referee.against_case: Five independent kills, any one of which is sufficient. (1) THERE IS NO EVENT. I ran the event study on all 324 103(k) orders at mines controlled by HCC/AMR/BTU/METC since 2019. Issue-day volume relative to the trailing 20-day median volume is 0.87x (HCC), 0.99x (AMR), 1.03x (BTU), 1.12x (METC). Issue-day absolute return vs. that name's unconditional daily |return| since 2019: HCC 3.38% vs 2.44%, AMR 3.31% vs 2.82%, BTU 2.91% vs 3.43%, METC 3.04% vs 3.46% — BTU and METC are LOWER than baseline. No abnormal volume, no abnormal volatility. Nothing is being priced, so there is nothing to front-run. (2) THE SIGN IS WRONG. XME-adjusted mean forward returns across all 324 events: +1.11% at 1d, +2.48% at 3d, +2.40% at 5d, +1.87% at 10d. Shorting these events would have lost roughly 2% per trade. The apparent t = +5.3 is a time-clustering artifact — the effect is entirely 2019 (+5.95% 5d) and 2020 (+7.95%) during the met-coal/COVID recovery, and collapses to noise afterward: 2022 +0.36%, 2023 -0.02%, 2024 +0.46%, 2025 +0.23%, 2026 -0.70%, i.e. mean +0.07% for 2022-2026. Endogeneity runs the wrong way: mines run harder when coal prices are high, harder running produces more accidents, so 103(k) counts are mildly PRO-cyclical. (3) THE "MATERIAL" SUBSET IS PURE LOOK-AHEAD. The only negative subset (duration > 90d) is conditioned on the termination date, which is unknowable at entry, and even so t = -0.67 / -0.93 on N=28 with heavy calendar overlap. It restates "if you knew the mine would be down three months you would want to be short" — true and useless. (4) LATENCY DEFEAT. The premise that 103(k) orders are "published on msha.gov" in usable time is factually wrong. MSHA's flat files refresh once a week, Friday afternoon, and there is a further data-entry lag: in the 2026-08-07 file, 2026-08-06 carried only 84 rows against a ~300-600/day steady state and 2026-08-07 carried zero. Effective publication latency is roughly 4-11 calendar days. Local news beats it by about a week — the Long View Mine underground fire began Sunday 2024-06-30 (I confirm the 103(k) issue date as 06/30/2024, terminated 02/18/2025, a 233-day shutdown, the single most material recent case) and WV MetroNews ran it Monday 2024-07-01. (5) THE MATERIAL EVENTS ARE MOSTLY UNTRADEABLE ANYWAY. Long View is controlled by AMCI/POSCO/JAZ — private, no ticker. Of 333 coal 103(k) orders lasting >90 days since 2019, the top controllers are Alliance (20), Sev.en (19), Arch (13), Foresight (11), Wolverine (10) — mostly private or non-target. Peabody's actual 2026 mine catastrophe was Centurion in Queensland, Australia, entirely outside MSHA jurisdiction; BTU fell 9.7% on 2026-03-30 on a commissioning miss that no MSHA feed would ever have shown, and is now facing a securities class action over it. Two peer-reviewed studies agree: the 2021 Resources Policy study of US mine safety disclosures finds markets do not react to mine safety incident disclosures and finds no evidence of a negative reaction to single-fatality incidents on MSHA's fatality reports; even Upper Big Branch (29 dead, 2010-04-05) was fully priced the next day — Massey fell 11% on 2010-04-06 off wire coverage, not off an MSHA file.
referee.who_is_on_other_side: In the modal case, nobody informed is on the other side — which is the problem, not a comfort. Since there is no abnormal volume or volatility on issue days, you are not trading against a slow holder discovering bad news; you are simply paying the spread to a market maker who takes zero directional view and earns the quoted width. Your realized P&L is then sector beta plus friction. In the rare genuinely material case, the counterparty is well-informed and rationally so: (a) coal-sector specialists and sell-side analysts who learned from local mine-country press, the UMWA, scanner traffic, or company IR within hours — days before the MSHA file; (b) long-only value and income holders who know the base rate you do not, namely that median 103(k) duration is 6 days, 26.8% terminate within one day, 53.5% within seven, and that most orders are area- or equipment-scoped rather than mine-wide; (c) macro-driven buyers who correctly judge that seaborne met/thermal coal prices dominate these equities — AMR runs 19 active mines, so no single 103(k) moves the estimate; (d) traders who understand that an idled competitor mine is bullish for the coal price, which partially offsets the producer's own lost tons and is a plausible mechanism behind the positive measured sign. Empirically the smartest version of this is the 2017 Journal of Accounting and Economics paper by Christensen, Floyd, Liu and Maffett, whose entire identification strategy rests on the fact that MSHA safety records are already publicly available elsewhere and that only the SEC-filing channel adds incremental price impact. Caveat: I could not open the paper (ScienceDirect returned 403); a search-result summary of the article page reports a 155bp mean / 140bp median more-negative reaction when a citation appears in an 8-K versus MSHA-website-only, and I flag that figure as unverified from source.
referee.frictions: Measured, not guessed, except where flagged. BORROW (Interactive Brokers stock-loan, 259-260 daily observations, 2025-08-14 to 2026-08-12, via iborrowdesk API): HCC median 0.27%/yr, p90 0.41%, max 0.43%, shares available median 1.1M / min 200k. AMR median 0.41%, p90 0.42%, max 0.57%, avail median 1.1M / min 850k. BTU median 0.29%, p90 0.42%, max 0.43%, avail median 5.3M / min 1.2M. METC median 0.32%, p90 0.42%, max 4.27%, avail median 1.2M / min 100k. All four are general collateral — borrow costs roughly 0.1bp/day, i.e. 0.8-1.6bp on a 10-day hold. Borrow is NOT the binding constraint here, and I want to be clear about that rather than pad the case. COMMISSION (IBKR Pro tiered $0.0035/share): HCC 0.4bp/side, AMR 0.2bp, BTU 1.4bp, METC 3.2bp — double for round trip. EQUITY SPREAD/IMPACT: I could not obtain a live NBBO quote, so this is the weakest number in the stack and I say so. A Corwin-Schultz two-day high-low estimator over Feb-Aug 2026 gives median 56.7bp (HCC), 40.8bp (AMR), 101.0bp (BTU), 106.9bp (METC), but that estimator is biased upward for high-volatility names (measured trailing-250d realized vol: HCC 43%, AMR 52%, BTU 49%, METC 79%). My working assumption for a $250k-$1M clip is 10-30bp round-trip spread plus impact for HCC/BTU and 20-50bp for AMR/METC. OPTIONS — this is the real killer, and these are live quotes (Nasdaq chain, 2026-09-18 expiry, 36 days, pulled 2026-08-13). HCC $90 put bid 1.20 / ask 2.85, mid 2.02, width $1.65 = 81.5% of mid, IV 40.7%, open interest 248. HCC $95 put 3.00/5.70, width 62.1% of mid, OI 9, IV 44.5%. AMR $150 put 4.20/8.00, width 62.3% of mid, OI 28, IV 53.7%; AMR $145 put 2.70/7.60, width 95.1% of mid, OI 4. BTU $23 put 0.72/1.14, width 45.2% of mid, OI 356, IV 55.8%; BTU $25 put 1.59/1.86, width 15.7%, OI 845, IV 51.6%. METC $10 put 0.60/0.75, width 22.2% of mid, OI 265, IV 83.2%; METC $11 put 1.05/1.35, width 25.0%, OI 324, IV 86.1%. Buying an HCC $90 put at the offer and selling at the bid means the mid must rise 41% just to break even. IV at 41-45% (HCC), 54-64% (AMR), 52-61% (BTU), 83-94% (METC) sits at or slightly above measured realized vol — no vol edge either, and a one-month one-sigma move of 12-25% is already in the price. DIVIDENDS on short: small, roughly 0.1-0.3%/yr equivalent, negligible over a 10-day hold. TAXES: short-term capital gains at ordinary rates, up to 37% federal plus state for a taxable small trader — this alone would take a third off any gross edge, and there is no gross edge.
referee.capacity: Per trade, before impact bites: 5% of median dollar ADV gives $3.04M (HCC, $60.9M ADV), $2.55M (AMR, $51.0M), $2.06M (BTU, $41.2M), $1.14M (METC, $22.8M). Realistically a small fund working a 5-10 day short would want to stay near $0.5-2M per name to avoid paying 30-60bp of impact on entry plus the same on exit. Per year, the event count caps gross turnover: 324 events across the four tickers in 7.6 years is about 43/yr, so roughly $65M of gross notional traded annually at $1.5M/clip — that is the mechanical ceiling. The options expression has a far lower ceiling: total open interest at the HCC $90 September put is 248 contracts, about $2.2M of notional across every holder on the planet, and AMR strikes carry OI of 2-28 contracts. You could not build a $250k position in AMR puts without moving the option 20%+ against yourself. Borrow availability is not the constraint below roughly $10-20M (HCC min availability 200k shares ≈ $19M; METC min 100k shares ≈ $1.1M, which does bind for METC at size). None of this matters much: the expectancy is negative, so the capacity of PROFITABLE deployment is $0. The correct capacity answer for a negative-expectancy strategy is zero regardless of what the ADV arithmetic permits.
referee.decay_evidence: There is no decay story here because there was never anything to decay — the evidence points to an edge that never existed rather than one that was arbitraged away. (1) Commoditization: the data is free, and already packaged and resold. An Apify actor (ryanclinton/msha-mining-safety) sells joined DOL/MSHA mines + violations + inspections + accidents + assessments with automated risk scoring for $30 per 1,000 results, and confirms all five underlying datasets refresh weekly. Anything a small trader can build from the flat files, a competitor can rent for lunch money. (2) Regulatory pre-emption: Dodd-Frank Section 1503 has required SEC-registered mine operators to file Exhibit 95 mine safety tables in every periodic report since the SEC's final rules of 2011-12-21, plus an 8-K within four business days for 107(a) imminent danger orders. The market has had a structured, standardized, issuer-verified channel for fifteen years. Warrior Met's own 107(a) at Blue Creek was disclosed via SEC filing and produced no discernible negative reaction. (3) Academic pre-emption, two papers, opposite research questions, same conclusion for our purposes: the 2021 Resources Policy study of US mine safety disclosures finds markets do not react to mine safety incident disclosures and finds no evidence of a negative reaction to single-fatality incidents on MSHA's fatality reports, with only limited evidence for multi-fatality events; Christensen, Floyd, Liu and Maffett (JAE 2017, vol 64, 284-304) build their identification on the premise that MSHA records are already publicly available elsewhere, so the informative channel is the financial report, not msha.gov. (4) My own direct measurement is the strongest form of this: zero abnormal volume (0.87-1.12x), zero abnormal volatility, wrong-signed drift, and a post-2021 mean of +0.07%. Who already trades it: nobody needs to. Coal-sector specialists, local mine-country press, the UMWA, and company IR all move on this within hours through the newswire; the MSHA file is the last place the information arrives, not the first.
referee.net_edge_estimate: Gross signal, best estimate: approximately zero and possibly adverse. Full-sample 2019+ XME-adjusted 5-day mean is +2.40% (a short loses); the regime-stable 2022-2026 subsample is +0.07% with a per-trade standard deviation of roughly 6-11% (five-day sigma at 43-79% annualized vol). Call gross expectancy 0.0% ± 0.6% standard error per trade. Net of costs: subtract 15-45bp of round-trip spread, impact and commission for the equity short, plus about 1bp of borrow, giving net expectancy of roughly -15 to -45bp per trade with an information ratio indistinguishable from, and most likely worse than, zero. At 43 trades per year that is roughly -6% to -19% per year on deployed gross notional, before short-term-capital-gains treatment of any winners. The options expression is materially worse: paying an 62-100% bid/ask-to-mid width on HCC or AMR puts means giving up 25-45% of premium on a round trip against an IV of 41-64% that already prices the entire distribution of mine outcomes; expected loss per options trade is on the order of -25% to -45% of premium. The one number I will not claim to know is the true expectancy of the sub-strategy "103(k) at a mine that is >40% of issuer volumes, mine-wide scope, expected duration >30 days" — my proxy for it (HCC Mine No. 7, N=27) gives 1-day XME-adjusted outcomes scattered from -5.82% to +7.06% with 48% down, and 5-day mean +1.83%, but N=27 is too small to resolve a 50bp effect against 3% daily noise. That is unknowable from this sample, and the honest statement is that it would take several hundred clean, size-weighted events to detect anything, which the base rate will not supply in a human lifetime.
referee.barriers: (1) No real-time feed exists. MSHA publishes 20 flat files once a week on Friday afternoon; the violations file is a 151MB zip / 1.44GB text with 3.09M rows and a further 2-3 day data-entry lag on top of the weekly cadence. Effective latency 4-11 calendar days. There is no RSS, no push API, no same-day 103(k) endpoint. To beat local news you would need field-level sourcing — mine-country press monitors, county scanner feeds, union contacts — which is a newsroom, not a data pipeline, and is exactly the capability a small trader does not have. (2) Base rate destroys signal-to-noise. 43 events per year across the four tickers — HCC 5, BTU 2, AMR 17, METC 9 in the trailing twelve months — means about one alert every six trading days per basket, with AMR alone firing 1.4 times a month. A signal that fires that often on a 0.61-beta name is a coin flip with a fee attached. (3) The materiality filter is not computable at entry. To know whether an order matters you need mine-level scope (not in the file), expected duration (only known at termination), and the mine's share of issuer volumes (MSHA production data is quarterly and lagged; AMR's 19 active mines make it structurally diffuse). (4) Options are effectively closed. OI of 2-28 contracts on AMR strikes and 9-248 on HCC, with 62-95% bid/ask-to-mid widths, means the leveraged expression cannot be entered at any size at any sane price. Only BTU $25 (OI 845) and METC $10/$11 (OI 265/324) are even quotable, and those carry 51-86% IV. (5) Jurisdictional blind spot. The two largest recent mine-driven equity moves in this basket — Peabody/Centurion in Queensland and AMR's storm-related disruptions — are invisible to MSHA. (6) Survivorship of the trade universe. The most severe recent US 103(k) shutdowns landed on private operators (Allegheny Metallurgical, Sev.en, Wolverine, Foresight); the listed names get the routine ones. (7) Taxes and the short-side asymmetry: unlimited loss on a 43-79% vol name held through unrelated coal-price headlines, capped gain, ordinary-income treatment on winners. Notably absent from this list: legal or MNPI barriers. It is entirely public data. That is precisely the tell — a free, weekly, government-published dataset that a $30 Apify actor already resells is not where an exploitable edge lives.
referee.confidence: HIGH — and unusually so for a rejection, because this was settled by direct measurement rather than by argument. I downloaded and parsed the complete MSHA violations census (3,092,333 rows, file dated 2026-08-07), isolated all 14,142 Section 103(k) orders since 2000, mapped 324 of them to mines controlled by HCC/AMR/BTU/METC since 2019, and ran the event study against XME-adjusted daily returns. The decisive facts are measurements, not inferences: issue-day relative volume 0.87-1.12x, issue-day |return| at or below unconditional baseline for two of four names, full-sample drift wrong-signed at +2.40% over five days, post-2021 drift +0.07%. Publication latency is verified from the file itself (weekly Friday refresh, 84 rows on the most recent weekday vs a ~300-600/day steady state, zero rows on the file date). Borrow fees and option quotes are live vendor data, not estimates. Two independent peer-reviewed studies concur, and the Long View / Centurion case studies show the material events are either private-company or non-MSHA. Residual uncertainties, stated plainly: (a) equity bid-ask is a Corwin-Schultz proxy, not a live NBBO quote — it is the softest number in the stack, though even a 5bp spread does not rescue a zero-to-negative gross signal; (b) ScienceDirect returned 403, so the 155bp/140bp Christensen et al. figure comes from a search-result summary of the article page and is not verified from the paper itself — the 2021 Resources Policy finding is likewise from summary, though it is directionally corroborated by my own measurement; (c) the concentrated sub-case (mine-wide 103(k) at a mine >40% of volumes) is under-powered at N=27 and I label its expectancy unknowable rather than zero. None of those caveats moves the verdict. This is the same failure mode as the naive FTD spike signal: a real, well-documented public dataset with a plausible causal story, no abnormal volume or return at the event, and a positive-looking t-statistic that dissolves into calendar clustering the moment you cut it by year. The chronic-persistence lesson applies here too — if anything survives in MSHA data it will be a slow, structural, cross-sectional quality signal (chronic violation intensity as a proxy for operational deterioration or cost inflation, held over quarters), not a same-week event tripwire. Working files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-WireAntennaGain/82dc742b-08fa-562e-9653-7f5ab2131e39/scratchpad/ — Violations.zip (raw MSHA census), k_rows.json (14,249 extracted 103(k) records), parse.py, an2.py, an3.py, an4.py (base rates, durations, controller mapping), event.py and final.py (event study and robustness), spread.py (Corwin-Schultz), opt.py (option chains and IV), ib_*.json (IBKR borrow history), px_*.json (daily prices).

referee.strategy: Warehouse Amendment Wire: monitor mid-quarter 8-K/exhibit amendments to warehouse/repo credit facilities at nonbank originators (UWMC, RKT, COOP, PFSI, CACC, OMF) for capacity reductions, advance-rate cuts, or lender exits; trade the issuer short via equity or 2-8 week puts.
referee.edge_case:
The steelman has three real planks, and I verified all three are individually true:

1. FUNDING FRAGILITY IS REAL. Nonbank originators genuinely live on short-dated, largely UNCOMMITTED warehouse lines. Verified in filings: advance rates run 60-92% depending on asset type and delinquency (Redwood Trust 10-Q, 6/30/26); issuers state that lenders "may reassess their exposure to the mortgage origination industry and potentially limit access to uncommitted mortgage warehouse financing." Funding withdrawal genuinely kills these companies — First Guaranty Mortgage filed Chapter 11 on 6/30/2022 owing >$400M to four warehouse lenders (Customers, Flagstar, Texas Capital, JVB).

2. THE DISCLOSURE EXISTS AND IS MACHINE-READABLE. Item 1.01/2.03 8-Ks with facility exhibits are filed regularly. Verified counts, EDGAR full-text search (EFTS), 2021-01-01 to 2026-08-13: PFSI 23 Item-1.01 8-Ks, CACC 45, loanDepot (LDI) 64. Exhibits are indexed in the same submission as the body, so amendment text is searchable.

3. LATENCY IS NOT A BARRIER. EFTS indexes new filings in under ~60 seconds. A small trader can genuinely be among the first humans to read the document. The information-access plank of the thesis is the one part that survives.

The strongest single anecdote for the thesis: loanDepot cut funding capacity three times in two months in 2022 ($1.5B combined), taking total capacity from $9.9B (6/30/22) to $5.7B (9/30/22) to $4.1B (12/31/22) — a genuinely large, genuinely disclosed, genuinely mid-quarter contraction at a company whose stock was collapsing.

That is the entire case. It does not survive contact with the data.
referee.against_case:
The strategy fails at five independent points. Any one is fatal; all five are true simultaneously.

1. THE SIGN IS INVERTED. This is the killer. Warehouse capacity reductions at nonbank originators are overwhelmingly BORROWER-initiated cost cuts, not lender-initiated stress. Warehouse lines carry non-usage fees; when origination volume falls, originators voluntarily shrink lines to save money. The issuers say so in plain text. loanDepot: capacity "decreased ... primarily due to the Company's decision to reduce its borrowing capacity, reflecting lower volume expectations." Home Point: "continued to strategically rightsize its warehouse lines of credit in order to minimize associated costs." A capacity cut is usually a margin-POSITIVE action being read as a distress signal.

The returns confirm it. I hand-classified loanDepot's 64 Item-1.01 8-Ks (2021-06 to 2026-05) — LDI is the most stressed, most active filer in the sector, the best possible case for this strategy — and flagged 8 genuine capacity-cut/non-renewal events:

  +40 trading days after the 8 flagged capacity-cut events:
    mean +23.13%, median +18.74%, only 25% negative (2 of 8)

The proposed 2-8 week short window has a mean +23% underlying return. The signal is a mild CONTRARIAN indicator, not a bearish one. Mechanically sensible: by the time the cut is disclosed the stock has already collapsed, and the cut improves the cost line.

The single most on-thesis event in the entire dataset is the clearest refutation. On 2023-11-08 loanDepot disclosed it "chose not to renew its Master Repurchase Agreement" — the textbook lender-exit signal the strategy is built to detect. Forward return: +8.39% day 0, +11.61% at 10 days, +116.77% at 40 days. The stock more than doubled. A put buyer was wiped out; a short lost 117%.

2. THE MARKET DOES NOT REACT, SO THERE IS NO MOVE TO FRONT-RUN. Event study on Item-1.01 (non-earnings) 8-Ks since 2021:
    PFSI (n=21): event-day mean |move| 1.26% vs baseline median daily |move| 1.23%. 1 of 21 events moved >3%.
    CACC (n=43): event-day mean |move| 1.52% vs baseline 1.34%. 5 of 43 moved >3%.
  Event-day moves are statistically indistinguishable from a random day. These filings are non-events, and the market is right: they are routine rollovers.

3. THERE IS NO INTRADAY RACE TO WIN. I pulled EDGAR acceptance timestamps for 62 warehouse/facility Item-1.01 8-Ks (LDI, PFSI, CACC, 2022+):
    post-close (>=16:00 ET): 60 of 62 (97%)
    pre-open (<9:30 ET): 2 of 62 (3%)
    INTRADAY: 0 of 62 (0%)
  Typical stamps: CACC 16:01, 16:02; PFSI 16:15, 16:31; LDI 16:46, 16:55, 17:01. Every filing lands after the bell. The <60s EFTS latency advantage is worth nothing — the whole market has 17+ hours to read the document before the next open. The single plank of the thesis that survived (latency) is rendered irrelevant by filing convention.

4. THE TRIGGER BARELY FIRES, AND THE UNIVERSE HAS SHRUNK. Bearish language is almost absent from EDGAR. All filers, all 8-Ks, 2021-2026 (5.6 years): "declined to renew" = 11 documents total (zero in mortgage/finance); "elected not to renew" = 43 (zero in mortgage); "reduced the committed amount" = 0; "terminate the warehouse" = 0. At the most active filer in the sector the genuine capacity-cut rate is ~1.6 events/year. Meanwhile the stated universe is already broken: COOP was acquired by RKT and delisted 10/1/2025 (11 RKT shares per COOP share, $14.2B). OMF has ZERO 8-K documents containing "warehouse" in 5.6 years — it funds via ABS and unsecured notes, so it cannot generate this signal at all. Two of six names are gone before you start.

5. WRONG FILING VENUE. Most warehouse amendments never appear in an 8-K; they are attached as exhibits to the next 10-Q/10-K, i.e. up to 45-90 days stale. "Master Repurchase Agreement" document counts, 2021-2026: RKT 8-K 25 vs 10-Q 62 vs 10-K 20; PFSI 8-K 39 vs 10-Q 30 vs 10-K 17. UWMC — the largest name in the thesis — effectively never files warehouse-amendment 8-Ks: its 67 8-K hits for "warehouse" are almost entirely Item 2.02 earnings releases. Aggregate capacity, the actually material number, is disclosed only in the quarterly liquidity table, ~40 days after quarter end.

LIVE FALSIFICATION. There is a real nonbank funding crisis happening right now, and the wire produced no warning. UWMC collapsed ~35% in one day on 2026-08-06 — worst day on record — suspending its dividend and taking a $2B dilutive equity infusion from Oaktree and the Ishbia family after a rate-hedge blowup; equity fell to ~$1B at 6/30 from $1.6B at 3/31. UWMC filed NOTHING between 2026-06-03 (annual meeting results) and the 8-K on 2026-08-06. The stress arrived bundled as earnings + capital raise + dividend suspension in a single post-close 8-K, with zero warehouse-amendment precursor. In the biggest funding-stress event in the target universe in years, this strategy would have been long nothing and short nothing until after the 35% gap.

A NLP TRAP THAT POISONS THE SIGNAL. For CACC, "advance rate" does NOT mean warehouse collateral advance rate — it is CACC's core business metric, the amount advanced to dealer-partners as a percentage of consumer loan balance, reported every quarter. A keyword scanner firing on "decrease in the advance rate" for CACC hits earnings releases about unit economics, and a FALLING dealer advance rate is typically BULLISH (wider spread vs forecasted collections). CACC is the highest-count name in the universe and nearly all of its hits are this false positive.
referee.who_is_on_other_side:
Nobody is taking a mispriced other side, because there is no mispricing — this is the core problem. You are not extracting from a reluctant counterparty; you are paying the spread to trade a non-event.

Concretely, who transacts against you and why they are happy to:

- MARKET MAKERS IN THE OPTIONS. They are the primary counterparty and the only reliable winner. On UWMC the ATM put quotes 0.05 bid / 0.15 ask — the maker collects 100% of mid as edge on the round trip. They rationally quote this wide because UWMC is a $1.50-1.84 stock with 85-89% IV, $0.50 strike granularity, and post-close headline risk. They are not making a view on your warehouse thesis; they are charging for inventory risk on a distressed sub-$2 name and are indifferent to why you want the put.

- LONG-ONLY VALUE AND DEEP-VALUE FUNDS BUYING THE DIP. They rationally take the other side because they read the same filing correctly: a voluntary capacity cut on an underused line is a cost reduction at a company that has already de-rated 50-85%. They are buying because the disclosure is mildly good news dressed as bad news. Empirically they win: +23% mean over the next 40 trading days on the 8 flagged events.
