pitfalls.mitigation: The repo already solved this: 425 zips (~591 MB raw) consolidate to a 235 MB zstd Parquet at parquet/ftd_all.parquet, built by build_parquet.py in a couple of minutes. Partition by year, sort within partition by (cusip, settlement_date), and add the knowledge_date column during the build so no downstream consumer can forget it.

concrete_specs: SEC FTD current files: https://www.sec.gov/files/data/fails-deliver-data/cnsfails{YYYYMM}{a|b}.zip — 'a' = settlements 1st-15th, 'b' = 16th-EOM. Derived round-trip friction as a percentage of notional, IBKR Pro Tiered at the entry tier, short then cover, excluding borrow and spread — $0.50 stock: ~1.52% (0.700% commission per side + 0.040% clearing per side + 0.039% TAF + 0.002% Sec31). $1.00: ~0.76%. $2.00: ~0.38%. $5.00: ~0.154%. These are the numbers that decide whether a signal is tradeable.

The 1%-of-trade-value commission cap starts binding below roughly $0.37/share (where $0.0035 commission + $0.0002 clearing exceeds 1% of price), i.e. sub-$0.37 names cost ~1% per side in commission alone, ~2% round trip. Whether the $0.00020/share clearing charge sits inside or outside that cap is not stated on the pricing page — confirm with IBKR before modelling sub-$0.40 names.

execution.topic: Order types, venues, and microstructure for executing short-biased and event-driven trades in US small/micro-cap equities ($0.50–$5)

practices.practice: Treat Rule 201 (SSR) as the default state for your entry signal, not an edge case
practices.detail: Verbatim from SEC Release 34-61595: trading centers must prevent 'the execution or display of a short sale order of a covered security at a price that is less than or equal to the current national best bid if the price of that covered security decreases by 10% or more from the covered security's closing price as determined by the listing market for the covered security as of the end of regular trading hours on the prior day,' and must impose it 'for the remainder of the day and the following day.' A short-biased/event book entering after a -10% day is structurally trading SSR-restricted names on the entry bar AND the next session. Build the SSR flag into the signal pipeline before sizing, not into the fill logic afterward. Note the asymmetry: SSR restricts only the short sale side; buying to cover is entirely unrestricted, so exits are never blocked by Rule 201.

practices.practice: Under SSR, use midpoint pegs — the midpoint is above the NBB, so a midpoint short is compliant when a bid-hitting short is not
practices.detail: Rule 201 prohibits display/execution at or below the NBB. With any positive spread, the midpoint sits strictly above the NBB (a $2.00 x $2.01 market has a $2.005 midpoint = NBB + $0.005), so a sell-short midpoint peg is executable while a marketable short is being repriced or cancelled. This is the single most useful SSR workaround and requires no 'short exempt' marking. Two caveats: (1) on a locked market (bid == ask) the midpoint equals the NBB and the order becomes non-executable; (2) confirm your broker does not pre-emptively block the order on a naive at-or-below-bid check. IEX M-Peg and D-Peg both qualify, are non-displayed, are Min-Quantity eligible, and take a limit price.

practices.practice: Post, never take, and treat the post-vs-take decision as the largest controllable cost in the book
practices.detail: Modelled on a $2.00 name, 10,000 shares ($20,000 notional): taking costs ~57.5 bps per side (17.5 bps IBKR Tiered commission + 15.0 bps exchange take fee + 25.0 bps half-spread on a $0.01 spread) = ~115 bps round trip. Posting the same size earns ~-15.5 bps per side (commission net of a $0.0016 BZX add rebate, capturing rather than paying the half-spread). The swing is ~73 bps per side / ~146 bps round trip. Against a strategy whose own research characterises the edge as 'a small negative median,' round-trip take costs of ~115 bps consume most or all of the signal. Passive execution is not an optimisation here, it is the difference between a viable and a non-viable strategy.

practices.practice: Know the LULD band regime for your exact price bucket — in $0.75–$3.00 names the bands give you almost no protection
practices.detail: Verified band table (LULD Plan): Tier 1 = S&P 500, Russell 1000 and select ETPs; Tier 2 = all other NMS securities except rights and warrants (i.e. essentially every micro-cap in this universe). Above $3.00: Tier 1 ±5%, Tier 2 ±10%. Between $0.75 and $3.00 (both tiers): ±20%. Below $0.75 (both tiers): the lesser of $0.15 or 75%. Bands double during the opening period (9:30–9:45) and during the last 25 minutes (3:35–4:00, for Tier 1 and Tier 2 securities at or below $3.00). So a $2.00 short can run 40% against you in the first 15 minutes before a limit state is even possible. Traders who assume LULD is a stop-loss backstop are mispricing the tail on precisely the names where the tail matters.

practices.practice: Watch the $3.00 boundary as a hard regime change in halt protection
practices.detail: A Tier 2 name at $3.05 has a ±10% band; the same name at $2.95 has a ±20% band — the protection halves the instant it crosses $3.00 (and the band is based on the price level, so this flips intraday). For a short book, drifting below $3.00 doubles the distance the stock can travel before a pause, and simultaneously moves you into the price bucket where bands double at the open and close. Tag every position with its band regime and re-tag on price moves through $3.00 and $0.75.

practices.practice: Avoid the open (9:30–9:45) for entries; use the close deliberately, with LOC rather than MOC
practices.detail: The open combines doubled LULD bands, the widest spreads of the day, and stale opening-cross imbalance information. The close is the opposite: it is a single-price event with no spread to cross, and Nasdaq states the closing auction is 'almost 10% of Nasdaq's average daily volume.' Use LOC, never MOC — an unbounded MOC into a large imbalance in a thin name can print double-digit percentages away from the last sale. LOC bounds that. Read the Net Order Imbalance Indicator before committing.

practices.practice: Work the auction timetable exactly — the cancel deadline, not the entry deadline, is what traps you
practices.detail: Nasdaq closing cross (verified, Nasdaq Closing Cross FAQ): MOC/LOC/IO accepted before 3:50; at 3:50 early dissemination begins and orders may still be entered but MAY NOT BE CANCELLED OR MODIFIED; at 3:55 Nasdaq stops accepting MOC, LOC accepted until 3:58, IO until 4:00; 3:58 LOC entry stops; 4:00 cross. NYSE: MOC/LOC may be entered, modified or cancelled until 3:50; after 3:50 they may be entered only on the contra side of a published MOC/LOC Significant Imbalance, and cannot be modified or cancelled at all. The operative risk is that from 3:50 you are committed. An LOC left in a name that halts at 3:52 cannot be pulled.

practices.practice: Read the NOII/imbalance feed before sending closing interest
practices.detail: Nasdaq disseminates NOII from 3:50, every 10 seconds until 3:55 (paired shares, imbalance side, imbalance quantity, current reference price), then every 1 second from 3:55–4:00 adding the Near Indicative Clearing Price (includes continuous book) and Far Indicative Clearing Price (closing interest only). The Near/Far divergence is the tell for how much of the indicated print is real closing demand versus continuous-book liquidity that may evaporate. NYSE publishes informational imbalance every 1 second from 3:50 until the close, including paired quantity, unpaired quantity, total imbalance, closing-only interest price and continuous book clearing price.

practices.practice: Use hidden midpoint liquidity rather than displayed icebergs in genuinely thin books
practices.detail: IEX D-Peg rests outside the NBBO and steps to the midpoint except when the Signal (crumbling quote) is on; M-Peg pegs to the midpoint and holds priority over a D-Peg exercising discretion into the midpoint; P-Peg is the conservative variant that steps only to the NBB/NBO. All three are non-displayed, Min-Quantity eligible, accept an optional limit price and are book-recheck eligible. Note they are NOT reserve/iceberg eligible and not post-only. The Signal is the point: it protects a resting order from being picked off at the moment the quote is about to move, which is exactly the adverse selection that destroys passive fills in thin names.

practices.practice: Size child orders to your ability to cover in a bad tape, not to average volume
practices.detail: For a negative-skew short, the binding constraint is not entry participation, it is exit capacity during the squeeze. Keep child orders at 5–10% of trailing interval volume for entry, but size the total position against what can be covered in a hostile session. Volume typically rises during a squeeze, which helps, but it rises at a price 20–40% away, which is the whole problem. The relevant question is not 'can I get out' but 'at what price can I get out.'

practices.practice: Never send a market order in this universe; use marketable limits with an explicit cap
practices.detail: A market order in a $1–5 name with a thin book walks the ladder. Use a marketable limit priced at a defined offset (e.g. NBO + 1–2 ticks for a cover) so the worst fill is bounded. This matters most on the cover side, which is the side you will be forced to trade at the worst moment, and where SSR provides no protection because covering is unrestricted.

practices.practice: Reconcile the borrow leg against the strategy's own breakeven before trading the signal
practices.detail: The repository's own FTD study puts the breakeven annualised borrow fee for the cheap-stock decay effect at only 25–55%, which it correctly notes is 'the same order as actual HTB fees.' In this universe the borrow cost is not a rounding error, it is comparable to the entire gross edge. Pull indicative fee and shortable-quantity data before entry and re-check it daily, because rates reprice intraday and a locate is not a guarantee against recall.

practices.practice: Treat recall and buy-in as a correlated tail, not an independent operational nuisance
practices.detail: Borrow recall arrives when utilisation spikes — which is precisely when the stock is squeezing. A forced buy-in executes at the market's convenience, not yours, and stacks on top of a LULD-halted, gapping tape. This is the same negative-skew event as the price tail, not a separate risk, so do not diversify against it by adding more crowded shorts. Prefer names with genuine borrow depth, or express the view in defined-risk options.

practices.practice: Consider defined-risk options where the borrow or SSR constraint binds hardest
practices.detail: Rule 201 restricts short sales of the covered security; it does not restrict buying puts, and the academic literature explicitly documents this route (see 'Circumventing SEC Rule 201 short sale restrictions with options,' Journal of Banking & Finance / ScienceDirect). Options also cap the fat positive tail that is the signature risk of this book. The trade-off is that the market maker's borrow cost is already embedded in the option price via put-call parity, so you pay the borrow either way — but you pay it as a known premium rather than an open-ended liability. The repo's own verdict on the FTD trade was that it is 'unresolved as a defined-risk put trade — needs options/IV data,' which is the right place to resolve it.

practices.practice: Rebuild your assumptions about hidden odd-lot liquidity — odd lots became visible in 2026
practices.detail: Under the Market Data Infrastructure rules the SIPs began disseminating odd-lot quotation data with a Nasdaq UTP hot cut on 27 April 2026 and an SEC compliance date in early May 2026 (sources differ slightly on the exact date; both are in the past as of August 2026). The new Best Odd-Lot Order (BOLO) field publishes the highest-priced odd-lot buy above the NBB and the lowest-priced odd-lot sell below the NBO. Slicing into sub-100-share pieces no longer conceals intent the way it did before 2026. Odd lots still do not constitute protected quotations, so they can be traded through.

pitfalls.pitfall: Your marketable short during SSR is silently converted into a passive resting order, so you believe you are short when you are not
pitfalls.mitigation: Per the Nasdaq Reg SHO FAQ, once the SIP indicates the circuit breaker is on, 'short sale orders that are limited to the national best bid or lower and short sale market orders will be re-priced by NASDAQ and BX to one minimum allowable price increment above the national best bid (Permitted Price),' and are then continuously re-priced as the NBB moves, down to the original limit price. No rejection is generated. Alert on the difference between intended and actual fills for every SSR name, and reconcile positions intraday rather than at EOD. Never assume a 'market' short filled.

pitfalls.pitfall: IOC and ISO short orders are NOT repriced during SSR — they simply cancel, returning zero fill and no error
pitfalls.mitigation: Nasdaq Reg SHO FAQ: 'During the Short Sale restriction period, IOC orders requiring that all or part of the order be executed immediately will be executed to the extent possible and then cancelled, and will not be re-priced. Intermarket Sweep Orders (ISOs) not marked short exempt will be handled in the same manner as IOC orders.' If your entry logic sweeps with IOC, SSR days produce systematic silent non-entry. Switch to midpoint pegs or resting limits above the NBB on SSR names, and log every zero-fill IOC against the SSR flag to detect this.

pitfalls.pitfall: Routing strategies quietly stop routing during SSR, concentrating your order on one venue
pitfalls.mitigation: Nasdaq Reg SHO FAQ: 'NASDAQ will passively post to the NASDAQ book any short sale orders that are entered using a strategy that normally routes (STGY, SCAN, etc.) to other destinations in order to not violate Reg SHO.' Your smart-router silently becomes a single-venue post. Expect materially lower fill rates on SSR days and plan entry over a longer horizon rather than escalating aggression.

pitfalls.pitfall: Stop-loss orders do not protect you through a LULD halt — they execute at the reopening print
pitfalls.mitigation: There is no trading during the 5-minute pause, so a stop is not a stop; it becomes a market order into the reopening auction, which can print 20–40% away in a $0.75–$3.00 name where the band is 20% (40% at the open/close). Do not rely on stops for tail control on these names. Use position sizing, defined-risk options, or pre-committed maximum loss per name as the actual control.

pitfalls.pitfall: Micro-caps halt repeatedly in the same session, so 'wait for the halt to clear' is not a plan
pitfalls.mitigation: Measured directly from the live Nasdaq halt feed on 13 August 2026: roughly 19 LUDP (LULD pause) entries across about 9 distinct symbols, with one name (FGI) halting approximately 7 times in the session and resumptions typically 5–10 minutes after the halt. A squeeze in a micro-cap is a ratchet of halt, reopen higher, halt again — during which you cannot cover. Assume you will be locked out for the duration of the adverse move and size accordingly. (Note: this feed is a rolling ~49-item window, so treat these counts as a snapshot rather than a complete market-wide daily census.)

pitfalls.pitfall: Per-share commissions are catastrophic as a percentage of notional on low-priced stocks
pitfalls.mitigation: IBKR Fixed at $0.005/share on a $0.60 stock is 83 bps per side in commission alone; at $0.40 the 1%-of-trade-value cap binds and you pay a full 100 bps per side. On a $2.00 stock, Fixed is 25 bps and Tiered ($0.0035/share) is 17.5 bps per side. Use Tiered rather than Fixed for this universe, and set a hard minimum price filter — below roughly $0.50 the commission structure alone can exceed any plausible edge.

pitfalls.pitfall: Taking liquidity in a sub-$1.00 name costs 30 bps in exchange fees before you pay a single tick of spread
pitfalls.mitigation: Cboe BZX charges 0.30% of total dollar value to remove liquidity in securities priced below $1.00, while adding liquidity in the same names is free (no charge and no rebate). IBKR explicitly warns clients about 'ECN charges for removing liquidity when sending marketable orders for low priced stocks (under USD 2.50).' In sub-$1 names, adopt an absolute rule: post only, never take. If a position drifts below $1.00, your exit cost structure has changed and the position should be re-evaluated on that basis alone.

pitfalls.pitfall: You cannot cancel closing-auction interest after 3:50, which becomes a trap when the name halts
pitfalls.mitigation: Both Nasdaq (from 3:50, MOC/LOC/IO 'may not be canceled or modified') and NYSE (after 3:50, MOC/LOC 'cannot be modified or canceled') lock you in. Decide closing-auction participation before 3:50 with full knowledge that it is irrevocable, and reduce auction size in names already showing intraday LULD activity.

pitfalls.pitfall: MOC orders in thin names are unbounded risk at the single most concentrated moment of the day
pitfalls.mitigation: Use LOC. Note the Nasdaq repricing nuance: an LOC entered between 3:55 and 3:58 is accepted at its limit price 'unless its limit price is more aggressive than either the 3:50 p.m. ET or 3:55 p.m. ET Reference Prices, in which case the LOC order will be re-priced to the more aggressive of the two Reference Prices' — so a very aggressive late LOC will not achieve the price you typed.

pitfalls.pitfall: Imbalance-Only orders get repriced to the 4:00 BBO and frequently do not fill at all
pitfalls.mitigation: Per Nasdaq's own worked example, an IO to sell priced at $9.95 was repriced to the 4:00 Nasdaq ask of $10.15 and received no fill, while an LOC at $10.00 executed. IO orders 'to buy (or sell) that are priced more aggressively than the 4:00 p.m. ET Nasdaq bid (or ask) will be adjusted to the Nasdaq bid (or ask) prior to the execution of the cross.' If you need the fill, use LOC, which has genuine price standing; use IO only when you are genuinely indifferent and are supplying stabilising liquidity.

pitfalls.pitfall: Iceberg refresh patterns are a readable signature in a thin book
pitfalls.mitigation: Repeated identical-size prints at the same price level advertise a reserve order to anyone watching the tape, and in a micro-cap the watching population is small and attentive. Prefer genuinely non-displayed liquidity (IEX M-Peg/D-Peg, midpoint dark) over displayed reserve orders, or randomise display size and price level if you must show. Accept that hidden orders lose queue priority to displayed orders as the cost of concealment.

pitfalls.pitfall: Two Reg NMS changes land on the first business day of November 2026 and will alter your cost model mid-strategy
pitfalls.mitigation: The $0.005 minimum pricing increment (for NMS stocks at or above $1.00 with a time-weighted average quoted spread of $0.015 or less) and the reduced Rule 610 access fee caps ($0.0010/share for stocks at or above $1.00; 0.1% of the quotation price below $1.00) were delayed by SEC exemptive relief to the first business day of November 2026 — roughly two and a half months out as of August 2026. The D.C. Circuit denied challenges to these amendments on 14 October 2025, so they are proceeding. Many liquid $1–5 names quote penny-wide and will qualify for half-penny ticks, which narrows spreads (lower crossing cost) but also halves the queue value of a passive post. Re-derive the post-vs-take breakeven after implementation rather than carrying today's 73 bps figure forward.

pitfalls.pitfall: Assuming SSR blocks your exit
pitfalls.mitigation: It does not. Rule 201 constrains only short sale orders. Buying to cover is unrestricted at any price, including hitting the offer, at all times. Do not build exit logic that defers covering on SSR days — the constraint is entirely on the entry side.

pitfalls.pitfall: Treating the SSR flag as a single daily boolean when it has three distinct states
pitfalls.mitigation: The Nasdaq Reg SHO Price Test Indicator carries three values: 0 = no restriction; 1 = restriction in effect due to an intra-day price drop in the security; 2 = restriction remains in effect (i.e. the carry-over second day). Nasdaq sends a full pre-opening spin of the indicator for every listed security at the start of each trading day, then intraday updates only for securities newly breaching the 10% threshold. Consume state 2 explicitly — that is the day-after case that a naive 'did it drop 10% today' check will miss entirely.

concrete_specs: Rule 201 trigger (verbatim, SEC Release 34-61595): short sale restriction applies when the security 'decreases by 10% or more from the covered security's closing price as determined by the listing market for the covered security as of the end of regular trading hours on the prior day.'

Rule 201 restriction: prevents 'the execution or display of a short sale order... at a price that is less than or equal to the current national best bid,' in force 'for the remainder of the day and the following day.'

Nasdaq/BX/PSX SSR repricing: short sale limit orders at or below the NBB, and short sale market orders, are repriced to one minimum price increment above the NBB ('Permitted Price'), and continuously repriced as the NBB moves, down to the order's original limit price.
Nasdaq SSR + IOC/ISO: IOC orders execute to the extent possible then cancel and are NOT repriced; ISOs not marked 'short exempt' are handled identically. Expect zero-fill, no-error outcomes.
Nasdaq SSR + routing: orders using routing strategies (STGY, SCAN, etc.) are passively posted to the Nasdaq book instead of routed away.
Nasdaq SSR + auctions: Nasdaq uses the National Best Bid at the time of the cross to determine short-order eligibility, while using the Nasdaq BBO to determine the actual auction price.

Reg SHO Price Test Indicator values: 0 = no restriction; 1 = restriction in effect due to intra-day price drop; 2 = restriction remains in effect. Full pre-opening spin daily for every Nasdaq-listed security.
LULD tiers: Tier 1 = S&P 500, Russell 1000 and select ETPs. Tier 2 = all other NMS securities except rights and warrants (covers essentially this entire universe).
LULD bands above $3.00: Tier 1 ±5%, Tier 2 ±10%. Between $0.75 and $3.00: ±20% both tiers. Below $0.75: lesser of $0.15 or 75%, both tiers.

LULD band doubling: bands double during the opening period (9:30–9:45) and during the last 25 minutes (3:35–4:00) for Tier 1 and for Tier 2 securities at or below $3.00. A $2.00 name therefore has a ±40% band in the first 15 minutes.

LULD mechanics: reference price is the average trade price over the immediately preceding five-minute period; a limit state persisting more than 15 seconds triggers a 5-minute trading pause; reopening is via auction on the primary listing exchange.

Live halt endpoint (verified working, August 2026): http://www.nasdaqtrader.com/rss.aspx?feed=tradehalts — fields include Issue Symbol, Issue Name, Halt Date, Halt Time, Market, Reason Code, Resumption Date, Resumption Quote Time, Resumption Trade Time.
Halt reason code LUDP = LULD volatility pause (LUDS = straddle-condition variant). Codes T1, T3, T12, H11 and M were also observed live in the feed on 13 August 2026.
Empirical halt observation (13 August 2026 feed snapshot): ~19 LUDP entries across ~9 distinct symbols; FGI halted ~7 times in one session; LUDP resumptions typically 5–10 minutes after halt.

Nasdaq Closing Cross timeline: before 3:50 MOC/LOC/IO accepted → 3:50 early NOII dissemination begins, orders accepted but NOT cancellable or modifiable → 3:55 MOC entry stops, full dissemination begins → 3:58 LOC entry stops → 4:00 IO entry stops, cross runs at the NOCP.

Nasdaq NOII cadence: every 10 seconds from 3:50–3:55 (paired shares, imbalance side, imbalance quantity, current reference price); every 1 second from 3:55–4:00, adding Near Indicative Clearing Price (includes continuous book) and Far Indicative Clearing Price (closing interest only).
Nasdaq LOC repricing: an LOC entered 3:55–3:58 is accepted at its limit unless more aggressive than the 3:50 or 3:55 Reference Price, in which case it is repriced to the more aggressive of the two.

NYSE closing timeline: MOC/LOC entry, modification and cancellation until 3:50; after 3:50 entry only on the contra side of a published MOC/LOC Significant Imbalance, with no modification or cancellation permitted. Informational imbalance published every 1 second from 3:50 until the close.

NYSE opening timeline: Pillar gateways open 6:30 a.m.; opening imbalance disseminated every 1 second from 8:00 a.m.; opening process begins 9:30 a.m.; securities that cannot open within 10% of the reference price must be opened manually by the DMM.

NYSE Closing Offset (CO) order: limit only, no validation against imbalance publication, yields to all other closing interest, executes only against the opposite side of an imbalance and never adds to one — the most conservative way to supply closing liquidity.

IEX order types for SSR-constrained shorts: M-Peg (midpoint, non-displayed), D-Peg (rests outside NBBO, steps to midpoint except when the Signal is on), P-Peg (steps only to NBB/NBO). All Min-Quantity eligible, optional limit price, book-recheck eligible; none are reserve/iceberg eligible or post-only. M-Peg holds priority over a D-Peg exercising discretion into the midpoint.

Round lot in $1–5 names remains 100 shares; the amended tiered round-lot definition (implemented on or before 3 November 2025) only shrinks round lots for higher-priced stocks. Odd lot = 1–99 shares in this universe.

Odd-lot transparency now live: Nasdaq UTP hot cut 27 April 2026, SEC compliance date early May 2026. New SIP messages include Odd Lot Quote (short/long form), Combined Quote, and a BOLO (Best Odd Lot Order) appendage. BOLO to buy = highest-priced odd-lot buy above the NBB; BOLO to sell = lowest-priced odd-lot sell below the NBO. Odd lots remain unprotected quotations.

Upcoming (first business day of November 2026): $0.005 minimum pricing increment for NMS stocks at or above $1.00 with a time-weighted average quoted spread of $0.015 or less; Rule 610 access fee caps drop to $0.0010/share (at or above $1.00) and 0.1% of quotation price (below $1.00). SEC estimated ~1,800 stocks / ~66% of share volume affected by the tick change. D.C. Circuit denied challenges 14 October 2025.

Operational rule of thumb set: no market orders in this universe; post-only below $1.00; Tiered not Fixed commissions; price floor around $0.50 (where the 1% commission cap binds); LOC not MOC; all auction decisions final by 3:50; child orders 5–10% of trailing interval volume; tag every position with its LULD band regime and re-tag on moves through $3.00 and $0.75.
costs: Cboe BZX, securities at or above $1.00: remove displayed liquidity $0.0030/share; add displayed liquidity $0.0016/share rebate (verified, BZX fee schedule).

Cboe BZX, securities below $1.00: remove liquidity 0.30% of total dollar value; add liquidity free (no charge, no rebate). Routed executions (Parallel D, Parallel 2D, ROUT, ROUX, Post to Away) also 0.30% of total dollar value on either side.

Cboe BZX non-displayed adding liquidity fee codes HB/HV/HY show a $0.0080/share rebate and HI (non-displayed receiving price improvement) is free — UNVERIFIED whether these rates are tier-conditional; confirm against your firm's qualifying tier before relying on them.
IEX remove displayed liquidity: $0.0030/share standard, reduced to $0.0024/share for members adding at least 25,000 ADV of displayed liquidity; 0.15% of total dollar value below $1.00.
IEX remove non-displayed liquidity: $0.0010/share at or above $1.00; 0.10% of total dollar value below $1.00.
IEX add liquidity: displayed at or above $1.00 is free; non-displayed $0.0010/share (0.10% of TDV below $1.00).
IEX M-Peg / D-Peg removing displayed liquidity (fee codes TLK/TLBK): $0.0010/share at or above $1.00; 0.20% of total dollar value below $1.00.

Interactive Brokers US equities: Fixed $0.005/share, $1.00 minimum, 1% of trade value maximum. Tiered $0.0035/share (under 300k shares/month), $0.35 minimum, 1% of trade value maximum, plus pass-through exchange/regulatory/clearing fees and rebates.

IBKR sub-dollar orders (under $1.00) are commission-free for IBKR Lite only while the combined monthly volume of Open auction, Close auction, outside-RTH and sub-dollar orders stays at or below 10% of the account's monthly US stock volume; above that, the lesser of $0.005/share or 1% of trade value applies.

Modelled all-in taking cost, $2.00 name, 10,000 shares ($20,000): 17.5 bps IBKR Tiered commission + 15.0 bps exchange take fee + 25.0 bps half-spread (on a $0.01 spread) = 57.5 bps per side, ~115 bps round trip.

Modelled posting alternative, same trade: ~-15.5 bps per side (commission net of the $0.0016 BZX add rebate, capturing rather than paying the half-spread). Post-vs-take lever = ~73 bps per side, ~146 bps round trip.

Commission as a share of notional on low-priced names (IBKR Fixed $0.005/share): $2.00 stock = 25 bps/side; $0.60 stock = 83 bps/side; $0.40 stock = 100 bps/side, where the 1%-of-trade-value cap binds. IBKR Tiered on a $2.00 stock = 17.5 bps/side.

Borrow cost context from the repository's own FTD study: breakeven annualised borrow fee for the cheap-stock decay effect is only 25–55%, described in-repo as 'the same order as actual HTB fees' — i.e. financing cost is comparable in magnitude to the entire gross edge.

UNVERIFIED — live borrow data endpoints: IBKR publishes shortable-share counts and indicative borrow fee rates as a machine-readable file (commonly cited as ftp.interactivebrokers.com/usa.txt), and iBorrowDesk archives that feed. The IBKR pages returned HTTP 403/503 during this research, so confirm the current endpoint and schema directly before wiring it into a pipeline.

UNVERIFIED — closing auction share for micro-caps specifically. Nasdaq's stated 'almost 10% of average daily volume' in the closing auction is a market-wide figure; the micro-cap-specific share is typically lower and should be measured per name from your own tape before sizing auction participation.

execution.topic: Compliance and regulatory guardrails for a small short-biased trader in US small/micro-cap equities ($0.50–$5 names), ETFs and event trades — verified against primary sources as of 2026-08-13

practices.practice: Re-baseline the day-trading rules: the pattern-day-trader regime and the $25,000 minimum were ELIMINATED effective June 4, 2026
practices.detail: VERIFIED, and this overturns the premise of most guidance you will find online. SR-FINRA-2025-017 amended FINRA Rule 4210 effective June 4, 2026; FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10 (Apr 20, 2026, 'FINRA Adopts New Intraday Margin Standards to Replace the Day Trading Margin Requirements') states the new standards replace 'in their entirety the outdated day trading margin requirements, including the day trade count requirements for designating a customer as a "pattern day trader" and the $25,000 pattern day trader minimum equity requirement.' I downloaded the live Rule 4210 text from finra.org and confirmed it now contains ZERO occurrences of 'pattern day trader', '25,000', or 'day trad'. Replaced by new Rule 4210(a)(17)-(a)(19) and (d)(2) 'Intraday Margin'. CRITICAL CAVEAT: there is an 18-month phase-in ending October 20, 2027, and firms 'that need more time to implement the rule change will be permitted to phase in their implementation' — so your broker may still be enforcing the legacy $25k/4-trades regime today. Do not assume either way: email your broker's margin department and get the answer in writing before sizing an account under $25k.

practices.practice: Learn the new intraday margin standard, because it bites short-biased books specifically
practices.detail: VERIFIED from Rule 4210 text. New 4210(a)(17) defines 'IML' or 'intraday margin level' as 'the amount of cash that the customer could withdraw while still having the maintenance margin required' (expressed as a negative number when you'd need to add cash). (a)(18) 'IML-reducing transaction' includes any purchase or sale in the account (a short sale qualifies), option expiration that reduces IML, and any withdrawal. (a)(19) 'intraday margin deficit' is the largest negative IML during the day. Under (d)(2)(C) the member must require the deficit 'to be satisfied as promptly as possible'; it stays outstanding until satisfied or until close of business on the 15th business day. The practical shift: you must now carry maintenance margin excess at EVERY point intraday, measured at each trade, not merely at the close. A short entered at 10:00 that is underwater at 14:00 creates a measurable deficit even if you flatten by the bell.

practices.practice: Treat the 90-day freeze as the single largest operational risk to a short-only book
practices.detail: VERIFIED. Rule 4210(d)(2)(D): if a customer 'makes a practice of failing to satisfy intraday margin deficits as promptly as possible and fails to satisfy an intraday margin deficit by the close of business on the fifth business day after it occurs,' the member must enforce policies 'reasonably designed to prevent the customer from creating or increasing a short position or debit balance (other than by closing a short position) for 90 calendar days.' Read that literally: the penalty is a 90-day ban on NEW SHORTS while leaving you free only to cover. For a short-biased strategy that is a full business stoppage, not a slap. De minimis safe harbour: deficits that 'do not exceed the lesser of 5 percent of the equity in the margin account or $1,000', or that arose under 'extraordinary circumstances'. Engineer your sizing so any plausible intraday adverse move keeps the deficit under min(5% of equity, $1,000).

practices.practice: Size shorts off the maintenance margin requirement, never off the sale proceeds
practices.detail: VERIFIED verbatim from FINRA Rule 4210(c)(2)-(3): '$2.50 per share or 100 percent of the current market value, whichever amount is greater, of each stock "short" in the account selling at less than $5.00 per share; plus $5.00 per share or 30 percent of the current market value, whichever amount is greater, of each stock "short" in the account selling at $5.00 per share or above.' Your entire target universe sits in the punitive band. Compute the requirement per name before entry and treat it as the position's true capital cost.

practices.practice: Run a Rule 201 (alternative uptick) pre-trade check every morning and use limit orders exclusively for short entries
practices.detail: VERIFIED from 17 CFR 242.201. A 'covered security' is any NMS stock. The circuit breaker fires when 'the price of that covered security decreases by 10% or more from the covered security's closing price' as of the prior day's regular-hours close; 'the listing market for the covered security' makes the determination and 'shall immediately make such information available.' The restriction runs 'for the remainder of the day and the following day' — note it spans two sessions, which routinely surprises traders on day two. While active, trading centres must 'prevent the execution or display of a short sale order of a covered security at a price that is less than or equal to the current national best bid.' Operationally: you may only sell short ABOVE the NBB. Never send a market short or a marketable-limit short on a triggered name — it will be rejected, repriced or queued, and on a $0.80 stock with a $0.01 tick that repricing is a material slippage event.

practices.practice: Never short a name into a pending or plausible follow-on offering, then buy that offering — Rule 105 is effectively strict liability
practices.detail: VERIFIED from 17 CFR 242.105. It is unlawful to 'sell short ... the security that is the subject of the offering and purchase the offered securities' during the restricted period, defined as the shorter of the period '(1) Beginning five business days before the pricing of the offered securities and ending with such pricing; or (2) Beginning with the initial filing ... and ending with the pricing.' It applies to offerings 'conducted on a firm commitment basis.' There is no intent element — the SEC brings these as routine disgorgement-plus-penalty sweeps. This is acutely relevant because serial dilutive issuers (PLUG, HYZN and similar cash-burning micro caps) price overnight offerings off a shelf with little warning. The bona fide purchase exception exists but is narrow: it requires an offsetting open-market purchase during regular trading hours, reported to an effective transaction reporting plan, made after the last short sale and before pricing, and NO short sales in the final 30 minutes before the close on the day preceding pricing. Simplest compliant rule: if you were short the name at any point in the prior five business days, do not participate in the offering at all.

practices.practice: Keep locate and order-marking hygiene clean, even though the locate obligation legally sits with the broker
practices.detail: VERIFIED from SEC Reg SHO materials. Rule 203(b)(1) requires the broker-dealer to 'have reasonable grounds to believe that the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due before effecting a short sale order.' The bona fide market-making exception is narrow and 'excludes speculative selling' — it is not available to you. Rule 200(g) requires every order be marked 'long', 'short', or 'short exempt'. Your exposure is on the marking side: representing a sale as 'long' when you do not own and cannot deliver the shares is a Rule 200(g) violation attributable to you, not your broker. Retain locate confirmations and timestamped order marks; if you use a locate-provider broker for hard-to-borrow names, archive the daily locate receipts.

practices.practice: Model Rule 204 close-out and forced buy-in as a hard, un-negotiable exit you do not control
practices.detail: VERIFIED from SEC Reg SHO guidance. Fails on short sales must be closed out 'by the beginning of regular trading hours on the settlement day following the settlement date' (long sales and bona fide market making get to the third consecutive settlement day; a 35-calendar-day window under 204(a)(2) applies only to narrow 'deemed to own' delayed-delivery situations such as Rule 144 resales). Settlement has been T+1 since May 28, 2024, which compressed every one of these windows. Non-compliance puts the participant and the brokers routing through it into the 'penalty box': no further short sales in that security without a pre-borrow. Separately, a stock loan is callable at any time — you have no contractual right to keep the borrow, and a recall-driven buy-in lands exactly when the name is squeezing. Never build a thesis that requires holding a hard-to-borrow short through a specific future date.

practices.practice: Draw the research/manipulation line at your own disclosure and your own order book, and treat SEC v. Andrew Left as the governing template
practices.detail: VERIFIED from SEC press release 2024-89. The SEC charged Left and Citron Capital over 'bait-and-switch' conduct: publicly recommending long or short positions in 23 companies on 26 occasions while falsely representing that those recommendations matched his actual positions; reversing positions after the stock moved (averaging 12% moves); buying back stock immediately after telling readers to sell; falsely claiming a price target he would hold to ('$65') while selling far earlier ('$28'); and misrepresenting Citron as independent and never compensated by third parties despite compensation arrangements with hedge funds. Alleged ill-gotten profits: $20 million. Remedies sought included disgorgement, prejudgment interest, civil penalties, an officer-and-director bar and a penny stock bar. The lawful posture is simple: analysis of public data and taking a position on it is legitimate, including when your conclusion is negative. What converts it into fraud is a false statement — about your position, your holding intention, your independence, or your compensation. The safest configuration for a small trader is to publish nothing at all while positioned.

practices.practice: Never let execution tactics drift into order-book signalling
practices.detail: VERIFIED from FINRA Rule 5210 Supplementary Material .02. Members must publish only quotations they reasonably believe are bona fide. Layering is described as entering 'multiple limit orders on one side of the market at various price levels', after which 'the level of supply and demand for the security changes', the party 'enters one or more orders on the opposite side ... that are subsequently executed', and then 'cancels the Displayed Orders'. Spoofing is described as narrowing 'the spread for a security by placing an order inside the national best bid and national best offer', then executing 'an order on the opposite side of the market that executes against another market participant that joined the new inside market'. Both require a 'frequent pattern'. In a $0.50–$5 name with a wide spread and thin book, ordinary iceberg/refresh/ladder logic can innocently produce this exact fingerprint. Configure algos to avoid placing displayed orders you intend to cancel on the opposite side of a position you are working, and keep cancel/execute ratios logged per symbol.

practices.practice: Scrape regulator sites within their published access rules and stay strictly on the public-record side of the line
practices.detail: VERIFIED from SEC's webmaster FAQ. SEC explicitly states 'We allow scripted access to sec.gov content.' You must declare a User-Agent in the format 'Sample Company Name AdminContact@<sample company domain>.com', and the rate ceiling is 10 requests per second, 'carefully monitored to preserve equitable access.' Prefer the bulk channels over page scraping: full/daily index files, the Financial Statement Data Sets, the RESTful JSON APIs on data.sec.gov, the Latest Filings RSS feed, and the EDGAR Public Dissemination Service for near-real-time needs. The published semi-monthly fails-to-deliver files are public records and trading on them is entirely lawful — this repo already holds the full 2004–2026 archive (425 files) under research/data/ftd/, gathered exactly this way.

practices.practice: Hold the hard line between published public records and staged, embargoed or access-controlled content
practices.detail: Public-record data — EDGAR filings, SRO threshold lists, FTD files, FDA/court/agency dockets, published calendars — is fine to scrape and trade on, however unglamorous the retrieval. What is NOT fine: guessing or enumerating unlinked staging URLs, reverse-engineering an IR back-end to reach a release before publication, diffing sitemaps to find pre-release pages, or racing an embargoed wire feed. Those can constitute unauthorized system access and trading on MNPI. Note that misappropriation/hacking theories reach exactly this conduct even with no insider relationship. This project already applied that filter: the vol-2 idea catalogue documents that eight ideas were removed pre-publication for precisely this reason ('accessing staged or embargoed material ahead of publication can constitute unauthorized system access and trading on material nonpublic information'). Keep that rule; do not reintroduce those ideas. A useful bright-line test: if the publisher would be surprised that you have it yet, stop.

practices.practice: Keep the personal-trading boundary explicit and unbroken
practices.detail: Trading your own capital on public data requires no registration and is not investment advice. The boundary is crossed by three specific acts: managing or pooling other people's money (triggers adviser/fund registration analysis and state rules); receiving compensation for advice about securities; and being paid to promote a security, which triggers the Securities Act Section 17(b) anti-touting disclosure obligation. Note that the Left action shows the SEC will reach a publisher's trading even where he was not a registered adviser. Keep the research repo internally scoped, label outputs as personal research and not advice, and do not accept payment from anyone with a position in a name you cover. Note the existing research files already carry this framing ('These are research hypotheses, not investment advice, and none have been backtested') — retain it.

practices.practice: Set a scaling tripwire for position-reporting obligations before you need it
practices.detail: PARTIALLY UNVERIFIED — the SEC pages 404'd this session. Two thresholds to confirm with counsel before scaling: Form 13F for institutional investment managers exercising discretion over $100 million or more in Section 13(f) securities; and Rule 13f-2 / Form SHO monthly gross short position reporting for institutional investment managers, which I believe uses a $10 million or 2.5%-of-shares-outstanding threshold for reporting-company issuers with filing within 14 calendar days of month end, but I could NOT verify the figures or the current compliance date this session — treat all Form SHO numbers as unverified. A single-trader account is very unlikely to reach these, but a short position of $10M in one micro-cap is not a large book.

practices.practice: Do not count on a public borrow-rate tape arriving soon
practices.detail: VERIFIED from finra.org. FINRA SLATE (Securities Lending and Transparency Engine), the facility implementing SEC Rule 10c-1a and the FINRA Rule 6500 Series for reporting 'Covered Securities Loan' transactions, has a launch date of September 28, 2028, extended from an earlier date after the SEC approved a compliance-date extension. Until then borrow rates remain an opaque, broker-quoted, vendor-priced input. Budget for paid borrow data (S3, Ortex, S&P/IHS Markit) or accept that your borrow-cost assumptions are estimates.

pitfalls.pitfall: Building the account plan around the $25,000 pattern-day-trader minimum — or, having heard it was repealed, assuming your broker has already implemented the change
pitfalls.mitigation: Both errors are live simultaneously right now. The rule change is real and effective June 4, 2026, but the phase-in runs to October 20, 2027 and firms may implement on their own schedule within it. Note also that SEC investor.gov still publishes the OLD regime ('four or more day trades within five business days', '>six percent of the customer's total trades', 'at least $25,000') — I fetched it this session and it is stale. Do not rely on it. Get your broker's current policy in writing, and re-ask each quarter until October 2027.

pitfalls.pitfall: Sizing a sub-$5 short off the proceeds, then getting margin-called on a position that never moved against you much
pitfalls.mitigation: The $2.50/share floor means a cheap short consumes multiples of its own notional. At $0.75/share the maintenance requirement is $2.50/share = 333% of market value. Build the requirement into the position sizer as max(2.50, price) per share for names under $5.00, and max(5.00, 0.30*price) for names at or above $5.00. Refuse the trade if the requirement exceeds your per-name capital budget.

pitfalls.pitfall: Sending a market or marketable-limit short order on a name that has already triggered the Rule 201 circuit breaker
pitfalls.mitigation: Screen every candidate against prior-day close before the open: any name down 10% or more intraday from the prior close is restricted for the rest of that day AND the following day. On restricted names, use limit sell-short orders priced strictly above the current national best bid. Build the check into the order gateway so it cannot be bypassed manually — the two-day span means day-two entries are the common failure.

pitfalls.pitfall: Shorting a chronically dilutive micro cap, then buying the overnight offering at a discount — a textbook Rule 105 violation
pitfalls.mitigation: No intent is required and the SEC pursues these mechanically. Maintain a per-symbol 'last short sale date' field; hard-block any offering participation in a name shorted within the prior five business days. Given the target universe (serial ATM/shelf issuers), the cleanest policy is a blanket ban on participating in follow-on offerings in any name your strategy shorts.

pitfalls.pitfall: Assuming the borrow will be there tomorrow because it was there today
pitfalls.mitigation: Stock loans are callable without notice and hard-to-borrow names in this price band are the most recall-prone. Never structure a trade that requires holding a specific short across a specific date. Where the thesis genuinely needs a fixed horizon, express it with defined-risk long puts instead — options carry no locate requirement, cannot be recalled, and cap the loss at premium, which directly addresses the negative-skew problem.

pitfalls.pitfall: The signature risk of the book — a fat right tail against the short — colliding with the new intraday margin rule to produce a 90-day ban on new shorts
pitfalls.mitigation: This is the compounding failure mode specific to this strategy. A squeeze creates an intraday margin deficit; a pattern of unsatisfied deficits plus one unsatisfied past the fifth business day triggers the (d)(2)(D) freeze on 'creating or increasing a short position or debit balance' for 90 calendar days. Mitigate structurally: hold a cash buffer sized so that a 3-sigma adverse intraday move keeps any deficit inside the de minimis band of min(5% of account equity, $1,000); set hard per-name stops; and satisfy any deficit the same day rather than relying on the 15-business-day expiry or the 5-business-day grace.

pitfalls.pitfall: Publishing a bearish thesis — even informally on X, Reddit or a Substack — while trading around the position
pitfalls.mitigation: The Left action makes clear the SEC will reconstruct your fills against your publications. If you publish at all: state your position and that you may trade it at any time without notice, never state a price target you do not intend to hold to, never accept third-party compensation, and never cover into the readership you just told to sell. The zero-risk configuration for a small trader is to publish nothing while positioned.

pitfalls.pitfall: Treating elevated FTD counts or Reg SHO threshold-list membership as evidence of manipulation and saying so publicly
pitfalls.mitigation: Legally hazardous and empirically wrong. The repo's own fact-checked deep dive documents that FTD data is CNS-netted, semi-monthly, lagged, cannot be attributed to any account, and is roughly 78% ETF operational plumbing; peer-reviewed work (Fotak, Raman & Yadav 2014) associates higher fails with higher liquidity and pricing efficiency, not manipulation. Publishing unproven manipulation accusations against a named issuer or firm invites defamation exposure on top of securities-law risk. Treat every flag as a hypothesis; trade it silently.

pitfalls.pitfall: Routine execution algorithms in thin micro-cap books innocently generating a layering or spoofing fingerprint
pitfalls.mitigation: FINRA 5210 .02 keys on the pattern, and a wide-spread $1 stock with a two-deep book makes the pattern easy to produce by accident. Disable displayed-order laddering on the opposite side of a working position, avoid rapid place-and-cancel inside the NBBO, log cancel-to-execute ratios per symbol per day, and review any symbol-day exceeding a preset ratio.

pitfalls.pitfall: Scraping a regulator or issuer site into a block, a terms-of-service breach, or an MNPI problem
pitfalls.mitigation: Honour the published limits: declare a real User-Agent with a contact email and stay at or under 10 requests/second on sec.gov; prefer bulk index files and data.sec.gov APIs to page-by-page crawling. Never enumerate unlinked or staged URLs, never bypass an access control, never trade an embargoed release. Keep the eight-idea removal precedent from the vol-2 catalogue as a standing rule rather than a one-time cleanup.

pitfalls.pitfall: Reaching for a cash account to sidestep margin constraints, and hitting Regulation T free-riding restrictions instead
pitfalls.mitigation: You cannot sell short in a cash account at all, so this does not help a short-biased book. For the long/event side, selling a security bought with unsettled funds before those funds settle is free-riding and draws a 90-day restriction to settled-funds-only. If you run a cash sleeve, track settled cash explicitly rather than relying on displayed buying power.

pitfalls.pitfall: Assuming listed options are a compliance-free short substitute
pitfalls.mitigation: They do sidestep the locate requirement, recall risk and the $2.50/share short maintenance charge — genuine advantages here. But they do not sidestep Rule 105 (which reaches the short sale, so check the structure), they are not free of the borrow cost (put IV in hard-to-borrow names embeds the loan fee, so you rent the same expense), and structuring deep-ITM buy-writes or married puts to fake a Rule 204 close-out is itself illegal — see the SEC's optionsXpress action and the 2013 OCIE risk alert on options used to reset Reg SHO close-out obligations, both already catalogued in this repo's deep dive.

concrete_specs: FINRA Rule 4210(c)(2), verbatim: short maintenance margin is '$2.50 per share or 100 percent of the current market value, whichever amount is greater' for stock 'selling at less than $5.00 per share'. Worked examples for this universe: short 10,000 shares at $0.75 → proceeds $7,500, maintenance requirement $25,000 (333% of notional). Short 10,000 at $2.00 → proceeds $20,000, requirement $25,000. Short 10,000 at $4.00 → requirement $40,000 (the $2.50 floor is inactive above $2.50; 100% of MV governs).

FINRA Rule 4210(c)(3), verbatim: '$5.00 per share or 30 percent of the current market value, whichever amount is greater' at or above $5.00. The $5.00/share floor binds all the way up to $16.67/share (0.30 × 16.67 = 5.00); above $16.67 the 30% governs. So a $5 stock costs 100% of notional in maintenance margin, a $10 stock 50%, a $16.67 stock 30%.
FINRA Rule 4210(b)(4), verbatim: margin accounts require 'equity of at least $2,000'. This survived the June 2026 amendment and is now the only flat dollar minimum for a regular margin account.

SR-FINRA-2025-017, effective June 4, 2026: eliminates Rule 4210(f)(8)(B) and the day-trading margin language in (b), (f)(10) and (g)(13); establishes new (a)(17)–(a)(19), new (d)(2), and new (g)(1)(J)–(K). Announced in FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10 (Apr 20, 2026); interpretations and investor-education materials in Regulatory Notice 26-11 (May 19, 2026). Phase-in ends October 20, 2027.

Rule 4210(d)(2)(D) de minimis safe harbour, verbatim: you are not 'making a practice' of failing if deficits 'do not exceed the lesser of 5 percent of the equity in the margin account or $1,000'. Concrete sizing rule: for a $60,000 account the binding number is $1,000 (5% = $3,000, so the $1,000 leg is lesser); for a $15,000 account it is $750. Size so a worst-plausible intraday adverse move leaves the deficit under that figure.

Rule 4210(d)(2)(C)(iii): an intraday margin deficit 'shall remain outstanding until satisfied or until immediately after the close of business on the fifteenth business day after the date of the intraday margin deficit'. The 90-day freeze trigger is failure to satisfy 'by the close of business on the fifth business day after it occurs' combined with a practice of not satisfying promptly.

Portfolio margin: the $5 million equity threshold is preserved — accounts below $5 million must margin intraday risk 'substantially similar to' end-of-day margin. Portfolio margin is not a route around the new intraday standard for a small account.

17 CFR 242.201 trigger: a decline of '10% or more' from the prior day's regular-hours closing price, determined by 'the listing market'. Restriction runs 'for the remainder of the day and the following day.' Permitted price: strictly above the current national best bid — trading centres must block execution or display 'at a price that is less than or equal to the current national best bid.' Order-desk rule: on triggered names, short entries are limit-only, priced at NBB + at least one tick.

17 CFR 242.105 restricted period: 'the shorter of the period: (1) Beginning five business days before the pricing of the offered securities and ending with such pricing; or (2) Beginning with the initial filing ... and ending with the pricing.' Applies to firm-commitment offerings. Bona fide purchase exception requires an offsetting regular-hours purchase reported to an effective transaction reporting plan, made after the last short sale and before pricing, with no short sales in the final 30 minutes before the close on the day before pricing.

Reg SHO Rule 204 close-out deadlines: short-sale fails by 'the beginning of regular trading hours on the settlement day following the settlement date'; long sales and bona fide market making by 'the beginning of regular trading hours on the third consecutive settlement day following the settlement date'; 35 calendar days only for 'deemed to own' delayed deliveries (e.g. Rule 144 resale restrictions). Settlement is T+1 as of May 28, 2024. Non-compliance triggers a pre-borrow requirement ('penalty box') for further short sales in that security.

Reg SHO threshold security definition: CNS fails of at least 10,000 shares AND at least 0.5% of shares outstanding for 5 consecutive settlement days. Daily SRO threshold lists are published by NYSE, Nasdaq and Cboe and update far faster than the SEC's semi-monthly FTD file — use the SRO lists for entry timing, the SEC file for confirmation.

SEC EDGAR automated-access rules: declare a User-Agent in the format 'Sample Company Name AdminContact@<sample company domain>.com'; hard ceiling of 10 requests per second; SEC states 'We allow scripted access to sec.gov content.' Bulk alternatives: full-index and daily-index files, Financial Statement Data Sets, RESTful JSON APIs at data.sec.gov (submissions and XBRL 'company facts'), Latest Filings RSS, and the EDGAR Public Dissemination Service for near-real-time.

FINRA Rule 5210 Supplementary Material .02 defines the two prohibited patterns operationally — layering ('multiple limit orders on one side ... enters one or more orders on the opposite side ... that are subsequently executed; and following the execution of the Contra-Side Orders, the party cancels the Displayed Orders') and spoofing ('narrows the spread ... by placing an order inside the national best bid and national best offer ... then executes an order on the opposite side'). Both require occurrence 'in a frequent pattern'. Set an automated per-symbol-per-day cancel-to-execute ratio alert.

SEC v. Andrew Left / Citron Capital (SEC Press Release 2024-89) — the benchmark short-and-distort action: 23 companies, 26 occasions, recommendations that did not match actual positions, average 12% price moves exploited, a stated '$65' target while selling at '$28', undisclosed hedge-fund compensation while claiming independence, $20 million in alleged ill-gotten profits; SEC sought disgorgement, prejudgment interest, civil penalties, an officer-and-director bar and a penny stock bar.

FINRA SLATE (SEC Rule 10c-1a / FINRA Rule 6500 Series) launch date: September 28, 2028, extended from the original date. Participant Reporting Specifications last updated June 27, 2025. No public securities-lending rate tape before then — borrow-cost inputs must come from broker quotes or paid vendors.

Pre-trade compliance checklist to codify in the order gateway, per candidate short: (1) prior-day close vs. current price — Rule 201 triggered today or yesterday? → limit-only above NBB; (2) any short sale in this symbol within the last 5 business days AND any pending firm-commitment offering? → block offering participation (Rule 105); (3) maintenance requirement = shares × max(2.50, price) for price < $5.00, or shares × max(5.00, 0.30 × price) for price ≥ $5.00 — does it fit the per-name capital budget?; (4) locate confirmed and receipt archived; (5) order marked 'short' not 'long' (Rule 200(g)); (6) projected worst-case intraday deficit < min(5% of equity, $1,000).

Stale-source warning to hard-code into research hygiene: SEC investor.gov's 'pattern day trader' glossary page still describes the repealed regime ('four or more day trades within five business days', 'more than six percent of the customer's total trades', 'at least $25,000'). Verified stale this session (2026-08-13). Cite the live FINRA Rule 4210 text and Regulatory Notice 26-10 instead.
costs: Capital cost of a sub-$5 short (VERIFIED, derived from FINRA 4210(c)(2)): short $10,000 notional at $0.75 requires $33,333 of maintenance margin (2.50/0.75 = 3.33x notional). At $1.00 it is 2.5x notional; at $2.00, 1.25x; at $2.50 and above, 1.0x. Practical implication: a $100,000 account can carry roughly $30,000–$40,000 of notional short in sub-$1 names before maintenance margin alone is exhausted — before any buffer for the negative-skew tail.

Capital cost at or above $5 (VERIFIED, derived from FINRA 4210(c)(3)): 100% of notional at $5.00, 50% at $10.00, 30% at $16.67 and above. Shorting a $5.50 stock ties up nearly twice the capital per dollar of notional as shorting a $17 stock.

Reg T initial margin for short sales: 50% of market value, on top of which the FINRA maintenance floors above apply and typically dominate for names under $10. (Reg T 50% is standard and long-settled; not re-verified against the CFR this session.)

Hard-to-borrow financing: the repo's own empirical work on the chronic-fail signal computed a breakeven annualized borrow fee of only 25–55% — and noted that is 'the same order as actual HTB fees' for these names. Treat 25–55%+ annualized as the realistic borrow-cost band for chronically failing sub-$5 names, i.e. roughly 2–5% per month of notional, which alone consumes the measured edge (median −1.08%).

Borrow-fee accrual convention: fees accrue daily on the marked-to-market loan value and are debited monthly; brokers typically apply a collateral markup and a minimum charge. UNVERIFIED — Interactive Brokers' short-sale-cost page returned HTTP 403 this session, so I could not confirm IBKR's specific formula, collateral percentage or minimum. Pull your broker's current schedule directly before modelling.

Per-share locate fees at prime/locate-provider brokers (Cobra Trading, CenterPoint, TradeZero and similar) for hard-to-borrow micro caps. UNVERIFIED — Cobra Trading returned HTTP 403 this session. These are typically quoted per share with a per-locate minimum and are non-refundable if unused, but obtain the current rate card in writing; for a $0.75 stock a per-share locate fee is a very large percentage of notional and can exceed the expected edge outright.
Paid borrow/short-interest data (S3 Partners, Ortex, S&P Global/IHS Markit) is a required input until FINRA SLATE goes live on September 28, 2028. Pricing not verified this session.

Zero-cost inputs, verified available: SEC semi-monthly fails-to-deliver files (full 2004–2026 archive already in research/data/ftd/, 425 files), daily SRO Reg SHO threshold lists from NYSE/Nasdaq/Cboe, FINRA daily short-sale volume files, and EDGAR filings via data.sec.gov — all free, all public record, all lawful to trade on.

execution.topic: Monitoring, decay detection, and kill switches for short-biased and event-driven US small/micro-cap equity strategies

practices.practice: Monitor the MEDIAN trade return as the primary decay statistic, not the mean
practices.detail: With a realistic short-biased P&L distribution (typical winner +2.0% with 4% sd, 7% chance of a squeeze averaging -28%), Monte Carlo (200k draws) gives mean -0.07%, median +1.63%, sd 11.3%, hit rate 64.3%. Detecting 'mean edge has gone to zero' at 80% power needs 2,208-76,290 trades depending on tail frequency — operationally impossible for a small trader. The rolling-50-trade MEDIAN separates cleanly: edge intact gives p5=+0.38%, p50=+1.62%; edge dead (mu=0) gives p50=-0.37%, p95=+0.84%. Tripwire: rolling-50 median < +0.40% = 5% false-alarm-rate decay flag. Log the rolling-50 median daily; the rolling-50 MEAN is useless as a tripwire because even with the edge fully intact its 5th percentile is -3.05%.

practices.practice: Run a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) on trade sign instead of waiting for a fixed-N window
practices.detail: Fixed-N binomial tests are slow: detecting a hit-rate drop from 62% to 50% at alpha=0.05 one-sided, 80% power needs N=103 trades (N=144 at 90% power); 60%->50% needs N=150; 60%->55% needs N=600; 55%->50% needs N=614. An SPRT on the same data flags in a median of 35 trades. Concrete implementation for H0: p=0.64 vs H1: p=0.50 at alpha=0.05, beta=0.20 — maintain a running score S starting at 0; each winning trade adds ln(0.50/0.64) = -0.2469; each losing trade adds ln(0.50/0.36) = +0.3285. Alarm when S >= +2.77 (= ln(0.80/0.05)); reset/declare-healthy when S <= -1.56 (= ln(0.20/0.95)). Simulated performance: 92.7% probability of flagging a genuinely dead strategy, median 35 trades; only 3.8% false-alarm rate on an intact strategy. For a stricter gate (alpha=0.01, beta=0.10) use A=+4.50, B=-2.29: 97.3% power, median 67 trades, 0.7% false alarm.

practices.practice: Run three INDEPENDENT monitors, because no single statistic catches all three failure modes
practices.detail: (1) Central-tendency decay: rolling-50 median + trade-sign SPRT. (2) Tail-regime shift: a separate Bernoulli CUSUM on the count of adverse tail events. (3) Cost drift: EWMA of realized-minus-modeled slippage. Proof they are not redundant: when squeeze frequency doubles from 7% to 14% while the central edge is fully intact, rolling-50 hit rate only falls from 64% to 60% (p5 48%, p95 70%) and rolling-50 median only falls from +1.63% to +1.18% — both monitors miss it entirely — yet the rolling-50 MEAN collapses to a median of -1.98% and you are losing money. Monitors 1 and 2 are blind to each other's failure mode.

practices.practice: Define an adverse-tail-event CUSUM with pre-computed alarm counts
practices.detail: Define a tail event as any single trade whose adverse excursion exceeds 20% of entry notional (choose one definition and freeze it — MFE-against, not just close-to-close). Baseline q0 = your backtested rate; alarm rate q1 = 2*q0. For q0=7%, q1=14%: each tail event adds ln(0.14/0.07)=+0.693, each non-event adds ln(0.86/0.93)=-0.078, boundary +2.77. Pre-computed alarm counts: k>=6 tail events in 20 trades (expected 1.4), k>=7 in 30, k>=9 in 50 (expected 3.5), k>=12 in 80, k>=14 in 100 (expected 7.0). Post these numbers on the wall; the trader should be able to check the tail monitor without a computer.

practices.practice: Reconcile realized vs modeled execution cost on every fill with an EWMA control chart
practices.detail: For each fill record: arrival mid, decision price, fill VWAP, shares, gross commission, exchange fee, clearing fee, regulatory fee, borrow accrual, and route. Compute realized_cost_bps minus modeled_cost_bps and feed to an EWMA with lambda=0.10. Steady-state EWMA sd = per-trade sd * sqrt(0.10/1.90) = 0.229 * per-trade sd. Concrete 3-sigma control limits: per-trade slippage sd of 30 bps -> alarm at +21 bps above model; sd 50 bps -> +34 bps; sd 80 bps -> +55 bps. A cost-side breach without a median-side breach usually means liquidity got worse or you drifted into a worse price bucket — that is a sizing/routing fix, not a kill.

practices.practice: Pull four free daily files before the open and use them as hard-coded regime and eligibility gates
practices.detail: All four verified live on 2026-08-13. (a) SSR/short-sale-circuit-breaker list: https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/symdir/shorthalts/shorthalts{YYYYMMDD}.txt — CSV header Symbol,Security Name,Market Category,Trigger Time. If your name is on it, Rule 201 price test applies today; your short entry can only execute above the NBB, so any backtest assuming marketable short fills is wrong for that name. (b) Reg SHO threshold list: https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/symdir/regsho/nasdaqth{YYYYMMDD}.txt — pipe-delimited, 80 names on 2026-08-12. Threshold membership means elevated buy-in risk. (c) FINRA daily short volume: https://cdn.finra.org/equity/regsho/daily/CNMSshvol{YYYYMMDD}.txt — pipe-delimited, ~12,200 symbols, posted by 6:00 pm ET same day. (d) Live halts: https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/rss.aspx?feed=tradehalts — 50 most recent, ReasonCode LUDP/LUDS = volatility pause, T1 = news pending, T12 = additional info requested, H10 = SEC trading suspension.

practices.practice: Build a squeeze-regime thermometer from the daily SSR trigger count and freeze the percentile bands
practices.detail: Measured live over 25 sessions (2026-07-09 to 2026-08-12): daily SSR trigger count min 448, p25 535, median 593, p75 720, max 1040. Nasdaq Reg SHO threshold list size ranged 55-80 names over the same window. Note the sign: SSR triggers on a 10% DECLINE, so a high SSR count is broad small-cap selling (favourable for shorts). For the squeeze regime you want the opposite tail — count daily LUDP/LUDS halts from the halts RSS and track the count of Russell-microcap names closing up more than 20%. Freeze your bands from a trailing 250-session distribution and reduce gross short exposure by 50% when the upside-halt count exceeds its trailing p90.

practices.practice: Use FINRA short-volume ratio as a crowding flag relative to each name's own trailing baseline, never as an absolute level
practices.detail: Actual CNMS short-volume ratios measured 2026-08-03 to 2026-08-12: BYND 60.5-80.4%, PLUG 41.1-74.5%, CGC 39.2-64.0%, SPCE 46.9-60.1%, GME 58.7-79.8%, MARA 63.9-70.7%, AMC 23.7-38.1%. A 70% reading means nothing in isolation — market-maker hedging is reported as short volume. What is actionable is the deviation: flag when today's ratio exceeds the name's own trailing 20-session median by more than 15 percentage points (e.g. PLUG's jump to 74.5% on 08/10 against a ~48% trailing median), and treat that as a crowding/positioning warning that raises tail risk on the short side.

practices.practice: Pre-commit kill criteria in writing, with a date, before any capital is deployed
practices.detail: The document must specify, per strategy: (1) the exact statistic, (2) the exact threshold, (3) the observation window, (4) the action (halve size / stop new entries / flatten), (5) who can override and on what evidence, (6) the restart criteria. A workable default set for a short-biased small-cap book: HALVE SIZE on any one of {rolling-50 median < +0.40%; SPRT score >= +2.77; EWMA cost breach > 3-sigma}; STOP NEW ENTRIES on any two simultaneously, or on tail-CUSUM alarm; FLATTEN AND STAND DOWN on strategy-level drawdown exceeding the pre-computed p99 of the intact distribution. Sign and date it. The whole value of pre-commitment is destroyed if you write the thresholds after seeing the drawdown.

practices.practice: Calibrate drawdown kill switches against the drawdown distribution of the INTACT strategy, not against intuition
practices.detail: Simulated 250-trade paths at 10% of NAV notional per position with the edge fully intact: max drawdown p50 = 18.0%, p75 = 25.5%, p90 = 32.6%, p95 = 37.2%, p99 = 45.8%. With the edge dead: p50 = 40.0%, p90 = 53.4%, p95 = 57.0%. A naive 20% drawdown kill would fire on more than 40% of perfectly healthy runs, and a 30% kill still fires on ~15%. Either set the drawdown kill at the intact p95-p99 (37-46% here) and rely on the statistical monitors for early warning, or cut position notional. Halving notional to 5% of NAV roughly halves every drawdown percentile and lets you set a tighter, more useful kill.

practices.practice: Size so that no single tail event can trip the kill switch by itself
practices.detail: Simulated single-trade tail returns for this distribution: p2 = -35.8%, p1 = -55.2%, p0.5 = -75.1%, p0.1 = -120.3% (a short can lose more than 100% of notional). At 10% of NAV notional per position, that is a NAV hit of -3.58%, -5.52%, -7.51%, -12.03% respectively. If your stand-down kill is at 25% drawdown, a single p0.1 event consumes half of it. Rule of thumb: set per-position notional so that the p0.5 single-trade outcome consumes no more than 20% of the distance from your current equity to the stand-down level. Cap gross short exposure per theme (e.g. all EV/hydrogen/cannabis names count as one bucket) because squeeze events are correlated within theme.

practices.practice: Forward-test on paper with the full frictions stack for a pre-committed number of trades before risking capital
practices.detail: Minimum forward-test length should be set by the SPRT clear boundary, not by calendar time: run until the SPRT score reaches B = -1.56 (declares the edge consistent with the backtested hit rate) or until 50 trades, whichever is later. That typically requires 40-80 trades. Paper mode must include: (a) IBKR paper account for order mechanics, but (b) an independent shadow ledger that applies the real fee stack, the real borrow rate at the time, SSR eligibility from the shorthalts file, and forced no-fill during any LUDP halt window. IBKR paper trading does not model borrow cost, locate failure, or SSR — a paper P&L that ignores those will overstate a sub-$5 short strategy by 100-300 bps per trade. Require that the paper-vs-model cost EWMA stays inside its 3-sigma limits for the whole forward test before going live.

practices.practice: Stage capital in tranches gated on live-sample milestones
practices.detail: Tranche 1: 25% of target size until 25 live trades. Tranche 2: 50% until 50 live trades AND rolling-50 median above +0.40%. Tranche 3: 100% at 100 live trades AND SPRT score below 0 AND cost EWMA in control. This matters because N=103 is the fixed-N sample needed to detect a 62%->50% hit-rate decay at 80% power — you should not be at full size before you have the sample to know the strategy still works. Every de-gate is one-way per review cycle: you can drop a tranche instantly on an alarm, but you can only add a tranche at a scheduled review.

practices.practice: Treat borrow-fee change as a leading indicator, separate from P&L
practices.detail: Borrow rate is the market's real-time price of short crowding and it moves before your P&L does. Snapshot the indicative borrow rate and shares-available for every name in your universe at 09:00 ET and 15:45 ET daily and store the series. Alarm rules: (a) any name whose fee rate more than doubles day-over-day, (b) any open short whose fee rate exceeds 25%/yr, (c) any name whose shares-available falls below 5x your intended position size. A fee spike plus threshold-list appearance plus rising short-volume ratio is the classic pre-buy-in signature; exit before the recall, not after.

practices.practice: Implement the kill switch as an out-of-process supervisor with its own market-data path
practices.detail: The kill switch must not live inside the strategy process, because the most common real failure is that the strategy process hangs, loses its data feed, or its broker session silently expires. Run a separate supervisor daemon that (1) independently polls broker positions and P&L, (2) has its own price source, (3) has a heartbeat contract with the strategy (strategy writes a timestamp file every 5s; supervisor flattens if the heartbeat is older than 60s during RTH), and (4) can be triggered manually from a phone. Test the kill switch monthly in the paper account by deliberately killing the strategy process and confirming the supervisor flattens within the target window.

practices.practice: Run a fixed review cadence with the agenda pre-written, and separate observation from decision
practices.detail: DAILY (15 min, post-close): pull the four regime files; update SPRT score, rolling-50 median, tail-CUSUM, cost EWMA; check every open short against SSR list, threshold list, borrow-fee alarms; confirm no unreconciled fills. WEEKLY (60 min): realized-vs-modeled cost attribution by price bucket and by route; borrow accrual actuals vs assumed; count of missed/partial fills; list of names that hit LULD pauses while you were in them. MONTHLY (half day): re-estimate hit rate, median, and tail frequency on the trailing 250 trades and compare to the backtest confidence interval; recompute drawdown percentiles; kill-switch fire drill; review whether any kill criterion was breached and overridden, and why. QUARTERLY: full strategy re-validation on out-of-sample data only; explicit go/no-go on continuing each strategy. Never make a size or kill decision outside a scheduled review unless a pre-committed threshold fired — that is the whole point of pre-commitment.

practices.practice: Write restart criteria at the same time as kill criteria
practices.detail: Without restart rules, a kill switch becomes a permanent stop and you lose strategies to noise. A workable restart protocol: after a stand-down, the strategy returns to paper for a minimum of 30 trades; it may restart at 25% size only if (a) the SPRT run on the paper trades reaches the clear boundary B=-1.56, (b) the identified cause is documented and either resolved or shown to be transient (e.g. a rate regime, a specific meme cycle), and (c) the restart is approved at a scheduled review, not intraday. Explicitly forbid re-fitting parameters to the losing period — if the only way to make the strategy work is to change it after the loss, it is a new strategy and needs a full forward test.

practices.practice: Log a fixed per-trade record schema from day one, immutable and append-only
practices.detail: Minimum fields: trade_id, strategy_id, symbol, side, decision_ts, arrival_mid, entry_ts, entry_vwap, shares, exit_ts, exit_vwap, gross_pnl, commission, exchange_fee, clearing_fee, sec_fee, taf, cat_fee, borrow_accrual, net_pnl, net_pnl_pct, mfe, mae, max_adverse_excursion_pct, was_on_ssr_list, was_on_threshold_list, borrow_rate_at_entry, shares_available_at_entry, halted_during_hold (bool), halt_reason_codes, route, order_type, modeled_cost_bps, realized_cost_bps, regime_flags_json. Every monitor in this section is computable from these fields and nothing else. Store as append-only Parquet or SQLite with a write-once constraint; a monitoring system built on a mutable spreadsheet is not a monitoring system.

practices.practice: Correct for multiple testing across monitors and strategies
practices.detail: If you run 4 monitors on each of 5 strategies at a nominal 5% false-alarm rate, the probability of at least one spurious alarm per review period is 1-(0.95)^20 = 64%. Either (a) run the monitors at alpha=0.01 each (SPRT boundary A=+4.50 instead of +2.77), which raises the median trades-to-detect from 35 to 67 but cuts false alarms from 3.8% to 0.7%, or (b) require two independent monitors to breach before any size action, which is the practical default. Never re-run a monitor with a different window length after it fails to alarm — pick the window in advance and keep it.

pitfalls.pitfall: Using mean P&L or a rolling P&L curve as the decay detector on a negatively skewed short book
pitfalls.mitigation: Simulation shows the rolling-50-trade mean has a 5th percentile of -3.05% even when the edge is fully intact — a 'rolling mean below -3%' rule false-alarms 5% of the time, and detecting a true mean edge going to zero requires 2,208-76,290 trades. Use the rolling median (+0.40% tripwire, clean separation between intact and dead) and the trade-sign SPRT as primary detectors, and relegate the mean to the tail monitor's job.

pitfalls.pitfall: Setting the drawdown kill switch at a round number like 20% because it 'feels safe'
