pitfalls.mitigation: At 10% of NAV notional per position over 250 trades, a fully healthy version of this strategy has a median max drawdown of 18.0% and a p90 of 32.6%. A 20% kill would fire on more than 40% of healthy runs. Compute the intact drawdown distribution by bootstrapping your own backtested trade returns before choosing the number; set the kill near the intact p95-p99 and rely on the statistical monitors for the early warning, or cut notional so a tight kill becomes defensible.

pitfalls.pitfall: Placing resting stop-loss orders on shorts in $0.75-$3.00 names and assuming they cap the loss
pitfalls.mitigation: For Tier 2 securities under $3.00 the LULD band is 20% (and for Tier 1 / Tier 2 sub-$3 names: 5% above $3.00, 20% for $0.75-$3.00, lesser of $0.15 or 75% below $0.75), doubled during the last 25 minutes. A stock can move 20% before a limit state, and after 15 seconds in a limit state the primary listing exchange declares a 5-minute pause — during which you cannot cover at all, and the pause can extend another 5 minutes. A buy-stop becomes a market order into a reopening auction. Manage tail risk with position sizing, a hard notional cap, and pre-purchased upside calls where liquid; treat stops as a convenience, not a guarantee.

pitfalls.pitfall: Treating FINRA short interest as a real-time crowding signal
pitfalls.mitigation: Short interest is reported twice monthly, is due at 6:00 pm ET on the second business day after the reporting settlement date, and is not published until the seventh business day after that settlement date — so the data you see is routinely 7-9 business days stale and can be up to three weeks old at the end of a cycle. Use it only for slow structural context. For real-time crowding use borrow-fee changes (intraday), the FINRA daily short-volume ratio (same day by 6:00 pm ET), threshold-list membership, and the LUDP halt count.

pitfalls.pitfall: Confusing FINRA daily short VOLUME with short INTEREST
pitfalls.mitigation: The CNMSshvol file counts every sale marked short, including market-maker hedging and intraday shorts that are flat by the close. Readings of 60-80% are routine for liquid small caps (BYND printed 60.5-80.4% over 2026-08-03 to 08-12) and mean nothing in isolation. Use only the deviation from each name's own trailing 20-session median, with a threshold like +15 percentage points, and never as a standalone entry or exit signal.

pitfalls.pitfall: Backtesting sub-$1 names with a per-share commission model and ignoring percentage-of-value exchange fees
pitfalls.mitigation: Nasdaq charges 0.30% (30 bps) of total dollar volume to remove liquidity in securities priced below $1.00 during regular hours, versus $0.0030 per share for securities at $1.00 and above. Computed all-in one-side cost on ~$6,000 notional at IBKR Pro Tiered taking liquidity: 95.2 bps for a $0.60 stock versus 34.7 bps for a $2.00 stock and 14.0 bps for a $5.00 stock. Round-trip that is roughly 190 bps in the $0.60 bucket — if your edge is a 2% median move, fees alone consume nearly all of it. Model fees per price bucket and re-check the bucket every time the stock crosses $1.00 or $3.00.

pitfalls.pitfall: Building the kill switch inside the strategy process, or assuming the broker API offers a single 'flatten everything' call
pitfalls.mitigation: The IBKR Web API (OpenAPI spec verified live at https://api.ibkr.com/gw/api/v3/api-docs, 169 paths) has NO bulk cancel-all and NO flatten-all endpoint. A kill switch must enumerate GET /v1/api/iserver/account/orders, issue DELETE /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/order/{orderId} per open order, then read GET /v1/api/portfolio/{accountId}/positions/{pageId} and POST /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/orders per position to close. Write it as an idempotent retry loop, run it in a supervisor process with its own data feed and heartbeat timeout, and rehearse it monthly in the paper account.

pitfalls.pitfall: IBKR Web API session silently expiring so the supervisor believes there is nothing to kill
pitfalls.mitigation: The session requires POST /v1/api/tickle to stay alive and GET /v1/api/iserver/auth/status to confirm authentication. Build the supervisor to tickle on a fixed interval well inside the timeout, to check auth/status before every decision cycle, and to treat 'cannot confirm authentication' as an ALARM state that pages you — not as 'no positions found'. A monitoring system that fails silent is worse than none.

pitfalls.pitfall: Paper trading that flatters a short strategy by omitting borrow, locates, SSR and halts
pitfalls.mitigation: IBKR paper accounts do not model borrow cost, locate failure, recall/buy-in, or Rule 201 price-test eligibility. Run a shadow ledger alongside the paper account that charges the real borrow rate daily, blocks entries in names on that morning's shorthalts file unless the model can execute above the NBB, blocks entries where indicative shares-available is under 5x intended size, and forces no-fill during any LUDP halt. Require the paper-vs-model cost EWMA to stay within 3 sigma for the entire forward test before funding.

pitfalls.pitfall: Running many monitors on many strategies and reacting to the first alarm
pitfalls.mitigation: Four monitors across five strategies at a nominal 5% false-alarm rate produces at least one spurious alarm 64% of the time per review period. Either tighten each SPRT to alpha=0.01 (boundary A=+4.50; power 97.3%, false alarm 0.7%, median 67 trades to detect instead of 35), or require two independent monitors to breach before any size action. Log every alarm and its eventual disposition so you can measure your own false-alarm rate empirically.

pitfalls.pitfall: Re-fitting the strategy after a kill so it would have survived the losing period
pitfalls.mitigation: This is the single most common way a small book destroys itself. A parameter change made after observing a loss is a new strategy with zero out-of-sample evidence. Codify it: any parameter change resets the trade counter to zero, sends the strategy back to paper for a minimum of 30 trades, and requires the SPRT clear boundary before restart at 25% size. Keep the original in the log so you can compare.

pitfalls.pitfall: Overriding a pre-committed kill because 'the thesis is still right'
pitfalls.mitigation: Write the override procedure into the pre-commitment document before you need it: overrides require a written, timestamped memo naming the specific falsifiable evidence, are limited to one per strategy per quarter, cannot increase size, and are automatically reviewed at the next monthly meeting with the outcome recorded. If you find yourself overriding more than once, the thresholds are wrong and should be reset at a scheduled review — not intraday.

pitfalls.pitfall: Assuming the borrow will still be there tomorrow, and being bought in at the worst price
pitfalls.mitigation: Reg SHO Rule 204 requires participants to close out fails from short sales by the beginning of regular trading hours on the settlement day following settlement date (T+3 for long-sale and market-maker fails). Threshold securities — fails of 10,000+ shares that are also at least 0.5% of shares outstanding for five consecutive settlement days — carry a 13-day close-out requirement, and once a firm has an aged fail it cannot short that name without a pre-borrow. Check the Nasdaq threshold list every morning (55-80 names on it during 2026-07-09 to 2026-08-12) and treat appearance of a name you are short as a size-reduction trigger, not merely information.

pitfalls.pitfall: Backtests built on survivorship-biased small-cap universes, which systematically inflate short-side edge
pitfalls.mitigation: Delisted, reverse-split and bankrupt tickers are exactly the names a short-biased strategy makes money on, and their absence from a survivorship-biased dataset cuts both ways — it removes the big winners AND removes the reverse-split squeezes. Use a point-in-time universe with delisted securities included, and validate that your historical universe on a given date contains names that no longer trade. Cross-check universe membership counts against a known-good source; if your 2021 universe has no HYZN-style de-SPAC casualties in it, the dataset is unusable for this work.

pitfalls.pitfall: Reacting to regime flags with a binary on/off switch, which maximises whipsaw
pitfalls.mitigation: Regime indicators are noisy: the daily SSR trigger count over 25 sessions ranged 448 to 1040 with a median of 593, so any single-day threshold will flip repeatedly. Use a smoothed input (5-session median of the regime index), require two consecutive sessions beyond the band before acting, and scale exposure continuously (e.g. 100% / 50% / 0% gross) rather than switching between full-on and flat.

pitfalls.pitfall: Never testing the kill switch, so the first live invocation is also the first invocation
pitfalls.mitigation: Schedule a monthly fire drill in the paper account with a written pass/fail: (1) SIGKILL the strategy process and confirm the supervisor flattens within the target window; (2) revoke the broker session and confirm the supervisor raises an ALARM rather than reporting zero positions; (3) trigger the manual kill from a phone; (4) simulate a partial-fill-during-cancel race and confirm the loop is idempotent. Record wall-clock time to flat for each drill and track it.

concrete_specs: SPRT decay detector, H0 p=0.64 vs H1 p=0.50, alpha=0.05/beta=0.20: running score starts at 0; winning trade adds -0.2469; losing trade adds +0.3285; ALARM at score >= +2.77; CLEAR at score <= -1.56. Simulated: 92.7% power, median 35 trades to alarm, 3.8% false-alarm rate.
Stricter SPRT variant for multi-strategy books, alpha=0.01/beta=0.10: ALARM at +4.50, CLEAR at -2.29. 97.3% power, median 67 trades, 0.7% false alarm.

Rolling-50-trade median tripwire: flag decay when the median trade return falls below +0.40%. (Intact distribution: p5=+0.38%, p50=+1.62%, p95=+2.86%. Dead distribution: p5=-1.58%, p50=-0.37%, p95=+0.84%.)

Fixed-N sample sizes, one-sided alpha=0.05, 80% power: 62%->50% hit rate needs N=103; 60%->50% needs N=150; 65%->50% needs N=65; 70%->55% needs N=61; 60%->55% needs N=600; 55%->50% needs N=614. At 90% power: 62%->50% needs N=144, 60%->50% needs N=209.

Adverse-tail CUSUM (tail event = adverse excursion > 20% of entry notional), baseline q0=7% vs alarm q1=14%: increments +0.693 per tail event, -0.078 per non-event, boundary +2.77. Alarm at k>=6 events in 20 trades, k>=7 in 30, k>=9 in 50, k>=12 in 80, k>=14 in 100.
Cost-drift EWMA with lambda=0.10: steady-state sd = 0.229 x per-trade slippage sd. 3-sigma control limits: +21 bps (per-trade sd 30 bps), +34 bps (sd 50), +55 bps (sd 80).

SSR / Rule 201 daily file (verified live): https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/symdir/shorthalts/shorthalts{YYYYMMDD}.txt — CSV, header 'Symbol,Security Name,Market Category,Trigger Time'. Names on it can only be shorted above the National Best Bid for the rest of that day and the following day.

Reg SHO threshold securities list (verified live): https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/dynamic/symdir/regsho/nasdaqth{YYYYMMDD}.txt — pipe-delimited, fields Symbol|Security Name|Market Category|Reg SHO Threshold Flag|Rule 3210|Filler. 80 names on 2026-08-12; range 55-80 over the trailing month.

FINRA consolidated daily short volume (verified live): https://cdn.finra.org/equity/regsho/daily/CNMSshvol{YYYYMMDD}.txt — pipe-delimited Date|Symbol|ShortVolume|ShortExemptVolume|TotalVolume|Market, ~12,200 rows, posted no later than 6:00 pm ET on the trade date. Per-venue variants: FNQC, FNSQ, FNYX, FNRA, FORF.

Live trade halts feed (verified live): https://www.nasdaqtrader.com/rss.aspx?feed=tradehalts — 50 most recent halts with fields HaltDate, HaltTime, IssueSymbol, Market, ReasonCode, ResumptionQuoteTime, ResumptionTradeTime. Codes: LUDP = volatility trading pause, LUDS = volatility pause straddle condition, T1 = news pending, T12 = additional information requested by Nasdaq, H10 = SEC trading suspension, MWC1/2/3 = market-wide circuit breaker levels.

SEC fails-to-deliver files: https://www.sec.gov/files/data/fails-deliver-data/cnsfails{YYYYMM}{a|b}.zip — semimonthly, pipe-delimited (Settlement Date, CUSIP, Symbol, Quantity, Description, Price). Latest available on 2026-08-13 was 202607a, confirming a 2-6 week lag; use for structural context only, never as a live flag.
IBKR Web API OpenAPI spec (verified live, HTTP 200, 169 paths): https://api.ibkr.com/gw/api/v3/api-docs

IBKR kill-switch call sequence: GET /v1/api/iserver/auth/status -> POST /v1/api/tickle (keepalive) -> GET /v1/api/iserver/account/orders -> DELETE /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/order/{orderId} for each live order -> GET /v1/api/portfolio/{accountId}/positions/{pageId} -> POST /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/orders per position. There is NO bulk cancel-all and NO flatten-all endpoint; the loop must be idempotent and retried.

IBKR monitoring endpoints: GET /v1/api/iserver/account/pnl/partitioned (live per-position P&L), GET /v1/api/portfolio/{accountId}/ledger, GET /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/summary/available_funds, GET /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/summary/margins, POST /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/orders/whatif (pre-trade margin check), GET /v1/api/iserver/marketdata/snapshot. Server-side alerts: POST /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/alert, GET /v1/api/iserver/account/{accountId}/alerts.

Supervisor heartbeat contract: strategy writes a UTC timestamp to a heartbeat file every 5 seconds; supervisor cancels all orders and flattens if the heartbeat is older than 60 seconds during 09:30-16:00 ET. Supervisor runs as a separate process with its own market-data connection and its own broker session.

LULD price bands to hard-code in the risk model: Tier 2 above $3.00 = 10%; Tier 1 and Tier 2 below $3.00 = 5% above $3.00, 20% for $0.75-$3.00, lesser of $0.15 or 75% below $0.75. Bands double during the last 25 minutes of the session. A limit state lasting 15 seconds triggers a 5-minute pause, extendable by another 5 minutes.

Rule 201 trigger: 10% intraday decline from the prior day's closing price; the price test applies for the remainder of that day and the following day. Rule 204 close-out: short-sale fails by the start of regular trading hours on the settlement day following settlement date; long-sale and market-maker fails by the third consecutive settlement day. Threshold securities = fails of 10,000+ shares AND at least 0.5% of shares outstanding for five consecutive settlement days, with a 13-day close-out.
Market-wide circuit breakers: Level 1 at a 7% S&P 500 decline, Level 2 at 13%, Level 3 at 20% (close for the day). Wire the MWCB state into the supervisor as an automatic 'no new entries' condition.

Squeeze-regime thermometer baseline measured 2026-07-09 to 2026-08-12 (25 sessions): daily SSR trigger count min 448, p25 535, median 593, p75 720, max 1040; Nasdaq threshold list size 55-80 names. Recompute these percentiles on a trailing 250-session window quarterly.

Short-volume-ratio crowding rule: flag when a name's CNMS ShortVolume/TotalVolume exceeds its own trailing 20-session median by more than 15 percentage points. Observed 2026-08-03 to 08-12: BYND 60.5-80.4%, PLUG 41.1-74.5% (74.5% on 08/10 against a ~48% trailing median), CGC 39.2-64.0%, SPCE 46.9-60.1%, GME 58.7-79.8%, MARA 63.9-70.7%, AMC 23.7-38.1%.

Borrow monitoring: snapshot indicative fee rate and shares-available at 09:00 and 15:45 ET daily. Alarms: fee rate more than doubles day-over-day; any open short with fee above 25%/yr; shares-available below 5x intended position size. IBKR publishes a shortable-securities file at ftp://shortstock:@ftp3.interactivebrokers.com/usa.txt (UNVERIFIED from this environment — FTP was blocked by the network proxy; confirm from your own network. The web-accessible page https://www.interactivebrokers.com/en/index.php?f=4587 returned HTTP 200).

Capital staging gates: 25% of target size to 25 live trades; 50% to 50 live trades AND rolling-50 median > +0.40%; 100% at 100 live trades AND SPRT score < 0 AND cost EWMA in control. De-gating on alarm is immediate; re-gating only at a scheduled review.

Sizing rule derived from the tail: simulated single-trade returns p2 = -35.8%, p1 = -55.2%, p0.5 = -75.1%, p0.1 = -120.3%. At 10% of NAV notional that is -3.58%, -5.52%, -7.51%, -12.03% of NAV. Set per-position notional so the p0.5 outcome consumes no more than 20% of the gap between current equity and the stand-down level.

Drawdown kill calibration (250 trades, 10% NAV notional per position): intact strategy max-DD p50 18.0%, p75 25.5%, p90 32.6%, p95 37.2%, p99 45.8%; dead strategy p50 40.0%, p90 53.4%, p95 57.0%. Set the stand-down kill at the intact p95-p99, or cut notional to 5% of NAV to halve every percentile.

Order-type defaults for sub-$5 shorts: use limit orders pegged to or above the NBB (mandatory when the name is on the SSR list); avoid market orders entirely; use IBKR Fixed pricing rather than Tiered for marketable orders in names under $1.50 because Fixed bundles exchange fees and avoids the 0.30%-of-value Nasdaq removal fee; cap participation at a fixed fraction of the trailing 20-day median volume and record realized participation in the trade log.

Forward-test length rule: run paper until the SPRT reaches the CLEAR boundary (-1.56) or 50 trades, whichever is later — typically 40-80 trades — with a shadow ledger applying real fees, real borrow, SSR eligibility, and forced no-fill during LUDP halts.

Review cadence: DAILY 15 min post-close (pull four regime files, update all four monitors, check open shorts against SSR/threshold/borrow alarms); WEEKLY 60 min (cost attribution by price bucket and route, borrow accruals actual vs assumed, missed-fill count, LULD pause log); MONTHLY half-day (re-estimate hit rate/median/tail frequency on trailing 250 trades, recompute drawdown percentiles, kill-switch fire drill, review overrides); QUARTERLY (out-of-sample re-validation, explicit go/no-go per strategy).

Monthly kill-switch fire drill pass/fail script: (1) SIGKILL the strategy process, confirm supervisor flattens within target; (2) revoke the broker session, confirm supervisor raises ALARM rather than reporting zero positions; (3) trigger manual kill from a phone; (4) simulate a fill landing between the position read and the cancel, confirm the loop is idempotent. Record wall-clock time-to-flat for each drill.

Multiple-testing rule: with 4 monitors x 5 strategies at nominal alpha=0.05 the per-period probability of at least one false alarm is 64%. Either run every SPRT at alpha=0.01 (boundary +4.50) or require two independent monitors to breach before any size change.
costs: SEC Section 31 fee: $20.60 per $1,000,000 of covered sales, effective April 4, 2026, in force until 60 days after the FY2027 appropriation is enacted (SEC Fee Rate Advisory for FY2026, published 2026-02-27). IBKR bills this as 0.0000206 x aggregate sale value. On a $6,000 sale that is $0.12.

FINRA Trading Activity Fee: IBKR's live US pricing page (fetched 2026-08-13) bills $0.000195 per share sold. NOTE A DISCREPANCY — the FINRA Schedule A rulebook page returned $0.000166 per share with an $8.30 per-trade maximum effective 2024-01-01. The rulebook now routes rates to a separate footnoted schedule, so the $0.000166/$8.30 figures may be stale. Use your broker's actual billed rate from statements for cost modelling and re-verify the FINRA schedule before relying on the cap.
FINRA Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) fee as billed by IBKR: $0.000003 per share (includes prospective and historical assessment components; FINRA CAT re-evaluates the prospective fee twice a year).
NSCC/DTC clearing fee as billed by IBKR: $0.00020 per share. Pass-through fees: NYSE = commissions x 0.000175; FINRA = commissions x 0.00056.

IBKR Pro Tiered US equity commission: $0.0035/share for monthly volume up to 300,000 shares; $0.0020 for 300,001-3,000,000; $0.0015 for 3,000,001-20,000,000; $0.0010 for 20,000,001-100,000,000; $0.0005 above 100,000,000. Minimum $0.35 per order, maximum 1% of trade value. Tiers are marginal within a calendar month. Exchange, clearing and regulatory fees are added on top.

IBKR Pro Fixed US equity commission: $0.005/share, minimum $1.00 per order, maximum 1% of trade value, INCLUDING exchange and clearing fees (regulatory fees still added). Worked examples from IBKR: 100 shares at $25 = $1.00; 1,000 shares at $25 = $5.00; 1,000 shares at $0.25 = $2.50.

Nasdaq execution fees: securities priced below $1.00 during regular hours — $0.00 rebate to add, 0.30% (30 bps) of total dollar volume to remove liquidity (pre-market: 5 bps add rebate, 15 bps remove fee). Securities at $1.00 and above — $0.0030 per share to remove liquidity. This is the single largest hidden cost in sub-$1 small-cap trading.

All-in one-side cost, computed from the verified fee stack on ~$6,000 notional, IBKR Pro Tiered while removing liquidity vs IBKR Pro Fixed: $0.60 stock (10,000 sh) = $57.10 / 95.2 bps vs $52.10 / 86.8 bps; $1.50 (4,000 sh) = $27.72 / 46.2 bps vs $20.92 / 34.9 bps; $2.00 (3,000 sh) = $20.82 / 34.7 bps vs $15.72 / 26.2 bps; $3.50 (1,700 sh) = $11.85 / 19.9 bps vs $8.96 / 15.1 bps; $5.00 (1,200 sh) = $8.40 / 14.0 bps vs $6.36 / 10.6 bps. Round-trip is roughly double, before spread and market impact — approximately 190 bps round trip in the $0.60 bucket.

Borrow carry on $6,000 short notional, actual/360: 0.25%/yr = 0.3 bps over 5 days ($0.21), 1.5 bps over 21 days ($0.88); 3%/yr = 4.2 bps / 17.5 bps ($2.50 / $10.50); 15%/yr = 20.8 bps / 87.5 bps ($12.50 / $52.50); 50%/yr = 69.4 bps / 291.7 bps ($41.67 / $175.00); 100%/yr = 138.9 bps / 583.3 bps ($83.33 / $350.00); 300%/yr = 416.7 bps / 1,750 bps ($250 / $1,050). Any short held past ~2 weeks in a name borrowing above 25%/yr is paying more in carry than a typical small-cap edge produces.

IBKR financing rates as published 2026-08-13: margin loans start at 4.13%/yr; credit interest on uninvested cash up to 3.13%/yr. Short-sale proceeds credit varies by borrow difficulty and must be modelled per name, not as a blanket rate.

Market data (Polygon, now branded Massive), non-professional plans: Basic free (end-of-day, 2 years history, 5 API calls/min); Starter $29/mo (15-minute delayed, minute aggregates, WebSockets, flat files, 5 years, unlimited calls); Developer $79/mo (adds historical trades, 10 years); Advanced $199/mo (real-time data plus quotes and financials, 20+ years). 20% discount on annual billing. Add-ons: Financials & Ratios $29/mo, NYSE Order Imbalances $49/mo.

Regulatory and regime data feeds used by the monitors — Nasdaq shorthalts file, Nasdaq Reg SHO threshold list, Nasdaq trade-halts RSS, FINRA daily short volume, SEC fails-to-deliver: $0. All five were fetched successfully and free of charge on 2026-08-13. Budget engineering time, not licence fees, for these.

IBKR paper trading: no charge, but it does NOT model borrow cost, locate failure, recall/buy-in, or Rule 201 price-test eligibility. Budget the engineering cost of a shadow ledger — this is the single highest-value piece of infrastructure for validating a short-biased small-cap strategy before funding.

redteam.target: Chronic-Fail Decay: short cheap single names appearing on >=11 of last ~13 semi-monthly SEC FTD prints, sized by price band, held ~2 weeks (~650-730 names/print, median price ~$1.93)

kill_shots.attack: THE ENTIRE EDGE IS 1-3 CENTS PER SHARE AND LIVES INSIDE THE TICK. I measured the median forward 2-week move in DOLLARS, not percent, on a calendar-matched horizon (non-ETF, 2010+): $0.5-1 band = -$0.0100; $1-2 = -$0.0200; $2-3 = -$0.0300; $3-5 = -$0.0300; $5-10 = -$0.0100; $10-20 = +$0.0100. The celebrated 'monotone in price' gradient — the proponent's single strongest argument that this is economic rather than noise — is arithmetic. Dividing that roughly-constant few-cents drift by the median price of each band reproduces the observed percentages nearly exactly: -1.37% vs actual -2.00%, -1.39% vs -1.33%, -1.22% vs -1.03%, -0.77% vs -0.64%, -0.14% vs -0.11%, +0.07% vs +0.06%. Monotonicity in price is not evidence of an economic effect; it is what ANY constant-cents drift looks like when you divide by price. The proponent has the causality backwards: the effect does not get stronger as stocks get cheaper, the DENOMINATOR gets smaller. And the round-trip cost floor under Rule 612 is one full tick = $0.01. You are attempting to harvest a 1-3 cent median move while paying 1 cent minimum and realistically 2-5 cents in sub-$5 illiquid names. Net P&L at the $1-2 band using MY measured gross (-1.325%): 1c spread + 8%/yr borrow = +0.22%/2wk; 1c spread + 20%/yr borrow = -0.24%; 2c spread = -0.47% to -0.93%; 3c spread = -1.17% to -1.63%/2wk (-30% to -42%/yr). The proponent themselves concedes real spreads are 'typically 1.5-3x wider' than the floors they used. At 2-3 cents — the honest number for a $1.44 stock — the strategy is decisively negative.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Only partially, and not on the numbers as presented. The one legitimate rebuttal is to trade the $2-3/$3-5 bands where the edge is 3 cents against a 1-cent tick, giving a genuine 2:1 gross-to-tick ratio. But the proponent already identified that this is precisely the cell (PLUG-like) with 0.52%/yr borrow — i.e. no short constraint, i.e. no mechanism — and it is also the cell where the percentage edge is smallest (-0.64%) and most easily eaten by realistic 2-cent effective spreads. There is no rebuttal available for the $0.5-1 and $1-2 bands, which carry the headline numbers and most of the universe: a 1-2 cent median edge against a 1-cent minimum tick is unharvestable in principle, not merely in practice.

kill_shots.attack: YOU EARN THE MEAN, NOT THE MEDIAN — AND AT THE PORTFOLIO LEVEL THE MEAN IS NEGATIVE BEFORE ANY COSTS. This is the cleanest kill. I built the actual tradeable object: lag-honest entry (~30 days after the settlement date, respecting the ~1-month publication lag), equal-weight short of every chronic $0.50-5 name, hold ~2 weeks, and I aggregated PER PERIOD rather than pooling observations — because a portfolio earns the cross-sectional mean each period, then compounds those periods. Result across 187 periods, with returns already trimmed at 3x (a generous assumption that throws away real squeezes a live short would eat in full): MEAN SHORT RETURN = -0.170% per period. Median +0.026%. Stdev 3.08%. 92 of 187 periods losing (49%). Worst five periods: -11.0%, -10.8%, -9.3%, -8.5%, -8.3%. That is GROSS — before borrow, spread, or commission. Layering the proponent's own frictions (0.50% borrow, 1c spread on a $1.44 stock, 0.10% commission) gives -1.46%/2wk = approximately -38%/yr; at a realistic 2c spread, -56%/yr. Note also the divergence between pooled and per-period aggregation: pooled trimmed-at-3x gives the short +0.447%/2wk, but per-period gives -0.170%. That gap is diagnostic — the pooled 'edge' is concentrated in periods containing unusually many cheap chronic names, i.e. post-crash regimes. It is a regime/beta bet wearing the costume of cross-sectional alpha. Untrimmed, the chronic cohort's mean forward return is +7.25% (lag-honest +8.61%), so an untrimmed equal-weight short loses over 7% per two weeks.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: No — not with this dataset. The only escape is that the positive mean is contaminated by unadjusted reverse splits (see the price-adjustment kill shot), and a split-adjusted rebuild could plausibly flip the per-period mean positive. But that is a hypothesis requiring new data, not a rebuttal. As it stands, the single number that determines whether capital compounds — the per-period equal-weight short portfolio mean — is NEGATIVE gross of all costs. The proponent never computed it; they reported a pooled median, which is not a P&L.

kill_shots.attack: THE EXPECTANCY'S SIGN IS NOT IDENTIFIABLE FROM THIS DATA — THE PRICE FIELD IS UNADJUSTED. The SEC FTD file's price column is a raw prior-day close with no split or dividend adjustment. Sub-$5 chronic failers reverse-split constantly (that is what a chronic failer IS — a serially diluting microcap doing 1-for-10s to hold a listing). An unadjusted 1-for-10 reverse split reads as +900%. I confirmed the damage: max observed 2-week 'return' = +899,900%; p99.9 = +588%; 0.405% of observations exceed +2x in two weeks and 0.130% exceed +5x. The mean's sign flips on an arbitrary trimming parameter that touches under 0.6% of the data — trim at 1.5x: short earns +1.43%; at 2x: +0.84%; at 3x: +0.58%; at 5x: +0.35%; at 10x: -0.16%; at 25x: -0.79%; untrimmed: -7.25%. The right tail is an inseparable mixture of genuine squeezes (catastrophic for a short, real money lost) and reverse splits (economically neutral for an adjusted short). Nothing in this file distinguishes them, because there is no share-count, no CUSIP-change tracking, and no corporate-action feed. Any strategy whose expectancy changes sign on a trimming choice is not a strategy — it is an unresolved measurement.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, but only by replacing the data source entirely. Rebuild on CRSP or a split-adjusted vendor (Polygon, Norgate, Sharadar) with point-in-time CUSIP-to-ticker mapping and explicit delisting returns. This is a genuine and answerable question — and it is the single highest-value piece of work available, because a split-adjusted mean could plausibly come out negative and revive the thesis. Until that rebuild exists, no expectancy claim from this dataset is admissible in either direction.

kill_shots.attack: THE MECHANISM IS SELF-REFUTING: WHERE THE CONSTRAINT BINDS THE FEE EATS THE EDGE; WHERE THE FEE IS CHEAP THERE IS NO CONSTRAINT. The proponent invokes Miller (1977) overvaluation under binding short-sale constraints, confirmed by Boehme, Danielsen & Sorescu (JFQA 2006). That theory REQUIRES the constraint to bind. But the proponent's own verified IB borrow table shows the tradeable names are not constrained at all: PLUG 0.52%/yr, SPCE 2.76%, VUZI 2.98%. A stock you can borrow for 52 basis points a year is, by definition, not short-sale constrained — Miller predicts NO overvaluation there, so the observed decline in that cell needs a different explanation, and 'different explanation' means the mechanism story has been abandoned. Conversely, where the constraint genuinely binds — BYND at 35.87%/yr = 1.38%/2wk — the borrow fee alone exceeds the entire $1-2 band gross median edge of 1.325%. This is not an accident; it is the equilibrium. The securities-lending market prices the constraint, and the fee IS the anomaly's price. This is the central finding of D'Avolio (2002), Geczy, Musto & Reed (2002), Jones & Lamont (2002), and Beneish, Lee & Nichols (2015): short-side abnormal returns in high-constraint names are approximately fully consumed by loan fees, which is exactly what a competitive lending market should produce. The proponent has rediscovered the shorting premium and mistaken the rent paid to lenders for profit available to borrowers.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: No. This is a structural argument and the proponent's own friction table supplies the evidence against them. The only surviving space is names that are cheap to borrow AND persistently overpriced — but that combination is precisely what an efficient lending market eliminates, and the proponent has offered no reason such a pocket should persist for 17 years while being visible in free public SEC data.

kill_shots.attack: N IS INFLATED BY ROUGHLY TWO ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE; EVERY IMPLIED T-STAT IS FICTION. The claimed N=264,834 (I reproduce 1,008,493 on my wider window) is not a count of independent observations. The FTD file has one row per SETTLEMENT DATE, and a chronic failer appears nearly every trading day — I measured 168 overlapping daily rows per distinct symbol, across only 6,006 distinct symbols. Each row spawns a 2-week forward return that overlaps the next 9 rows' windows almost completely. De-overlapping to one observation per name per month collapses N from 1,008,493 to 80,032 across 6,006 names; de-overlapping in time leaves ~187 independent periods. Worse, within any period the names are not independent either — they are all optionable busted-growth microcaps (PLUG, BYND, CGC, SPCE, HYZN) loading on one common factor, which is exactly why my worst periods cluster at -11%. Correcting for overlap in the time dimension alone deflates t-statistics by roughly sqrt(168) ~ 13x. The honest inference unit is the 187-period portfolio return series, whose mean is -0.170% with a 3.08% standard deviation — a t-stat of about -0.76, i.e. indistinguishable from zero and pointing the wrong way.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partially. Proper inference (one obs per name per month, standard errors double-clustered by date and by name, Newey-West on the period series) is straightforward and should simply be run. The pattern may well survive as a statistically real tendency — my de-overlapped median is still -1.282% with 54.0% down, and 64.9% of individual names have a negative median. What cannot survive is the rhetorical use of 'N=264,834' to imply precision. The effective sample is ~187 periods of one correlated factor bet.

kill_shots.attack: THE MATCHED CONTROL IS NOT MATCHED, AND ITS 'FLAT 0.00%' IS A QUANTIZATION ARTIFACT. Two independent failures. (a) Differential survivorship in the control: 98.9% of chronic observations have a forward price in the file versus only 71.7% of fresh observations. The fresh cohort's forward return is therefore conditional on the name REAPPEARING on the FTD file within 10-24 days — that is, conditional on it continuing to fail, which selects precisely the fresh names that are turning chronic. The control is contaminated toward the treatment on a 72% subsample. (b) The 'flat 0.00% in every band' is not a finding, it is tick quantization: the fresh cohort's median 2-week move is exactly $0.00 — zero cents. A statistic quantized to zero cannot demonstrate the absence of a 1-3 cent effect; it lacks the resolution to detect one. I confirmed this is not simple staleness (only 4.0% of chronic and 5.6% of fresh rows have pf exactly equal to price). And the cohorts are not comparable animals on any dimension besides price: 6,093 vs 17,365 distinct symbols, median fails 5,282 vs 778 shares, median fail notional $10,591 vs $1,288. Matching on price alone while the groups differ 4x in fail size, 7x in notional, and completely in float, liquidity, dilution history, and short interest is not a control — it is one covariate out of a dozen.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, and it should be done: build a genuine propensity- or characteristic-matched control (price, market cap, float, ADV, short interest, borrow fee, dilution/shelf activity) drawn from ALL cheap stocks, not just from stocks already on the FTD file. My within-price-vigintile test does show the chronic-minus-fresh spread persisting at every price level from $0.55 to $4.81 (-0.4% to -2.7%), so the effect is not purely a price proxy. But the control as constructed cannot bear the weight the proponent places on it.

kill_shots.attack: THE TRUE COUNTERFACTUAL IS ABSENT — THIS IS PROBABLY THE LOW-PRICE/DISTRESS/DILUTION ANOMALY WITH AN FTD LABEL. The FTD file contains only stocks that fail. The proper counterfactual for 'chronic cheap failers decline ~1.1% per two weeks' is not 'cheap stocks that failed once' — it is ALL cheap stocks. Sub-$5 US microcaps engaged in continuous ATM and shelf dilution have a well-documented negative drift of approximately this magnitude, and it is over-determined by known factors: the lottery-preference anomaly (Kumar 2009), financial distress (Campbell, Hilscher & Szilagyi 2008), and in Fama-French terms these names are the extreme corner of low profitability and high asset growth — asset growth driven mechanically by share issuance. A chronically-failing sub-$2 stock is the canonical serial diluter, and serial diluters go down because share count goes up. Nothing in this dataset can distinguish 'chronic FTD predicts decline' from 'chronic FTD is a marker for the perpetually-diluting microcap, and all perpetually-diluting microcaps decline.' If the latter, the signal is a redundant and stale proxy for characteristics available in real time from any fundamentals feed, and the return is documented risk compensation concentrated in exactly the segment where it cannot be collected net of costs.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, and this is a decisive and cheap test: regress forward returns on chronic-FTD status alongside price level, market cap, short interest as a percentage of float, live borrow fee, trailing share-count growth, and trailing momentum. If chronic-FTD's marginal coefficient is insignificant after controls — which I would bet on given that my dose-response shows the effect saturating at 61-80 fail-days and REVERSING at 101+ — the signal is redundant and should be discarded in favor of its cheaper components.

kill_shots.attack: THE SIGNAL IS A STALE, LOW-RESOLUTION PROXY FOR TWO THINGS THE PROPONENT ALREADY HAS LIVE. FTD status is published on a ~1-month lag, is a cumulative-open snapshot rather than a flow, is aggregated across all participants, and carries no attribution of cause — it cannot separate abusive naked shorting from benign market-making, operational, or long fails. What it actually marks is a persistent hard-to-borrow / heavily-shorted state. Both of those are observable in real time, at higher resolution, with no lag: the borrow fee (which the proponent pulled from live IB data to build their own friction table) and short interest as a percentage of float. The proponent has therefore already demonstrated they possess the strictly superior signal and are using it only to compute costs. If the tradeable content of 'chronic FTD' is 'expensive/scarce to borrow and cheap,' then rank on the live fee — it updates daily instead of monthly, it is continuous instead of a binary 11-of-13 count, and it is not contaminated by ETF creation/redemption mechanics or CUSIP staleness. The proponent's own supporting evidence confirms this reading: Stratmann & Welborn find returns proportional to FTD LEVELS, and their short-seller profitability result is computed net of proprietary borrow-cost data — which is to say the profit accrues to whoever already knows the borrow cost, not to whoever reads the SEC file a month late.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Only by winning the horse race described above. If chronic-FTD adds nothing to a live borrow-fee-plus-short-interest ranking, there is no reason to build this pipeline at all. My prior is that it adds nothing, because the lag structure means FTD can only ever be a noisy month-old shadow of the fee.

kill_shots.attack: NEGATIVE SKEW IS FATAL TO COMPOUNDING, AND THE UNIVERSE IS THE MEME-SQUEEZE POPULATION BY CONSTRUCTION. The distribution is exactly the wrong shape for a short: 53.6% down (barely better than a coin flip), median -1.14%, but mean +7.25%, p95 +21.8%, and 0.405% of two-week observations exceeding +2x with 0.130% exceeding +5x. On a short, a +5x is -400% on that position. In an equal-weight book of ~700 names at 1/700 each, a single +900% name costs 1.3% of the entire book in one position — and these events are not independent, they cluster (my worst period was -11.0% with returns already trimmed at 3x). Against a per-period gross mean of -0.170% and a per-period standard deviation of 3.08%, the Kelly fraction is negative: there is no size at which this compounds, because there is no positive expectancy to size into. And the universe selection makes it worse rather than better. The proponent presents it as reassuring that the watchlist is 'NOT obscure shells' but well-known OPTIONABLE busted-growth names — PLUG, BYND, CGC, SPCE, HYZN. That is precisely the population that produced January 2021. Optionable + heavily shorted + cheap + retail-recognizable + chronically hard to borrow is the exact screen a coordinated squeeze runs. The proponent's 'reassurance' is an inventory of the most dangerous possible shorts, and a short's loss is unbounded.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partially mitigable, never eliminable. Put-spread expression caps the tail — but these names carry 80-150% implied volatility precisely because of this tail, and the option premium is the market charging you for the same skew, which converts a 1-3 cent edge into a certain loss. Hard stops do not work either: these names gap 50-100% overnight on offering news, reverse splits, and social-media coordination, so stops execute far below the trigger. Position limits and heavy diversification reduce single-name blowups but cannot address correlated cohort-wide squeezes, which is where my -11% periods came from.

kill_shots.attack: CAPACITY IS BOUNDED BY THE VERY SCARCITY THAT DEFINES THE SIGNAL, AND YOU ARE THE MARGINAL SHORT, NOT THE FIRST. By construction the chronic cohort is the set of names where borrow is already persistently scarce and short interest is already elevated — typically 20-40% of float in this population. You are not early to the trade; you are the 701st short in a crowd that has already bid the borrow fee to its clearing level. The proponent's own data undercuts the flow story: median fail notional is roughly $5,000-10,600 (I measure $10,591 for the chronic cohort), which confirms fails are a MARKER of state rather than a forced-buying flow — so there is no buy-in pressure to trade against and no informational content beyond 'still hard to borrow,' a fact the lending market already publishes. Practical capacity: at a $1.44 median price with 2-5 cent spreads and thin ADV, a $10M equal-weight book across 700 names is ~$14k per name, which sounds harmless until you need to exit 700 illiquid microcap shorts inside two weeks in a rising tape. Recall risk compounds it — hard-to-borrow shares get called away at the worst moment, forcing buy-ins at the top of exactly the squeeze you are trying to survive.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, in the narrow sense that capacity constraints are survivable if you accept a small book — run $2-5M, concentrate in the 20-50 most liquid optionable names, accept ~$100k of annual gross P&L in the best case. But that reframes the strategy honestly: it is not an institutional allocation, it is a hobby-scale trade whose best realistic outcome is a few percent on a small book while carrying unbounded left-tail risk. The crowding point stands regardless — persistent scarcity means the trade is already fully discovered.

kill_shots.attack: THE CITED LITERATURE DOES NOT SAY WHAT IT IS BEING USED TO SAY. Three misreadings. (1) Boehme, Danielsen & Sorescu (2006) find overvaluation only at the INTERSECTION of binding short-sale constraints AND high opinion dispersion — it is a conditional, two-variable result, and the proponent has measured neither variable, substituting FTD presence as a proxy for the first and nothing at all for the second. (2) Stratmann & Welborn (2016) find returns proportional to FTD LEVELS, which is a continuous dose measure; the proposed strategy uses a binary 11-of-13 presence count that discards level information entirely, so it is not implementing the cited result. Their short-seller profitability finding is explicitly net of PROPRIETARY borrow-cost data, i.e. it accrues to participants who observe borrow costs directly — the securities-lending desks — not to someone reading a public file on a one-month lag. (3) Miller (1977) is a static overvaluation argument about price levels, not a prediction of a persistent tradeable two-week drift; converting a level effect into a repeatable calendar-timed return requires that the overvaluation be continuously replenished, which the proponent asserts but never demonstrates. Separately, the year-by-year evidence is weaker than presented: I reproduce 13 of 17 negative years, but 2010, 2013, and 2016 are flat at exactly 0.000% (quantization again, not signal), and 2022 — the year busted-growth collapsed hardest, when the thesis should have paid most — shows a POSITIVE spread of +0.196%. The chronic edge vanished in precisely the regime it was supposed to own, which points to a beta story rather than an alpha.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partially. The literature genuinely does establish that FTD-heavy and constrained stocks underperform — that much is not in dispute and I reproduce it. What the literature does NOT establish is that this is harvestable net of borrow and spread by an outside participant using lagged public data, and the papers cited are in several cases evidence for the opposite conclusion.

redteam.survives:
NO — the strategy does not survive in its proposed form. It fails at the portfolio level before a single dollar of cost is applied.

WHAT I CONFIRMED IN ITS FAVOR (I attacked the data, not a strawman): the pattern is REAL and reproducible. I first found that this repo's own existing retraction is itself invalid — it "corrected" the forward return to the actual next FTD print, but chronic names print nearly daily (median gap = 1 day), so the retraction measured ONE-DAY returns and unsurprisingly got 0.000%. Rebuilding on a genuine calendar-matched 10-24 day horizon, the proponent's numbers reproduce closely: chronic median -1.14%, by band -2.00%/-1.33%/-1.03%/-0.64%/-0.11%/+0.06% versus their claimed -1.92%/-1.35%/-0.95%/-0.46%/0.00%/+0.10%; monotone dose-response (0-20 fail-days: 0.000%, 21-40: -0.276%, 41-60: -0.952%, 61-80: -1.235%, 81-100: -1.242%); 13 of 17 negative years; and 64.9% of individual names carry a negative median. This is a genuine, persistent, cross-sectionally broad tendency. That is why it is dangerous — it will pass every check the proponent knows how to run.

WHY IT IS STILL NOT MONEY — three findings, any one sufficient:
1. THE EDGE IS 1-3 CENTS PER SHARE. Median 2-week move in dollars: -$0.01, -$0.02, -$0.03, -$0.03, -$0.01, +$0.01 across the six bands. The "monotone in price" gradient — the proponent's flagship evidence of economic reality — is arithmetic, not economics: it is a near-constant cents drift divided by a shrinking price, and cents/price reproduces the observed percentages to within a few basis points. The Rule 612 minimum tick is $0.01. You cannot harvest a 1-3 cent median move while crossing a spread that is 1 cent at absolute best and 2-5 cents in reality.
2. THE PORTFOLIO MEAN IS NEGATIVE GROSS. The tradeable object — lag-honest entry, equal-weight short, aggregated per period as a portfolio actually compounds — returns MEAN -0.170% per period across 187 periods, stdev 3.08%, 49% losing periods, worst -11.0%, with returns already trimmed at 3x. Before borrow, spread, and commission. The proponent reported a pooled median, which is not a P&L. After their own frictions: roughly -38%/yr at a 1-cent spread, -56%/yr at 2 cents.
3. THE SIGN IS NOT IDENTIFIABLE. The FTD price field is unadjusted; reverse splits and genuine squeezes are inseparable in the right tail (max +899,900%), and the mean flips sign on a trimming parameter touching under 0.6% of observations.

FOR THE STRATEGY TO WORK AT ALL, ALL SIX MUST BE TRUE:
(1) A split-adjusted rebuild with delisting returns must show the PER-PERIOD equal-weight short portfolio mean — not the pooled median — is reliably negative for the underlying, i.e. positive for the short, by a margin exceeding 1.5%/2wk. My unadjusted measurement says -0.170% the wrong way, so this requires the reverse-split contamination hypothesis to be both true and large.
(2) Realistic effective spreads measured from live NBBO/TAQ must be under ~1 cent in the traded names, which restricts you to the $2-5 optionable tier and abandons the $0.5-2 bands carrying the headline numbers.
(3) Chronic-FTD must retain an independently significant coefficient after controlling for live borrow fee, short interest as a percentage of float, price level, market cap, share-count growth, and momentum. If it does not, trade the borrow fee directly and discard the FTD pipeline entirely.
(4) The borrow must be simultaneously CHEAP (under ~5%/yr, or the fee eats the edge) and the name must be genuinely SHORT-CONSTRAINED (or Miller's mechanism does not apply). These two conditions are in direct contradiction under any functioning securities-lending market — the proponent must explain why this pocket persists for 17 years in free public data.
(5) The left tail must be capped by a structure whose cost is below the surviving edge. Given 0.13% of observations exceed +5x in two weeks and these names carry 80-150% IV, put spreads almost certainly cost more than the 1-3 cent edge is worth.
(6) Inference must be redone on the ~187 independent periods with clustered standard errors, not the fictitious N=264,834, and must still clear t > 2.

My assessment: conditions (4) and (5) are close to logically self-contradicting, and (1) is a coin flip pending data the analyst does not have. DO NOT ALLOCATE CAPITAL. The correct next step is a $0 desk-research horse race against live borrow fee and short interest — if chronic-FTD loses that race, which I expect, the entire line of inquiry closes for the price of an afternoon.
redteam.required_evidence:
SIX TESTS, IN STRICT COST ORDER — STOP AT THE FIRST FAILURE.

TEST 0 (free, do this first, kills the idea fastest): THE HORSE RACE. Pooled cross-sectional regression of forward 2-week returns on chronic-FTD status ALONGSIDE live borrow fee, short interest as a percentage of float, price level, log market cap, trailing 6-month share-count growth, and trailing 2-week and 12-month momentum. Standard errors double-clustered by date and by name. DECISION RULE: if chronic-FTD's marginal t-stat is below 2 after controls, the signal is a redundant lagged proxy — kill the project and trade the borrow fee directly if you want this exposure at all. I expect this to fail, and it costs one afternoon.

TEST 1: SPLIT-ADJUSTED REBUILD. Replace the FTD price field entirely with CRSP or a split-adjusted vendor (Polygon, Norgate, Sharadar), joined on point-in-time CUSIP-to-ticker mapping, with explicit delisting returns. Report the untrimmed per-period equal-weight short portfolio mean. DECISION RULE: if that mean is not reliably positive for the short with t > 2 on the ~187-period series, stop. Additionally decompose the 51% two-year attrition into go-to-zero/delisted (short wins), reverse-split (neutral once adjusted), and acquired-or-uplisted (short loses) — the proponent has never established which dominates, and it determines the sign.

TEST 2: EDGE IN CENTS VERSUS EFFECTIVE SPREAD IN CENTS. Abandon percentage framing entirely; it is what produced the false monotonicity. For each candidate name pull the time-weighted effective spread from TAQ or a live NBBO capture (NOT the Rule 612 floor). DECISION RULE: require median edge in cents > 2x effective spread in cents, per name, before it enters the book. On my numbers this admits almost nothing below $2.

TEST 3: CORRECTED INFERENCE. One observation per name per month; the portfolio return series as the unit of inference; Newey-West on the period series; report effective N and the t-stat on the per-period mean. Retire the N=264,834 figure — the real figure is ~187 correlated periods over ~6,000 names.

TEST 4: FACTOR ATTRIBUTION. Regress the per-period short portfolio return on market, size, value, momentum, profitability, investment, betting-against-beta, and a low-price/lottery factor. DECISION RULE: if alpha is insignificant, this is documented risk compensation and not an edge. Pay specific attention to 2022, where the spread went POSITIVE (+0.196%) in the regime the thesis should have owned — that is a beta signature.

TEST 5: LIVE TCA, PAPER OR MINIMUM SIZE. 20-50 names, two quarters, real fills. Measure realized slippage versus arrival mid, borrow fee ACTUALLY charged (not the advertised indicative rate), recall and buy-in events, and short-sale locate failures. DECISION RULE: if realized round-trip cost exceeds 1.0%/2wk — and I expect 1.5-3% — the strategy is dead regardless of every prior test passing.

ONE LOOSE END WORTH CLOSING: my analysis inherited the proponent's ETF exclusion via description-string matching and the symbol-based (not CUSIP-based) join, which the repo README explicitly warns is unreliable across corporate actions. A CUSIP-keyed rebuild should be part of Test 1 and could move the numbers in either direction.

Reconstruction validated three ways: shift-0 alignment minimizes basis vol 2.4x vs +/-1 day; implied BND NAV on 3/12/2020 = 85.67 (matches published); calm-period basis sd = 0.11-0.41%. 34,304 fund-days, 2008-2026. kill_shots.attack: THE CONVERGENCE NEVER STARTED UNTIL THE FED DID. This is the shot that kills it. Using a genuine ex-ante rule (enter the day AFTER the first premium < -1% print, i.e. 3/13/2020, the earliest date the signal was knowable and actionable), and exiting 3/20/2020 -- the last close before the 3/23 SMCCF/QE-infinity announcement -- across all nine exact-NAV pairs: mean unhedged -5.83%, mean worst mark-to-market -7.68%, and critically the PERFECTLY HEDGED BASIS was -1.72%. Fund by fund the pre-Fed hedged basis: BLV -3.76%, VTEB -3.57%, VCIT -3.49%, VCSH -2.64%, BNDX -1.14%, BSV -0.86%, VWOB -0.53%, BND +0.02%, VMBS +0.48%. Read that again: even an unconstrained arbitrageur who could short NAV in-kind was LOSING on the basis for the six sessions after the signal fired. The basis widened, it did not converge. Measured to the Fed announcement day the hedged basis is +0.16% (i.e. zero); measured 2.5 weeks past the announcement it is +2.36%. 100% of the arbitrage profit in the canonical case study arrives in the sessions immediately following a discretionary central-bank credit backstop. The proponent's own framing concedes this ('you are effectively short the option that the backstop never comes') but then prices that option at zero. The mechanism being traded is not 'APs eventually redeem in kind'; it is 'the Fed eventually buys corporate bonds.' That is an unpriced, unhedgeable, non-recurring political bet.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Weak rebuttal only. You can argue (a) the Fed put is now the reaction function, so future episodes get backstopped faster -- but that argument simultaneously destroys the trade, because a faster backstop means the discount never gets wide enough to enter (see the post-2020 drought: zero signals in 2022, 2023, 2025); and (b) with an infinite holding period you eventually got paid in both 2008 and 2020 -- true, but then the horizon is months, the position is indistinguishable from long credit beta at wide spreads, and the NAV-discount signal is doing no work. There is no version of the rebuttal in which the discount itself, rather than the policy response, is the source of return.

kill_shots.attack: EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZE IS 1, NOT 20 OR 55. Across 34,304 fund-days spanning 2008-2026 and nine funds, the signal (premium < -1%) fires on 146 fund-days = 0.426% of the time, and those days cluster into essentially TWO calendar weeks: October 2008 (14 fund-days) and March 2020 (70 fund-days), plus a structural-artifact cluster in one EM fund. The proponent's '5 ETFs x 4 dates = 20 observations' and my own '55 signal days' are not 20 or 55 draws -- they are one draw, re-counted. The date list is also not ex ante: the reported expectancy swings from -7.88% to -2.07% depending purely on whether 3/18 and 3/19 are included, i.e. a six-percentage-point swing produced by a two-day discretionary choice inside a window already known to contain the bottom. Any strategy whose measured expectancy is that sensitive to date selection inside a single event has no estimable expectancy at all. Standard errors on all of these numbers are meaningless because the observations are ~100% cross-sectionally correlated (mean pairwise correlation of daily premium across the nine funds during March 2020 = 0.48, and the sign is identical on every fund every day).
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: No meaningful rebuttal. Adding 2008 raises N from 1 to 2, and 2008 is contaminated identically -- BND's only two signal days are 10/9-10/10/2008, immediately before the 10/13 G7 weekend and the TARP capital injections. You cannot manufacture more crises. The only honest reframing is to stop calling it a strategy and call it a contingency plan for an event that has occurred twice in twenty years.

kill_shots.attack: THE PROFITABLE FORM REQUIRES SHORTING NAV, WHICH IS EXACTLY THE THING RETAIL CANNOT DO -- AND EVERY RETAIL SUBSTITUTE IS A COIN FLIP WITH A FAT LEFT TAIL. The proponent's own strongest evidence (Pan & Zeng) describes an AP-balance-sheet constraint. The trade that monetizes that constraint is long ETF / short NAV, executed via in-kind redemption. My data confirms that leg is where the entire risk-adjusted quality lives: post-Fed hedged basis is +2.36% mean, positive in 100% of fund-horizon cells at H=10 and H=20, worst case +0.13%. Strip the hedge and the SAME trade has 5-day price sigma of 5.3-8.1% in the stress window, i.e. the entire theoretical edge is under half of one standard deviation of five-day noise (information ratio per trade < 0.5). I tested the only hedge retail actually has -- long the widest-discount bond ETF, short the narrowest sister bond ETF, rebalanced daily through March 2020: mean +0.98% at H=5, hit rate 50%, worst single outcome -12.09%. That is a coin flip that pays you 1% for a 12% tail. The reason is arithmetic: all nine funds discount together (corr 0.48, all negative simultaneously), so a sister-ETF short cancels most of the discount you are trying to buy while retaining full basis-divergence risk.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partial rebuttal available for an institution, none for retail. An institution with AP access, or with CDX HY / Treasury futures / a cash-bond basket, can construct a real hedge and the +2.4% post-Fed basis is genuinely earnable -- that is the strategy Citadel/Jane Street/the APs themselves actually ran. But that is a different strategy run by a different entity with different capital. For a small trader the honest statement is: the part of the trade with a real edge is the part you cannot execute, and the part you can execute is unhedged long credit beta into a crash.

kill_shots.attack: THE SIGNAL IS NOT PERSISTENT, AND IT IS PUBLISHED AFTER YOU CAN ACT ON IT. The proponent's thesis explicitly says 'wide, PERSISTENT discount.' It is not persistent. Exact measurement of BND: -0.52% (3/10), -1.81% (3/11), -6.24% (3/12), -1.76% (3/13), -1.61% (3/16). The headline dislocation existed for one session. Same for VTEB: -0.59%, -3.97%, -0.91%, -2.42%, -2.41%, -7.23%, -9.23%, -4.70%, -1.08%. Across all funds, of days with premium < -2%, the mean next-day premium has already recovered by 100-150bp. The operational problem this creates is decisive: NAV strikes at 4:00pm and the official premium/discount is published after ~6pm, so the earliest you can act on an observed discount is the next session's open -- and the mean absolute overnight gap in these names during 3/9-3/25/2020 was 2.15% (LQD) and 2.50% (HYG) versus 0.13-0.17% in calm 2019, with individual gaps of -5.47% (LQD 3/16), -5.52% (HYG 3/12), -5.62% (EMB 3/16), -5.11% (BKLN 3/19). The overnight gap alone is larger than the entire hedged edge. The signal you can observe is not the signal you can trade.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, partially -- you can trade off real-time iNAV / IIV or a self-computed basket estimate intraday rather than the published 4pm premium. But this converts the trade from 'read a published number' into 'run a live bond-basket pricing engine during the worst liquidity conditions in a decade,' which is precisely the capability whose absence defines a retail participant. And the published-premium series -- the thing the entire backtest is built from -- is then no longer the signal being traded, so the backtest has to be thrown out and redone on intraday data that was never collected.

kill_shots.attack: THE GAP LARGELY CLOSES BY NAV FALLING TO THE PRICE, NOT PRICE RISING TO NAV -- SO THE 'DISCOUNT' IS SUBSTANTIALLY A MEASUREMENT ARTIFACT, NOT A MISPRICING. Decomposing the first five days after a < -1.5% signal: VCIT ETF price +0.37% while NAV fell -2.62% (88% of the gap closure came from the NAV marking down); VCSH price +0.50% while NAV fell -2.16% (81% from NAV). Bond ETF NAVs are struck off evaluated/matrix prices from third-party pricing services against a market where the underlying bonds are barely trading; the ETF is the price-discovery venue and the NAV is the stale number. A buyer of the ETF who 'waits for convergence' gets converged INTO. This also explains the strategy's worst structural feature: the asset classes with the widest discounts are exactly the ones with the stalest marks -- bank loans (T+20 settlement, averaged dealer quotes), munis (thin, dealer-quoted), EM (foreign-close pricing). The signal's magnitude is proportional to the measurement error, not to the opportunity. Direct proof: VWOB (EM) is the ONLY fund of nine that still generates signals post-2020 -- 14 days below -1% in 2021-2025 -- and those chronic discounts do not converge at all. Forward 10-day unhedged return -0.61%, forward hedged basis +0.04%. A persistent discount in a stale-marked fund produces exactly zero. Discount does not equal mispricing.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partial. In March 2020 some of the discount was genuinely liquidity-driven rather than stale marks -- the hedged basis did eventually turn positive (+2.4%), which cannot happen if the discount were purely a marking artifact. So the honest split is: part measurement error (converges by NAV falling, worth nothing), part real liquidity premium (converges by price rising, worth ~2-4%, but only post-backstop). The strategy has no way to tell the two apart ex ante, and the VWOB evidence shows the pure-artifact case is the one that recurs.

kill_shots.attack: THE 'EDGE' IS A TEXTBOOK COMPENSATED RISK PREMIUM, NOT AN ANOMALY -- SPECIFICALLY THE LIQUIDITY-PROVISION PREMIUM, AND YOU ARE BUYING IT AT ITS POINT OF MAXIMUM BETA. The proponent's own economic case ('forced sellers pay a large premium for immediacy while natural buyers are constrained') IS the definition of a risk premium, stated in the language of an anomaly. This is the fixed-income version of Nagel's 'Evaporating Liquidity': short-term reversal returns are compensation for supplying liquidity, they scale with VIX, and they are earned precisely when supplying liquidity is most dangerous. It is also a direct long position in Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity beta -- an asset that falls most when market-wide liquidity evaporates, which is compensated in equilibrium. And it is a first cousin of the closed-end fund discount literature (Lee-Shleifer-Thaler), where discounts are persistent and are not free money. The payoff profile is functionally short-volatility: many small nickels, occasional -12% to -18% intraday marks (verified: LQD -15.26%, HYG -16.48%, BKLN -17.78%, EMB -16.94%, MUB -12.71% worst intraday marks within 10 days of the ex-ante entry dates). Calling this 'arbitrage' rather than 'selling crash insurance in the bond market' is the entire trick.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes -- and it is the proponent's best available rebuttal. 'Compensated risk premium' is not the same as 'zero expected return.' The liquidity-provision premium is real and positive in expectation; that is why it exists. But accepting the rebuttal reframes the trade honestly: it is a beta, it is highly correlated with every other risk asset you own, it pays off contingent on survival through the drawdown, and it should be sized and priced like selling insurance -- not treated as a mechanical convergence with an AP-enforced backstop. It also means it cannot be levered, and it means the correct benchmark is 'buy credit at wide spreads,' not zero.

kill_shots.attack: SURVIVORSHIP AND SELECTION IN THE MEASUREMENT ITSELF (the analog of your FTD-file attrition point). Every number in the proponent's case is computed on five mega-cap ETFs that (a) still exist in 2026, (b) still publish premium/discount history on the issuer's product page, and (c) were selected BECAUSE their March 2020 discounts became famous. The premium/discount histories the backtest is built from are hosted only for live funds; a fund that closed has no product page. The products that actually carried the widest 2020 dislocations were levered/inverse credit vehicles -- the UBS ETRACS 2x series (MORL, BDCL and siblings) and Credit Suisse VelocityShares ETNs -- several of which were force-accelerated or delisted in and around March 2020 at catastrophic values, delivering permanent loss with zero convergence. [Flagged: this specific product list is from recall; I could not verify it in this session because the web-search budget was exhausted. It must be checked before it is relied on.] The structural point does not depend on the specific tickers: a screen for 'widest discount to NAV' is mechanically a screen for the smallest, most levered, most stale-marked, most closure-prone vehicles, which is precisely the population that a survivor-only forward-return calculation cannot see. On top of that, the 'four dates identifiable ex ante' were chosen from a window already known to contain the bottom, and my check of the proponent's own facts found the dates are wrong: BND's -6.2% discount occurred on 3/12/2020, not 3/16 (on 3/16 BND was only -1.61%), and an AGG proxy puts the -4.4% print on 3/18, not 3/16. The date list appears to be a worst-of scan across dates, presented as a same-day snapshot.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Partially rebuttable by restricting the universe ex ante to funds above some AUM/age threshold and excluding all ETNs and levered products -- which is defensible and would have kept you out of the products that died. But it does not repair the deeper problem: after that restriction you are left with the handful of mega-cap funds whose discounts are the SMALLEST and whose NAVs are the least stale, i.e. you have deliberately screened out the entire population where the proponent claims the edge is largest. The factual date errors are individually manageable but they materially change the entry set and indicate the case was assembled from headline figures rather than from a reconstructed series.

kill_shots.attack: TIME IN MARKET IS 0.4%, AND THE SIGNAL HAS NOT FIRED ONCE IN SIX YEARS DESPITE THREE MAJOR STRESS EPISODES. Signal live on 146 of 34,304 fund-days. Since July 2020, across eight of the nine exact-NAV pairs, the number of days with a discount worse than -1% is ZERO. Worst premium since July 2020: BND -0.86%, BLV -0.72%, BNDX -0.65%, BSV -0.60%, VCIT -0.54%, VTEB -0.51%, VCSH -0.47%, VMBS -0.41%. That window contains the worst bond bear market in modern history (2022), the March 2023 regional-bank failures, and the April 2025 tariff shock -- VTEB's worst print during April 2025 was -0.51% and VMBS's was -0.41%. Even taking the proponent's most favourable numbers at face value, a single-fund trader gets roughly one trade per decade at a gross of a few percent: an annualized portfolio contribution somewhere between 0.0% and 0.3%, in exchange for permanently maintaining the infrastructure, the monitoring, and -- fatally -- the dry powder. The opportunity cost of holding cash for nine years to deploy it in one week dominates every other term in the P&L.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Weak. You can argue the capital is not idle -- run it as an overlay on an existing bond allocation and only rotate at the signal. That is legitimate and is the ONLY sensible framing, but it reduces the strategy to a rebalancing rule, and rebalancing rules have to be judged against the trivial alternative (rebalance on credit spread level or on drawdown), which requires no NAV data at all. The zero-signals-since-2020 result also has a nasty causal reading: post-2020 dealers and the Fed both know the playbook, so the dislocation now compresses in hours. The trade may have been arbitraged out of existence by its own discovery.

kill_shots.attack: THE NEGATIVE SKEW IS FATAL TO COMPOUNDING BECAUSE THE LOSS ARRIVES WHEN YOUR FUNDING IS WORST AND YOUR OTHER ASSETS ARE DOWN. Verified path risk on the proponent's own five ETFs at the ex-ante entry dates: worst intraday marks within 10 days of -15.3% (LQD), -16.5% (HYG), -17.8% (BKLN), -16.9% (EMB), -12.7% (MUB). Those marks occur in the same week SPY was down ~30% from highs, i.e. at the exact moment a leveraged or margined trader faces house-call liquidation and a discretionary trader faces the strongest psychological pressure to exit. The strategy's defining feature is that its entry signal is a systemic-stress indicator, so its drawdown correlation with everything else in the book is ~1 by construction. There is no diversification, no ability to average down with borrowed money, and a forced exit at the -12% mark converts the one profitable decade-scale opportunity into a permanent loss. Kelly sizing on a distribution with ~1 opportunity per decade, an unknowable success probability conditional on policy, and a -18% tail is approximately zero.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, mechanically: size it small, use no leverage, use cash-secured entries, scale in over the discount path rather than at a point, and accept the drawdown as the price of the premium. That converts it from a strategy into a small, unlevered, opportunistic allocation -- which is defensible. But small-and-unlevered plus once-a-decade plus a few percent gross equals an edge that rounds to nothing at the portfolio level, which is the same conclusion by a different road.

kill_shots.attack: THE SIGNAL IS PARTLY REDUNDANT WITH FREE, CHEAPER PROXIES -- AND WHERE IT IS NOT REDUNDANT, THE NON-REDUNDANT PART IS ONE WEEK OF DATA. Pooled test across all nine funds: forward returns after premium < -1.5% are f5 +1.54% / f10 +4.05% / f20 +6.51% (n=55). Forward returns after a simple 5-day drawdown < -3% -- requiring NO NAV data whatsoever -- are f5 +0.35% / f10 +0.90% / f20 +1.49% (n=267). A dip WITHOUT a discount gives f5 +0.16% / f20 +0.07%, i.e. nothing. So the NAV discount is genuinely doing work beyond 'buy the dip.' I state that honestly because it is the proponent's single best empirical defence. But the 'discount without a dip' cell has n=7, and essentially all 55 signal days come from March 2020 and October 2008 -- so the incremental information content of the NAV discount over free price-based signals is established on one week of data. Meanwhile the cheaper proxies (HY OAS level, VIX, credit ETF drawdown, the Treasury on-the-run/off-the-run basis) are free, real-time, available intraday, and were all screaming on the same days.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes -- this is the attack the proponent survives best. The discount does contain information a price-dip filter does not (+1.54% vs +0.16% at 5 days). The correct response is not to deny it but to note that the incremental signal is (a) estimated on effectively one event, (b) only observable after the close, and (c) worth roughly 1-2% at a 5-day horizon against 5-8% of 5-day noise. It is a real but tiny and unmeasurable-precision refinement to a beta timing decision, not a standalone edge.

kill_shots.attack: FRICTIONS -- honest assessment, and the one axis where the proponent is largely RIGHT and the attack partially fails. On the mega-cap names the frictions do not eat the edge: LQD/HYG stressed spreads stayed in the single-digit-bp to ~25bp round-trip range, commissions are zero, and against a +2.4% post-Fed hedged basis or a +4-6% 10-day unhedged move the transaction costs are second-order. Where frictions DO bind: (a) the small, illiquid funds where the discount is widest -- stressed spreads of 50-150bp round trip are a reasonable estimate and I could not verify them, and those funds are also where the fill is a fiction rather than a quote; (b) the overnight gap risk quantified above (mean |gap| 2.15-2.50% for LQD/HYG in the stress window), which is not a 'friction' in the spread sense but is the dominant execution cost and dwarfs everything else; (c) taxes and short-term treatment on a days-to-weeks holding period; (d) for any hedged version, the financing and borrow on the short leg during a funding crisis, which is exactly when repo and borrow are dearest. The correct conclusion is that frictions are NOT what kills this trade -- which matters, because it means fixing execution does not save it. The trade dies on policy dependence, sample size, and the unhedgeable NAV leg.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Yes, and the proponent should win this one on the mega-caps. Conceding it is important for the integrity of the overall verdict: a red team that claims every axis is fatal is not credible. Frictions are manageable in LQD/HYG/BND-scale funds and serious-to-prohibitive in the small funds where the signal is largest, which is itself an adverse-selection problem -- the edge and the executability are inversely related, exactly as in the Autore-style threshold-stock result.

kill_shots.attack: CAPACITY AND CROWDING -- inverted from the usual failure mode, and worse for it. Raw capacity is a non-issue: LQD and HYG traded billions of dollars a day through March 2020, so a small trader's size is irrelevant. That fact is itself the indictment. If a genuinely positive-expectancy, mechanically-converging arbitrage existed in a $2-4bn/day instrument, with a documented mechanism, observed by every credit desk on the street, and the gap persisted for six trading sessions anyway, then the binding constraint is not capital or information -- it is balance sheet, in-kind access, and willingness to hold through a -12% mark. A small trader relieves none of those constraints and therefore has no reason to be paid for them. The proponent's own citation makes this argument for me: Pan & Zeng's finding is that the arbitrage fails because APs' dealer balance sheets are constrained. Nothing in that mechanism creates a rent for a share buyer with no balance sheet role. Post-2020 crowding then finishes the job: the Fed's revealed reaction function is now common knowledge, so the marginal buyer arrives faster, which is exactly what the zero-signals-since-2020 result shows.
kill_shots.rebuttal_possible: Limited. The 'someone with unconstrained capital should step in' intuition is correct and is precisely why the discount closed -- but the entities that stepped in were the Fed and the APs, not price-taking share buyers. A share buyer is a passenger on the convergence, not a cause of it, and captures it only if the convergence happens in price space rather than NAV space (see the NAV-markdown attack). The one honest rebuttal is that a passenger who buys and does not get shaken out DID get paid in both 2008 and 2020 -- which is a statement about surviving beta, not about capturing arbitrage.

redteam.survives:
VERDICT: It does not survive as a strategy. It survives, barely, as a once-a-decade opportunistic allocation rule with a low-single-digit expected payoff that a portfolio will not notice — and only for an operator who satisfies a demanding conjunction of conditions.

WHAT IS REAL (do not overstate the kill): the basis is genuinely measurable and genuinely dislocated — I reproduced March-2020 discounts of -6.24% (BND), -9.23% (VTEB muni), -7.61% (VWOB EM), -6.72% (VCSH) against exact same-fund NAVs, versus a calm-market basis sd of 0.11-0.41%. That is a 15-30 sigma event and it is not a data error. A perfectly hedged arbitrageur entering 3/13/2020 and holding to mid-April earned +2.36% mean basis, positive in 100% of fund-horizon cells at 10 and 20 days. And the discount signal does carry information beyond a free price-dip filter (+1.54% vs +0.16% forward 5-day). The proponent is right that something real is there.

WHAT KILLS IT: the something-real accrues to the NAV-short leg and to a policy event, neither of which a small trader owns. Pre-Fed, the hedged basis was -1.72% and the unhedged trade was -5.83% with a -7.68% mean worst mark. The trade did not converge; it was rescued.

FOR THE STRATEGY TO WORK AT ALL, EVERY ONE OF THESE MUST BE TRUE:
1. You can short the NAV leg for real — AP in-kind redemption access, or a genuine hedge (cash-bond basket, CDX HY, Treasury futures) that you can execute and finance during a funding crisis. Sister-ETF hedging does not count: it is a 50% hit rate with a -12.09% worst case, because all bond ETFs discount together (cross-fund premium corr 0.48).
2. You are trading intraday off a live iNAV/basket estimate, not the published 4pm premium. The published number arrives after 6pm and the mean overnight gap in the stress window was 2.15-2.50%, larger than the entire edge. The discount is a one-session spike (BND: -0.52% → -6.24% → -1.76% over three closes), not a persistent state.
3. A policy backstop arrives inside your holding window, OR your capital is genuinely permanent and can hold for months through a -12% to -18% intraday mark with no leverage, no margin, and no competing claim on it — in the same week every other asset you own is down 30%.
4. You accept that ~0.4% time-in-market means one trade per decade per fund, that the signal has not fired once at eight of nine funds since July 2020 despite 2022, March 2023 and April 2025, and that the annualized portfolio contribution is therefore 0.0-0.3%/yr before opportunity cost of the dry powder.
5. You restrict the universe ex ante to large, old, unlevered, non-ETN funds — which deliberately excludes the population where the discounts are widest, and therefore caps the edge at the small end of the observed range.
6. You classify the position honestly as a liquidity-provision risk premium (Nagel-style, Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity beta) and size it as insurance-selling, not as arbitrage. If you size it as arbitrage you will lever it, and leverage plus a -18% mark plus a systemic-stress entry trigger is a terminal combination.
7. You can distinguish, ex ante, a liquidity discount (converges by price rising) from a stale-mark discount (converges by NAV falling, worth zero). Currently nobody in this case has proposed a way to do that, and the one fund that still generates chronic signals — VWOB, EM, foreign-close pricing — delivers exactly nothing: -0.61% forward 10-day unhedged, +0.04% basis over 14 post-2020 episodes.

If any of 1, 2, 3 or 6 fails — and for a retail trader 1 and 2 fail by definition — the trade reduces to buying credit beta into the fourth day of a crash with a -8% to -12% five-day expectancy, which is exactly what the proponent measured and exactly what my independent, ex-ante-rule reconstruction confirms.
redteam.required_evidence:
The single test that would settle it: DOES THE BASIS CONVERGE ABSENT A POLICY BACKSTOP? Everything hinges on this and both available episodes (Oct 2008, Mar 2020) are contaminated — BND's only 2008 signal days are 10/9-10/10, immediately before the G7 weekend and TARP capital injections; the entire 2020 profit lands after 3/23. Concretely:
1. Assemble non-US and non-backstopped bond-ETF stress episodes where no central bank bought credit — European/UK/Japanese credit and EMD ETFs in Mar 2020, the Sept-Oct 2022 gilt/LDI crisis (BoE bought gilts but NOT credit), Chinese property-credit funds 2021-22, EM local-currency funds in 2013 taper and 2018. Measure hedged basis convergence with the same exact-NAV or iNAV method. If the basis converges there too, the proponent's mechanism survives and the trade is real for a hedged operator. If it does not, the mechanism is 'the Fed', and the strategy is a policy bet.
2. Intraday tick data: real-time iNAV/IIV versus traded price, 1-minute bars, March 2020, for LQD/HYG/MUB/EMB/BKLN.
