verdictSummary.strategy: Create-to-Lend Borrow-Fee Harvest on XRT-type "hard-to-borrow" ETFs: buy and hold a persistently high-short-interest sector ETF, enroll the shares in a retail fully-paid lending program (IBKR SYEP / Fidelity FPL / Schwab SLFP), hedge the market exposure, and harvest the cost-to-borrow as net carry.
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH — and higher than I am normally willing to be on a rejection, for three specific reasons.

1. THE CORE RESULT IS ALGEBRAIC, NOT STATISTICAL. It requires no backtest, no sample period, and no distributional assumption. An options-hedged lender earns rf − borrow × (1 − split × util). For any positive borrow fee and any split below 100%, that is strictly less than rf. There is no parameter choice — no borrow fee, no utilization rate, no volatility regime — that flips the sign. This is not "the edge is probably too small"; it is "the edge has the wrong sign by construction." I stress-tested it at 50% and 60% splits and at 25%, 50% and 100% utilization; all nine combinations lose to T-bills before costs.

2. THE FACTUAL PREMISE IS DIRECTLY FALSIFIED BY OBSERVED DATA, NOT INFERENCE. The strategy is predicated on XRT being persistently hard to borrow with a high sustained fee. The measured fee is 1.07% with 500,000 shares freely available (ChartExchange/IBKR, 2026-08-12). Even at the peak of the 2021 meme-stock episode, S3's Ihor Dusaniwsky publicly noted XRT at 2.32% — cheaper to short than GME at 1.70%. The premise is not merely optimistic; it is inverted, and the academic literature explains why: XRT is the "short favorite" that intermediates most shorting AT LOW FEES, which is exactly why its short interest is 568% of float.

3. I VERIFIED THE HEDGE-PRICING CLAIM EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. Rather than asserting that options price the borrow, I pulled live CBOE quotes and inverted put-call parity across every liquid strike with a proper dividend schedule. Implied borrow came out at 0.79%, 1.11%, 1.43% and 1.57% against a 1.07% quoted cash fee. The options market has it right to within the bid-ask. That closes the only loophole through which this trade could have worked.

CALIBRATION AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND. My confidence is in the VERDICT, not in every input. Three numbers I could not verify and have flagged rather than fabricated: XRT-specific realized SYEP utilization (no broker publishes it; IBKR's own pages returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt, so all IBKR program terms here come from secondary sources and IBKR's own guides subdomain rather than the primary pricing page); IBKR's wholesale lending rate versus the 1.07% retail short charge; and the paywalled long-run XRT fee history. Critically, all three uncertainties push the conclusion in the SAME direction — the wholesale rate is typically below the retail short charge, and lower utilization means less income — so resolving them can only make the trade worse.

I would revisit only on a genuinely different setup: a lender split above 100% (does not exist), an ETF where option-implied borrow sits materially BELOW the achievable lending rate (I found the opposite), or AP status enabling real create-to-lend with full fee capture and redemption optionality. None is available to a small trader. This same failure mode — a dramatic surface statistic (568% short interest) that is a mechanical artifact rather than evidence of scarcity — is precisely the pattern the analyst's FTD work already identified. Recommend declining without further work.

verdictSummary.strategy: Illiquid-Underlying ETF NAV-Discount Convergence — buying HY/muni/bank-loan/EM bond ETFs when they trade at a wide, persistent discount to NAV during market stress, on the thesis that APs will eventually arbitrage the gap closed (March 2020 as case study).
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that the verdict is LIKELY-ILLUSORY, for a small trader or small fund.

Reasons for high confidence: (a) The direct empirical test is unambiguous and I computed it myself from raw price data — 95% of identifiable wide-discount entries lost money over 5 days, averaging -7.88%, in the single most favorable episode that has ever existed for this trade. A strategy that fails on its own best case study does not require further testing. (b) The structural barriers (no create/redeem, no way to short NAV) are absolute, not matters of degree, and they are independent of any statistical question. (c) The cost stack alone kills it: I verified live option quotes of 12-30% of mid on HYG and 30-200% on LQD, versus an average crisis signal of 1.0-1.4%, using BlackRock's own numbers. (d) The revealed preference of the APs — the only parties who could do the real arbitrage, who had every incentive, and who passed for two weeks — independently confirms the discount was compensation for risk rather than mispricing. Four independent lines of evidence converge on the same answer.

Reasons it is not stated as certainty: (a) My forward-return test is effectively one event across correlated instruments; overlapping windows on five funds in one crisis is closer to n=1 than n=30, and I have not run a multi-decade panel of daily premium/discount data — I attempted to obtain iShares' historical premium/discount series and the SEC/BIS underlying data and could not retrieve machine-readable history. (b) I could not verify March 2020 borrow rates, March 2020 option bid-ask widths, or the VXHYG implied-vol path (the index returned no time series), so the hedge cost is inferred from realized vol (50-58% annualized) rather than from observed IV prints. (c) I could not verify April 2025 tariff-shock discount magnitudes, which would be the cleanest test of decay.

Notably, every one of these gaps concerns evidence that would make the strategy look WORSE, not better — stressed borrow and stressed option spreads are strictly higher than the calm-market figures I used, so my cost stack is conservative. The verdict would only flip on evidence that discounts systematically predict positive risk-adjusted forward returns at identifiable entries, and I found the opposite.

I would upgrade to NO-EDGE if given a full daily premium/discount panel confirming no predictive power out of sample; the reason I stop at LIKELY-ILLUSORY is that a genuine liquidity risk premium does exist here — it is simply earned by balance sheet, and unavailable to the trader in question.

verdictSummary.strategy: Daily Short-Volume Reversal using FINRA's free daily short-sale volume file (short heavily short-sold names, buy lightly short-sold names), gated by an SEC fails-to-deliver (FTD) filter, motivated by Diether–Lee–Werner (2009, RFS 22:2).
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH that there is no exploitable net-of-cost edge here for a small trader or small fund, for four converging reasons that do not depend on each other.

(a) The originating paper's own cost arithmetic is negative: 1.39%/month gross versus 2.7%/month execution cost, stated by DLW in the published text, in the best-case 2005 sample, on price>=$5 stocks, using exchange-marked tick data superior to anything public today.
(b) The specific horizon this strategy trades has a direct, peer-reviewed null result in the public-data era — Wang-Yan-Zheng (JFE 2020): "abnormal short-term shorting flows do not predict future returns or anticipate bad news."
(c) My own measurement of the current file shows the cross-sectional dispersion that a sort would exploit is a liquidity artifact — ratio IQR falls monotonically from 0.661 in sub-1k-share names to 0.171 in >10M-share names, 75.6% of variance is within-name daily noise, and the extreme deciles have ~1/12th the volume of the median name.
(d) The gate makes it worse, not better: only ~5 names/day pass both filters, at median $1.47/share where the 170% margin rule, Rule 201, absent options, and deep-special borrow all apply simultaneously.

MEDIUM on the precise magnitude of the negative expectancy, because I could not run an independent return backtest (no free price feed reachable through the proxy) and could not verify current per-name borrow fees or per-market-cap effective spreads with an authoritative source. My spread figures lean on a 2014 SEC study of 2013 data, and my borrow-fee framing leans on D'Avolio (2002) plus a vendor aggregate whose methodology I could not check. Those uncertainties affect how negative the answer is, not its sign.

LOW confidence only on one sub-question: whether the correct sign is negative or actively inverted. SqueezeMetrics' commercial DIX product asserts high short volume proxies BUYING, with intraday returns uniformly positive above a 35% ratio — but that is a vendor white paper, not peer-reviewed, and I did not independently verify it. Either way it argues against the trade as specified; it just changes whether the strategy is dead or backwards.

Recommendation: do not put this on the book. If any variant is worth further work, it is the slow one Wang-Yan-Zheng actually validated — long-horizon accumulated shorting flow with a one-year decay — which is a low-turnover signal in liquid names, is essentially a proxy for short interest, and is already sold by multiple vendors. The daily-reversal-plus-FTD-gate construction should be retired for the same reason the analyst retired naive FTD spikes: it is a sort on noise in names too small to trade.

verdictSummary.strategy: Section 103(k) Coal Tripwire — monitor MSHA Section 103(k) accident/control orders on msha.gov and short the affected US-listed coal issuer (HCC, AMR, BTU, METC) into the expected production disruption.
verdictSummary.confidence: HIGH — and unusually so for a rejection, because this was settled by direct measurement rather than by argument. I downloaded and parsed the complete MSHA violations census (3,092,333 rows, file dated 2026-08-07), isolated all 14,142 Section 103(k) orders since 2000, mapped 324 of them to mines controlled by HCC/AMR/BTU/METC since 2019, and ran the event study against XME-adjusted daily returns. The decisive facts are measurements, not inferences: issue-day relative volume 0.87-1.12x, issue-day |return| at or below unconditional baseline for two of four names, full-sample drift wrong-signed at +2.40% over five days, post-2021 drift +0.07%. Publication latency is verified from the file itself (weekly Friday refresh, 84 rows on the most recent weekday vs a ~300-600/day steady state, zero rows on the file date). Borrow fees and option quotes are live vendor data, not estimates. Two independent peer-reviewed studies concur, and the Long View / Centurion case studies show the material events are either private-company or non-MSHA. Residual uncertainties, stated plainly: (a) equity bid-ask is a Corwin-Schultz proxy, not a live NBBO quote — it is the softest number in the stack, though even a 5bp spread does not rescue a zero-to-negative gross signal; (b) ScienceDirect returned 403, so the 155bp/140bp Christensen et al. figure comes from a search-result summary of the article page and is not verified from the paper itself — the 2021 Resources Policy finding is likewise from summary, though it is directionally corroborated by my own measurement; (c) the concentrated sub-case (mine-wide 103(k) at a mine >40% of volumes) is under-powered at N=27 and I label its expectancy unknowable rather than zero. None of those caveats moves the verdict. This is the same failure mode as the naive FTD spike signal: a real, well-documented public dataset with a plausible causal story, no abnormal volume or return at the event, and a positive-looking t-statistic that dissolves into calendar clustering the moment you cut it by year. The chronic-persistence lesson applies here too — if anything survives in MSHA data it will be a slow, structural, cross-sectional quality signal (chronic violation intensity as a proxy for operational deterioration or cost inflation, held over quarters), not a same-week event tripwire. Working files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-WireAntennaGain/82dc742b-08fa-562e-9653-7f5ab2131e39/scratchpad/ — Violations.zip (raw MSHA census), k_rows.json (14,249 extracted 103(k) records), parse.py, an2.py, an3.py, an4.py (base rates, durations, controller mapping), event.py and final.py (event study and robustness), spread.py (Corwin-Schultz), opt.py (option chains and IV), ib_*.json (IBKR borrow history), px_*.json (daily prices).

verdictSummary.strategy: Warehouse Amendment Wire: monitor mid-quarter 8-K/exhibit amendments to warehouse/repo credit facilities at nonbank originators (UWMC, RKT, COOP, PFSI, CACC, OMF) for capacity reductions, advance-rate cuts, or lender exits; trade the issuer short via equity or 2-8 week puts.
verdictSummary.confidence:
HIGH — that no exploitable edge exists in the direction specified. My confidence is tiered by how each finding was established, and the load-bearing findings are the mechanical ones, which are not estimates:

NEAR-CERTAIN (direct measurement, no modeling, large or complete samples):
- 0 of 62 warehouse/facility Item-1.01 8-Ks were filed during market hours; 97% post-close (16:01-17:01 ET), 3% pre-open. Read directly from EDGAR acceptance timestamps. This alone voids the latency premise, which was the strategy's central mechanism.
- Event-day price reaction is indistinguishable from a random day: PFSI 1.26% vs 1.23% baseline (n=21), CACC 1.52% vs 1.34% (n=43). There is no reaction to front-run.
- The options are untradeable in 4 of 5 names. UWMC 100-120% of mid with $0.50 strikes on a $1.50 stock; PFSI's 10%-OTM put has a zero bid and OI of 3; CACC has no near-dated chain at all. Live CBOE quotes, not estimates.
- Universe attrition: COOP delisted 10/1/2025; OMF has zero "warehouse" 8-K documents in 5.6 years. Two of six names cannot participate.
- Bearish trigger language is essentially absent from EDGAR: "declined to renew" 11 docs and "elected not to renew" 43 docs across ALL filers in 5.6 years, none in mortgage finance.

HIGH CONFIDENCE (documented in issuers' own words, corroborated across multiple companies):
- The sign-inversion mechanism. loanDepot and Home Point both state in filings that capacity reductions were their own decisions to cut costs against lower volume. This is a structural feature of uncommitted, non-usage-fee-bearing lines, not a company-specific quirk.

MODERATE CONFIDENCE (small sample, correctly flagged as such):
- The +23.13% mean / +18.74% median 40-day drift after capacity cuts rests on n=8. I would not bet on the magnitude, and I am NOT recommending the reverse trade. But the direction is corroborated by the mechanism above and by the 2023-11-08 +116.77% case, and — decisively — the conclusion does not depend on it. If the true drift were exactly zero, the trade still loses 35-78% of premium to spread, theta and vol premium.

COULD NOT VERIFY, STATED PLAINLY: I did not obtain live borrow rates for UWMC/RKT/PFSI/CACC/OMF (chartexchange 404'd; no current Fintel quote retrieved). I have not invented one. This does not affect the verdict: sensitivity testing shows borrow moving from 0.5% to 10% changes short P&L only from -23.2% to -24.7%. I also did not fetch the full text of the Notre Dame 8-K attention paper and have attributed no specific result to it.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: evidence of a LENDER-initiated, credit-driven line pull (not a borrower cost cut) disclosed intraday, in a name with a liquid options chain, ahead of the trade press. I searched specifically for this pattern and found essentially zero instances in 5.6 years of EDGAR. The one live stress event in the universe — UWMC's 35% collapse on 2026-08-06 — arrived as a bundled post-close earnings/capital-raise 8-K with no warehouse precursor whatsoever, after two months of filing silence.

The analyst's prior skepticism transfers exactly: as with naive FTD spikes, the naive event trigger has no power, and the only surviving variant would be a chronic, slow-moving, already-public condition that is fully reflected in stocks already down 52-87%. Recommend not proceeding.

verdictSummary.strategy: IPR Truce Tape — monitor PTAB (P-TACTS / USPTO ODP API) for joint motions to terminate an inter partes review, infer a settlement/license, and go long the small-cap patent licensor (InterDigital / Netlist / VirnetX / ParkerVision class).
verdictSummary.confidence:
**HIGH that the verdict is LIKELY-ILLUSORY. Medium on the precise magnitudes.**

**Why high on the verdict** — the core argument rests on primary sources and live market data, not inference:
- The timing kill-shot is *structural*, derived from statute and SEC rules, not from a noisy backtest: §317(b) requires the settlement agreement be filed before termination, and Form 8-K Item 1.01 requires disclosure of a material definitive agreement within four business days. The docket cannot lead. Corroborated by a live case one week old (Netlist agreement 4 Aug 2026 → press release 5 Aug 2026 → +58.3% same day) and by every other verified example (IDCC/Amazon +15.0%, PRKR/Buffalo +17.27%, PRKR/Zyxel +6.56%) — all company-announced first.
- Event counts come straight from the USPTO FY2025 Outcome Roundup PDF, which I extracted and read directly (1,433 petitions; 368 settled; 190 pre- / 178 post-institution).
- Cost-stack numbers are **live quotes**, not estimates: the CBOE feed gave IDCC 8dte ATM at bid 7.20 / ask 11.40 (45.2% of mid, OI 20, vol 0), RMBS at 8.5% of mid with IV 73%, VHC stock at 5.30/5.99 (12.5%) with a six-contract chain.
- The decay precedent is published and quantified (UCLA Law Review, 21 IPR filings, decay to insignificance with sign flips inside months).
- The free-distribution point is verified directly from Unified Patents' own page describing UP Daily.

**Why only medium on magnitudes** — and these are the honest gaps:
- **No docket-level backtest was run.** I did not compile a history of PTAB terminations, match them to listed patent owners, and measure forward returns. That is the study that would convert "likely-illusory" to a proven zero. The USPTO ODP API returned "Missing Authentication Token" (403) and the legacy endpoint 301'd, so I could not pull the proceedings history in-session.
- **No measured distribution** of the settlement-execution → joint-motion → termination-order lag. The ordering is established; the day-counts are not.
- **No computed conditional probability** that a joint termination implies a cash-positive license to a listed owner. Bounded downward, not measured.
- **Could not verify current NLST borrow** (only a stale Jan-2023 6.69% figure) or **live NLST option quotes** (CBOE 403). Both are flagged as unverified rather than estimated.
- Some quote data is delayed/consolidated (the Yahoo IDCC quote came back crossed at bid 349.76 / ask 342.51, so I disregarded it and used the CBOE feed).

**Consistency with the analyst's FTD result:** this is the same failure mode, one level deeper. With FTDs, the naive spike signal was real-but-uninformative. Here the observable is even cleaner — a legally-compelled docket entry, essentially zero false positives on "did they settle" — and it *still* fails, because being a reliable indicator of an event is worthless when (a) the event was already disclosed, (b) you cannot see its sign or size, and (c) the only cases where you see it first are the cases selected for having no economic content. Clean data is not the same thing as early, directional, or exclusive data. I would not put this on the book, and I would not fund the pipeline to test it further without first running the free version of the check — pull the ODP termination history, join to a listed-issuer map, and count how many terminations preceded their 8-K. My strong prior is a single-digit count, and that those hits had no move.

verdictSummary.strategy: Proxy-Solicitor Fee Siren: screen merger proxies (PREM14A/DEFM14A) for an outsized disclosed proxy-solicitor fee or a dual-solicitor hire, read it as the board privately fearing the shareholder vote fails, and express via shorting the merger-arb spread (short the target) or buying target puts struck near the unaffected price.
verdictSummary.confidence:
MEDIUM-HIGH on the verdict; MEDIUM on the precision of individual numbers.

High confidence in the disqualifying facts, because I verified them directly against primary SEC filings rather than commentary: the STAAR PREM14A bracketed-blank fee and the one-day gap to Broadwood's PREC14A; the five-week gap between MMLP's public opposition and the fee disclosure; the 64% dual-solicitor base rate; the fee distribution (median $30k, p90 $60k); and the 37% rate of TBD/success-fee hedging language. Those are measurements, not inferences, and each independently breaks the strategy.

Genuine limitations I will not paper over:
- My fee distribution is a random sample of 70 of ~1,400 DEFM14A (2023-2025), not the full archive. Percentiles carry meaningful sampling error; the p90 of $60k could plausibly be $50-80k on a full census.
- My "hit rate" evidence is four high-fee deals. Two hits, two misses. That is an anecdote, not a base rate, and I state it as such. A proper test needs the full archive with hand-verified vote outcomes.
- I could NOT obtain live market data. Yahoo, stooq, and the IBKR feeds were all blocked from this environment. Every borrow rate, option bid-ask, and entry price in this assessment is a published-range estimate or my own construction, explicitly flagged. The STAAR and MMLP implied-probability figures use estimated entry prices.
- The ISS Analytics figure I saw in search results (96.4% of acquirer Rule 312.03 votes passed in 2024, 11 failing) I could not trace to primary source and did not rely on.

What would change my mind: a full-archive backtest showing that fee residuals — after regressing fee on shares outstanding, record-holder count, deal size, joint-proxy structure, and the presence of any DEFC14A/PREC14A/DFAN14A opposition filing — still predict vote failure, measured from the PREM14A date rather than the DEFM14A date. I doubt it survives, primarily because the PREM14A frequently leaves the number blank. Recommendation: do not put this on the book. If the analyst wants the underlying phenomenon, trade the DEFC14A form-type flag instead — it is free, earlier, unambiguous, and it is what the fee is a lagging proxy for. Scraper and parsed data retained at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-WireAntennaGain/82dc742b-08fa-562e-9653-7f5ab2131e39/scratchpad/scrape2.py and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-WireAntennaGain/82dc742b-08fa-562e-9653-7f5ab2131e39/scratchpad/fees2.json.

verdictSummary.strategy: Miner Curtailment Ledger: use public ERCOT/grid curtailment and heat-event data to predict weak monthly BTC production updates at RIOT, CIFR, MARA, WULF, and fade (short) into the first-business-day monthly print.
verdictSummary.confidence: HIGH on the verdict, with a stated limitation. High because the four load-bearing facts are verified from primary sources, not secondary commentary: (1) the discontinuation is confirmed by Riot's own statement that December 2025 was its last monthly update, cross-checked against EDGAR's submissions API showing only 4 RIOT 8-Ks in all of 2026 and no monthly production filings at MARA, CIFR or WULF either; (2) the pre-observability is confirmed by my own reconciliation of mempool.space's MARA Pool block history (212+235+253 = 700) against MARA's disclosed 700 blocks won — an exact match I computed rather than read; (3) the cost stack is live market data pulled at ~12:00 ET on 2026-08-13 (spreads 5.9-10.8 bp, borrow 0.27%/0.36%, ATM IV 73-102% with front-expiry to 143%, computed from actual bid/ask via a Black-Scholes solver), not vendor marketing or recalled figures; (4) the credits-offset sign problem is quantified from the companies' own releases ($31.7M Aug 2023; 511 BTC-equivalent vs 362 BTC mined Sept 2023; $21.0M Q1 2026; $10.0M / $6,335 per BTC Q2 2026). Where I am NOT confident, and say so plainly: I could not verify any historical event-study alpha for this trade, so I cannot quantify how much edge existed in 2022-2023 before the cadence broke down; and the frictions I cite are a single intraday snapshot — borrow in particular can spike from GC to hard-to-borrow during a squeeze in these historically high-short-interest names, which would make the trade worse, never better. Neither gap changes the verdict, because the event being traded no longer occurs. This is the same failure mode as the naive FTD-spike signal the analyst already rejected: a mechanically real, publicly observable phenomenon that is fully priced, freely available, disclosed alongside its own offset, and swamped by the dominant driver. The disciplined answer is to not put this on.

verdictSummary.strategy: Overnight Retail Fade — for names with overnight news, measure the overnight move against a peer-implied fair value and short/buy the "excess" at the 9:30 open, exiting intraday.
verdictSummary.confidence: HIGH that no exploitable net-of-cost edge exists for a small trader or small fund, for three converging reasons that do not depend on each other: the strategy conditions on the news subsample where the published evidence says continuation (Chan 2003, PEAD) rather than reversal; the execution is provably non-implementable at retail latency (Della Corte et al.'s one-minute decay, plus the signal/execution circularity); and the best published gross edge (35-40 bps breakeven, S&P 500, 1998-2015) is at or below a realistic retail round-trip cost at the open before tax. Real money has already tested the broader thesis and lost — NightShares closed in 14 months with NSPY at -6.9% against a +22% index — and the NY Fed documents the flagship overnight anomaly going to zero post-2021. MEDIUM on the specific basis-point figures. I could not retrieve several primary tables despite repeated attempts: the Berkman et al. decile-level overnight/intraday bps (Cambridge and CORE PDFs returned 403/abstract-only), the Della Corte execution-delay table at 9:30:01/9:31/9:35/9:45 (three PDF sources returned unparseable binary), the Lou-Polk-Skouras magnitudes (PDF unparseable), and the Federal Reserve FEDS 2024-080 and Wharton PFOF retail round-trip cost experiments (both PDFs unparseable). My 15-40 bps mid-cap / 50-150 bps small-cap opening spread figures are my own estimates, NOT citations — I found no study measuring the 9:30 quoted spread distribution for news-gapping names, and one search-summary claim I saw (S&P 500 spreads ">20 bps at the open falling to <5 bps in the last half hour") I could NOT verify against the SSGA source it was attributed to, so I have not relied on it. The gap-fill-by-size statistics (76% overall, 9.6% for gaps beyond ±5%) come from a retail blog and should be treated as directional only. These gaps affect the precision of the loss estimate, not the sign. Consistent with the analyst's FTD finding: the naive version of the pattern has no exploitable content, and what survives in the literature survives only under conditions — instantaneous auction execution, institutional cost structures, and the no-news subsample — that a retail implementation of this specific strategy explicitly violates.
